#3453. 30 Best Cartoon Network Shows From The 2000s, Ranked

Although Cartoon Network started becoming popular in the '90s, it was in the 2000s when its shows really took off. The network had some great cartoons that started in the 2000s, and many of these series carried over into the 2010s, proving that this was the best network on TV at the time for cartoons. Not only did the network have some great shows carrying into the decade, but it introduced some seriously memorable cartoons in the 2000s as well, giving Cartoon Network an entire decade of animated dominance.

Alongside the launch of Adult Swim in 2001 — the network's spinoff block of programs aimed at adults — Cartoon Network's regular programming simultaneously pushed the boundaries of animation for children. Today's more limited lineup presents a totally different landscape for the network, and so many continue to look back to the best Cartoon Network shows from the 2000s for next-level content and a hit of nostalgia from what was considered the Golden Age of Cartoon Network.

With several spin-offs and a revival, it's not too far-fetched to say that Total Drama continues to be one of the best Cartoon Network shows from the 2000s. The Survivor-like animated series is essentially a satirical depiction of reality TV, with each season revolving around a group of teenagers who join a competition and try to avoid elimination. It's certainly a show with more mature themes, as the competitors (much like on regular reality TV shows) develop relationships, fight, and backstab each other to stay in the game.

Total Drama was created by Jennifer Pertsch and Tom McGillis, premiering initially in Canada before moving over the US Cartoon Network channel a year later in 2008. While it takes most of its inspiration from Survivor when it comes to its satire, it parodies many conventions found across the wider genre of reality TV — and the results are hilarious.

Mexican wrestling is one of the country's most famous cultural exports, present in everything from WWE, thanks to wrestlers like Rey Mysterio, to Hollywood with movies like Nacho Libre. In 2002, Cartoon Network did its own spin on the sport with the animated show Mucha Lucha, which was also the first ever series created with Macromedia Flash. It's set in the town of Luchaville, where almost every resident wears a Lucha Libre costume and has a signature move.

Not only is Mucha Lucha among the best wrestling TV shows, but it's also the first Western animated series focused on pro wrestling. Mucha Lucha stars Rikochet, Buena Girl, The Flea, and El Rey — students at the Foremost World-Renowned International School of Lucha. Though not as well-remembered as many of the other best Cartoon Network shows from the 2000s, Mucha Lucha's over-the-top depiction of the Mexican art of Lucha Libre makes it a must-see.

The 2000s were an interesting time for animated kids' shows, as the genre was moving away from some of the risqué humor of '90s offerings like Ren & Stimpy and into safer territory. This is what makes Chowder, released in 2007, feel like such an oddity. Chowder isn't about the popular soup, but it does involve an aspiring young cook named Chowder. Chowder is an interesting character that's a mix between a cat, bear, and rabbit. Despite wanting to be a chef, he gets involved in comical scenarios due to his impulse control issues.

He often eats customers' meals due to being always hungry — but that's not all. Chowder can also regurgitate items, and his stomach is basically its own storage unit. Considering Chowder's sexist jokes and oftentimes inappropriate material, there are some parts that haven't aged well, and it's more of an adult cartoon than one that's aimed at children.

Dorothy, Horace, and the other colorful residents of Soap City serve as supporting characters to the conflicts between the nerdy and nature-loving Lucien and the aggressive and blue-skinned scrap rat Wayne. While The Cramp Twins is one of many forgotten Cartoon Network shows from the era, that doesn't stop it from ranking among the best 2000s Cartoon Network shows. It has all the hallmarks that made the network's original content so popular during the decade, and almost every episode hits the mark when it comes to including laugh-out-loud humor.

From the lovable Otto Osworth to the excitable Larry 3000, the titular Time Squad is tasked with maintaining the flow of time and ensuring that the future remains a flawless utopia. Undoubtedly one of the best Cartoon Network shows from the 2000s, Time Squad served almost like an after-school history class in the best ways possible, as the team of travelers meet figures like Abraham Lincoln and Sigmund Freud on their adventures.

The squad had to correct history's course by guiding these significant people down the right paths. Notably, while the comic book debut of Marvel's Kang the Conqueror far predates Time Squad, the cartoon aired over two decades before the Time Variant Authority debuted in Loki. Time Squad portrayed a far more lighthearted take on the idea of guardians of history, however, and while it's not as popular as some other Cartoon Network shows from the 2000s, it is certainly among the most imaginative.

Xiaolin Showdown was a 2000s Cartoon Network show that capitalized on the popularity of anime thanks to series like DragonBall Z, Sailor Moon, and Pokémon. In a world where martial arts and magic have become the norm, it's up to a group of Xiaolin warriors to make sure that evil forces don't steal the mystical artifacts known as the Shen Gon Wu, which can change everything in a good or terrible way, depending on who wields them.

One of the best Cartoon Network shows from the 2000s, Xiaolin Showdown shows the struggles of brave characters like Omi and Kimiko Tohomiko as they travel the world to look for powerful artifacts and take on formidable enemies along the way. The series also raises some surprisingly mature questions about morality, with some of its heroes being tempted to use the artifacts for their own benefit.

With original series creator Craig McCracken already working on the Foster's Home for Imaginary Friends reboot, there's no better time to rewatch what many consider one of the best 2000s Cartoon Network shows. Foster's Home represents the onset of truly surreal storytelling in Cartoon Network's regular programming. In this world where imaginary friends are physically real and coexist with humans, a young boy named Mac is pressured by his mother to abandon his imaginary friend, Bloo.

They soon discover a foster home for abandoned imaginary friends. As long as Mac visits Bloo there, he is safe from adoption, a heartwarming premise that gives way to hilarious narratives. Foster's Home for Imaginary Friends was also notable not just for its hilarity and incredibly unique animation style (even by Cartoon Network's standards), but also because it had more tear-jerking and genuinely emotional moments than any other show on the network.

Few Cartoon Network shows from the 2000s, or any other decade for that matter, feature a trio of characters as memorable as Billy, Mandy, and Grim. Echoing Ingmar Bergman's The Seventh Seal, Grim, the personification of death, loses a limbo match against the dim-witted and cheerful Billy and his ego-driven and cynical best friend Mandy, forcing the Grim Reaper to be under the servitude of these children.

As would be expected from the premise, the scenarios and characters in The Grim Adventures of Billy and Mandy are incredibly horror-flavored, though the show isn't scary, instead portraying some dark concepts in an incredibly upbeat light. Unsurprisingly, many consider The Grim Adventures of Billy and Mandy to be foremost among the classic Cartoon Network shows that deserve movie adaptations. Curiously, viewers may not have realized Grim's constant desire to kill the two children at the beginning of the show.

While the majority of Cartoon Network shows in the 2000s featured original characters, the network was also host to many licensed properties with recognizable names and faces. Starring Looney Tunes characters in an even stranger setting, Duck Dodgers is a sci-fi adaptation of a short 1953 theatrical cartoon of the same name.

Featuring Daffy Duck as the eponymous protagonist, the show starts off with a humorous origin story, as Duck Dodgers finds himself in the far future after being accidentally frozen for over three centuries. He meets iconic characters in space like K'chutha Sa'am (Yosemite Sam), Witch Hazel (Leezah the Wicked), and Wile E. Coyote (a parody of the alien from Predator). The myriad references to franchises like Star Trek and even Bond films make the short-lived series even better to watch as an adult today.

No list of the best Cartoon Network shows from the 2000s would be complete without Codename: Kids Next Door. Like many original Cartoon Network programs, Codename: Kids Next Door took an established concept and put a spin on it that was beyond unique. In this case, it was spy movies and secret agents. Five kids — Numbuh 1 to Numbuh 5 — are trained by the organization known as Kids Next Door, undergoing oaths to protect children and battle adulthood.

These kids are in charge of Sector V, where their main base of operations is a high-tech tree house that's ridiculously much bigger from the inside. While the oathbound agents of Kids Next Door are typically decommissioned at the age of 13, it was later revealed that the most competent agents get recruited into Teens Next Door to spy on evil teens.

#3452. 25 Years Later, Dumbledore's Best Sorcerer's Stone Line Is Still The Greatest Harry Potter Quote

In the wizarding world of Harry Potter, Albus Dumbledore is often referred to as one of the wisest and most powerful wizards in history ... so, it's lucky for the titular boy wizard that Dumbledore just happens to be the headmaster of his magical academy. In the original Harry Potter film franchise (which is getting a new life, in a way, with the forthcoming HBO Harry Potter TV show), Harry Potter, as played by Daniel Radcliffe (who may not watch the HBO reboot series), leaves his humdrum life with his mean non-magical relatives behind and starts attending Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry, run by Dumbledore (Richard Harris in the first two movies before the legendary actor passed away in 2002, at which point Michael Gambon took over). There, he meets his best friends Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger (Rupert Grint and Emma Watson), learns how to cast magic spells, and has his first encounter, so to speak, with the Dark Lord Voldemort who tried to kill him as a baby.

Let's all be honest: Dumbledore sort of gets all the best quotes in the Harry Potter franchise. After all, his entire purpose is to dispense wisdom, so he drops a lot of stone-cold bangers. But what's his most memorable quote from the first movie, "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone" (which hit theaters on November 16, 2001)? We think we've pinpointed the perfect Dumbledore line from this film 25 years after its release.

During his first Christmas at Hogwarts, Harry receives the Cloak of Invisibility from an anonymous friend who leaves him a note telling Harry it belonged to his late father James. Emboldened by this gift, Harry starts exploring the halls of Hogwarts by night, and one evening, he stumbles upon a room containing a mirror that shows him not only James but his late mother, Lily, and even the extended family he never got a chance to meet. Understandably, the orphaned Harry becomes obsessed with visiting the mirror every night, and despite his confusion when Ron sees something completely different in said mirror, he returns until he finds Dumbledore waiting in the mirror's little room.

Dumbledore explains that it's called the Mirror of Erised, and it shows you your deepest desire. That's why Harry sees the family he never knew, and it's also why Dumbledore tells Harry, "It does not do to dwell on dreams, Harry, and forget to live." Dumbledore is right: Harry's devotion to seeing his family every night in the mirror is a short-term comfort that's terrible for the child's overall mental health, and even though Dumbledore tells him the mirror is moving to a different location anyway, Harry does promise not to look for it again.

Not only that, but in the third act of "Sorcerer's Stone" (as Harry looks for the titular object), we learn that the mirror is part of the defense system that keeps the Stone safe when Harry stares into it and receives the stone not to use but to have. In this way, Harry isn't dwelling on dreams, he's utilizing the mirror to achieve a vital goal.

Spoilers for Season 2, Episode 6 of Marshals are ahead! You can stream the series with a Paramount+ subscription and catch new episodes on CBS every Sunday.

The episode of Marshals that just aired on the 2026 TV schedule is inspired by a tragedy that actually happened to one of its stars and American Indian Affairs Coordinator, Mo Brings Plenty, and his family. In 2024, his nephew, Cole Brings Plenty, died, and a coroner ruled out foul play. His family disagreed with that, and they’re still looking for answers. In this week's episode of Marshals, Mo’s nephew, Troy, is found dead, and he and Kayce work to prove that it was a murder, not suicide. Ultimately, the case is left unsolved, and according to Mo Brings Plenty, that was a very important detail to include.

Knowing that “Roughstock” was inspired by his own experiences, I asked Mo Brings Plenty, who plays Mo in Marshals and Yellowstone, about details in the episode he was happy to see included. He immediately noted that he was glad the case was left unsolved, because that kind of outcome happens in real life, often, as the actor explained:

Oh, I was happy to see that when the police officer said he just kind of blew it off, because that's really the case. And so I was happy that we showed that legitimate part of it. Not every officer is that way, but in some cases, in some states - primarily states that have a high American Indian population - that occurs.

When I spoke to Mo in March this year about an episode of Marshals having to do with missing American Indians, he told me they “haven’t got any answers for” what happened to his nephew, Cole.

In this episode of Marshals, it’s made very clear that while Troy’s case will stay open, it will likely go unsolved. It’s obvious that it’s not being prioritized by law enforcement, and despite the marshals best efforts, there is no solution as to who killed Troy by the end of the episode. When I asked Mo why it was important for this episode to go without a solution to Troy’s case, he said:

Because the wheel of justice doesn't turn for us as American Indian people, and of course we're tax-paying people as well. And so, you know, first responders get their funding through taxpayers, tax funding, and so when it doesn't work for us, then it's so frustrating. It's like, ‘Well, why are we even paying taxes?’ And so that's one of the things that is impactful for me, and that I need to continue to speak about because it is occurring.

In the case of Mo’s real nephew, Cole, he was found dead a few days after he was reported missing and named as a suspect in a domestic violence case. Two years later, Mo spoke to THR and claimed that his nephew’s death had gone “uninvestigated,” while the Lawrence Police Department said there was “no foul play involved in Cole’s death.”

When I spoke to Mo about this topic recently and how it was represented on this Yellowstone show, he said:

It's sad for me and my family, especially when I hear the cry for other nationalities and in foreign countries, when the very same thing is occurring to us as the original inhabitants within this country, we're basically flying over mission fields to get to mission fields.

According to the U.S. Department of the Interior Indian Affairs, there are “approximately 4,200 missing and murder cases that have gone unsolved.” And when I asked Mo Brings Plenty if Marshals could ever circle back to Troy’s unsolved case, he said:

Absolutely, it could definitely happen. But you know, there are so many stories. I mean, my family is not the only family. This isn't the first time something like this has occurred in real life. You know, there are many stories, many families, different situations, different circumstances that are going through the same thing.

Overall, he was clear that there are lots of stories like his that should be shown on Kayce’s Yellowstone spinoff. He’s not the only one who has lost a loved one in this way and was left without answers, and he’s hoping to see more of those stories depicted on Marshals.

Now, to see how Mo’s story continues, you can watch the next episode of Marshals on November 22 at 8:30 p.m. ET, and you can stream it the next day on Paramount+.

#3450. How To Rob A Bank Pays Tribute To A Bruce Willis Movie With A Clever Easter Egg

There's something of a paradox when it comes to making legitimately good crime action movies. On the one hand, most filmmakers want the action to be as accurate and based in reality as possible, whether it be robbing a bank, taking down a security truck, or whatnot. On the other hand, they don't necessarily wish to inspire criminals who would copycat a crime they happened to see in a movie, especially as that's an instance where all publicity doesn't necessarily equal good publicity. (Remember the brouhaha over a crime allegedly inspired by 1995's "Money Train," a case which only just reached a resolution a few years ago?)

The irony of the new crime action film "How to Rob a Bank" is that it intentionally wishes to exist on the edge separating these two sides. The film, written by Mark Bianculli and directed by David Leitch, concerns a group of friends who, upon becoming radicalized by the various injustices of the current U.S. wealth gap, decide to become bank robbers. Their gimmick is hiding their crimes in plain sight, filming themselves in the act and detailing exactly how they did it for their YouTube channel (all while hiding their identities, naturally).

Thus, Leitch and Bianculli have to include a bunch of real-world tactics and hardware without going too far. To help accomplish this, they have their bandits (who've dubbed themselves the Wolf Pack) borrow a technique from the sequel to the bonafide action classic that is "Die Hard," i.e. 1990's "Die Hard 2." And while the characters never mention the movie on-screen, the inclusion of a trick used by that film's villains works as both an Easter egg homage to that movie as well as a bit of real-world verisimilitude, as this particular tactic does sound like it could actually work.

In "Die Hard 2," the terrorists holding Washington Dulles International Airport hostage around Christmas are former U.S. Army soldiers who've been corrupted by a military drug lord. After Bruce Willis' John McClane their plans while getting a quip or two in, the airport brass call in a military counter-terrorism unit. Then, during the subsequent firefights between the counter-terrorism unit and the terrorists, each group makes a point of switching to clips for their machine guns labeled with blue instead of red stripes. Eventually, McClane discovers this code means blue for blank rounds and red for live rounds, revealing that both units are working together.

While the terrorists in "Die Hard 2" have devised a fairly elaborate scheme, the blank-vs-live rounds element seems fairly simple and self-explanatory. In other words, it has an authenticity about it, which is why its use in "How to Rob a Bank" feels smooth rather than belabored. The Wolf Pack want to make their robberies feel threatening to the authorities they encounter and only elect to use live rounds to save their own skins. As such, adopting the blue and red labeled gun clips makes for an easy to understand visual code, so much so that the characters in the film barely have to explain it to the audience.

For those who know "Die Hard 2," this is a cute Easter egg calling back to that film's intuitive code system. Yet, for those who don't know, the element still completely works, and its realism adds to the movie's credibility. Who knows if anyone has used it (or will) in real life, but it helps "How to Rob a Bank" exist on that edge.

#3449. ChatGPT's New GIF Generator Is Fun, but Won't Replace Us Humans (Yet)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

When it comes to generating AI images, both Gemini and ChatGPT do a passable job. In most cases, the results will look AI-generated, but they likely won’t have glaring spelling issues or missing limbs. Now, OpenAI is trying something new, introducing GIF support for ChatGPT. It's the company's first "moving images" feature since OpenAI shut down Sora, and while you can generate hyper-realistic videos in Gemini, this new ChatGPT feature is trying to fill in the gap, in a small way.

OpenAI is pitching the new feature as an animation tool, not exactly as a way to create looping videos—though that’s how I ended up using it. You give ChatGPT a prompt, as detailed as you can make it, and the chatbot produces a GIF in just a few seconds. You can start with your own drawings or images, too. ChatGPT uses sketches as the base for animations, though it can turn any still image into animated GIFs. Like other AI editing tools, you can edit it if ChatGPT didn't quite get it right: You can ask ChatGPT to make the GIF longer or shorter, remove certain objects, change the style, slow down transitions, among other edits.

AI art can be quite sterile, but I was surprised by how adding motion and animation to the mix makes generating images a lot more fun. Unlike traditional GIFs, which usually pull from existing video clips, you can turn anything you want into a GIF, which is especially cool if you're using your own art. In my testing, I found this to be the most rewarding part. It’s not always possible to one-shot a GIF with a single prompt. But after a few rounds of edits, I ended up creating some GIFs that I actually wanted to share in my WhatsApp groups.

That being said, I think human-made GIFs are still the gold standard here. For example, I asked ChatGPT to generate a video of someone brewing a pour-over, with a gooseneck kettle, showing the coffee blooming process. It did okay, but it’s nothing like actually making a pour-over. The kettle doesn’t move in circles, the water doesn’t rise evenly, there are no bubbles, and the steam is all over the place.

Compare that to the GIF below, which comes from a royalty-free video. Even though it’s a compressed, low-quality, and noisy GIF, it still shows the movement of the pour, the water rising, and even the bubbles. The details captured by a real video just aren’t there in ChatGPT GIFs. If that’s what you’re expecting, you will be disappointed. But I don't think that's the point of this feature anyway.

I found that ChatGPT excels when you’re making something fun, and you don’t look into the details too much. It pulled off a loop of a cat playing with a ball, and it was great at making a festive GIF for Diwali. It even made a GIF based on a photo. I asked it to create a fun promotional GIF for my JBL Bluetooth speakers, and it did the job quite well. At first, the transitions were too jarring, and the movement just made no sense. After some editing, though, I got it to a decent place.

Still, the main issue with ChatGPT GIFs is that complex movement and transitions aren’t nailed down. A hand shifts position weirdly between frames, and colors and objects appear out of nowhere. But if you can get over these issues, you can make some fun, lighthearted GIFs and memes to share with your friends on Instagram or WhatsApp.

#3448. Patrick Stewart Had A Small But Important Role In One Of The Best Animated Movies Of The '90s

It feels impossible to do justice to the late Sir Patrick Stewart with mere words, but we can attempt it. One part of his incredible legacy is voice acting; how could he not try his hand there when he had such a magnificent voice? Stewart's defining voice role is probably the eccentric CIA Deputy Director Avery Bullock on "American Dad." Casting him against type there is the whole joke. Patrick Stewart, famous for playing dignified, fatherly authority figures like Captain Jean-Luc Picard and Professor Charles Xavier, is the one saying all of Bullock's ridiculous, profane, and unhinged lines, which become even funnier read in his baritone voice.

The folks behind the biblical epic "The Prince of Egypt" also knew the weight Stewart's voice carried. At Steven Spielberg's suggestion, DreamWorks Animation adapted the first stretch of the Book of Exodus, or how the prophet Moses (Val Kilmer) — raised as an Egyptian prince — discovered his true heritage and led his people out of bondage. Patrick Stewart plays Pharaoh Seti, adoptive father of Moses and the man who ordered the massacre of Hebrew babies that made Moses' mother send him away. Stewart/Seti has only a few scant scenes in the movie's first act, but he casts a shadow as wide as any pyramid over the rest of the film.

As with later DreamWorks pictures, "The Prince of Egypt" employs celebrity voice casting: Kilmer as Moses, Ralph Fiennes as Moses' brother/Seti's son Pharaoh Rameses, etc. But here, it mostly works — mostly. Jeff Goldblum as Moses' brother Aaron is a distracting bit of casting where you hear the actor first, not the character. "Prince of Egypt" doesn't disguise Stewart's voice either (you probably couldn't with a voice of such power), but it complements his character to a chilling effect.

In "The Prince of Egypt," Seti first appears admonishing his two sons for being reckless in a chariot race. He's especially harsh on his heir, Rameses, explaining that "one weak link can break the chain of a mighty dynasty." When Moses asks his father to go easier on Rameses, Seti offers understanding (and pure dramatic irony): "Moses, you will never have to carry a burden like the crown I will pass to Rameses."

Pretty typical Patrick Stewart, right? Seti is stern but reasonable, some of the same qualities that made Captain Picard such a respected leader. His respect-commanding voice is even more effective as a disappointed father, too; would you want to hear "I'm disappointed in you" from that voice?

But then Moses learns the truth about where he came from, and how. Seeing his son in despair, Seti is gentle but also doesn't deny he had a generation of Hebrew babies murdered as population control. The animation and Stewart's performance work in perfect sync. In Seti's whispered tone, he sounds genuinely pained. Even if his claim "sometimes, for the greater good, sacrifices must be made," rings hollow here, Seti's thousand yard stare tells us that maybe he does feel the weight of what he did and realizes he's damned for it.

But then the kicker comes: He tries to "comfort" Moses that the babies cast into the Nile "were only slaves." The dissonance of Seti loving his own family and also being a genocidal enslaver is potent, but sadly believable. Fittingly, this is also the last time we see him in the film, because the bond he shared with Moses has been severed.

"The Prince of Egypt" is one of the most gorgeously animated films ever made, and it's not only the animation that's beautifully crafted. The storytelling is sharp and mature. It sits at the very fine line of being simple enough for kids and complex enough for adults; Moses and Rameses being turned from beloved brothers to enemies by forces much bigger than themselves is painful to watch.

Right off, "The Prince of Egypt" is an unconventional title for the Exodus story; after all, the whole story is about Moses rejecting that life for his people by birth. (Compare it to the 1956 biblical epic titled "The Ten Commandments.") But the movie paints Moses' deliverance of his people as bittersweet, since it cost him the brother he loved.

Though not nearly as controversial as Nikos Kazantzakis's book (and later Martin Scorsese's film) "The Last Temptation of Christ," "The Prince of Egypt" similarly invents human drama from scripture. "Last Temptation" works from the tenet that Jesus was both fully divine but also fully human. So, then, wouldn't he be afflicted by man's foibles and doubts? The Book of Exodus holds that Moses was raised as an Egyptian in the Pharaoh's own family. Wouldn't Moses, then, feel pained about having to turn his back on the home where he was raised, even if he recognized the necessity of God's plan for him?

Part of the tragedy is that this only flows one way. After Moses learns the truth, he can't look at the enslaved Hebrew workers without thinking their birthright is also his. Conversely, neither Seti nor Rameses clock that the son/brother they love would've been just another of those slaves. It's an excellent use of Patrick Stewart, twisting our relationship to his fatherly presence and providing an undercurrent of darkness to it.

#3446. I Ain't Got No Body: The Various Non-Corporeal Aliens In Star Trek Explained

Welcome to Trekspertise, a series where we break down the technology, history, details, and decisions that make the Star Trek universe so complex — and so fun.

One of the primary features of "Star Trek" is theoretical biology. Given the wide panoply of alien species on display throughout the franchise, audiences have been invited to ponder alternate evolutionary paths besides the one that happened to bring us into being on Earth. What kind of planetary conditions would be required to form, say, a hyper-intelligent crystalline being? How did a horta evolve? What will we evolve into in the future? Will our brains adapt to become psychic over time? According to the "Star Trek: Voyager" episode "Threshold" (one of the show's most outraging to fans), it was revealed that humans will eventually evolve into giant salamanders.

This leads to a few logical evolutionary extremes, like the fact that some species on "Star Trek" have evolved into beings of pure energy. "Star Trek" has many examples of non-corporeal aliens who can only be perceived as light, as a psychic presence, as a sound, or as a vision beamed directly into our inferior, corporeal brains. To cite a notable example: In the original series episode "Is There In Truth No Beauty?," audiences were introduced to the Medusans, a highly intelligent, telepathic, and empathic species whose light-constructed bodies are so wildly complex that any human looking at them would instantly go mad. Only a mentally disciplined species like the Vulcans could look at a Medusan, and even then required a special filtered visor (pictured above).

These kinds of aliens expand the audience's mind as to what can be considered life.

In looking at fictional non-corporeal species, "Star Trek" expands our horizons. We're invited to ponder new perspectives about basic concepts like evolution, time, the nature of consciousness, and, perhaps, our own relationship to the cosmos. Non-corporeal entities are one of the coolest ideas "Star Trek" has to offer, and their recurring nature is a constant reminder that life is more complex, and the cosmos more ineffable, than we could ever hope to imagine.

On "Star Trek," non-corporeal aliens tend to appear as lights or clouds or glowing mists of energy. One might recall the smoke-like alien that made Kirk nervous in the episode "Obsession," one of the more underrated episodes of the show. Others might immediately think of Zefram Cochrane's glowing, cloud-like "companion" in the episode "Metamorphosis." That entity had the ability to sort of intuitively communicate with Cochrane (Glenn Corbett), and could also heal diseases and sustain human life beyond its usual biological barriers. A common theme of non-corporeal entities on "Star Trek" is that they are godlike and powerful, able to tap into the powers of the universe in ways we don't understand.

The Medusans may be one of the most popular non-corporeal entities on "Star Trek," but fans of "Deep Space Nine" would surely want me to acknowledge the wormhole aliens, a.k.a. The Prophets. In that show's pilot episode, "Emissary," Benjamin Sisko (Avery Brooks) travels into a stable wormhole and encounters bodiless creatures who can only communicate with him by appearing as people from his memories.

The wormhole aliens from "Deep Space Nine" are so, well, alien, they don't understand concepts like linguistic communication or linear time. They don't see cause leading to effect, but rather a widespread series of events that happen all at once. Sisko has to do the impossible, and explain the human habit of seeing time as a straight line.

And, of course, there are many species of godlike beings on "Star Trek" who often take the form of humans, despite not having physical bodies. Q (John de Lancie) from "Star Trek: The Next Generation" is one of these beings, as is Trelane (William Campbell) from the original series. Those two beings tend to see corporeal humans as lesser species and amuse themselves by taunting and playing with them. Less whimsical is Kevin Uxbridge (John Anderson), a member of a powerful energy species called the Douwd. Kevin took the form of a human, married, and witnessed his wife killed, leading him to, in a moment of ill-temper, commit instant galaxy-wide genocide of a single species. He's the deadliest character in all of "Star Trek."

The list goes on. Q tormented the Calamarain, which exist as ionized gas. There are the Organians, the Lights of Zetar, and the godlike Metrons, the latter of whom oversaw the fight between Kirk (William Shatner) and the Gorn in the episode "Arena," and plenty of other examples. In most cases, non-corporeal entities are so far beyond human experience, it's difficult to communicate with them, much less come to some kind of diplomatic understanding.

But sometimes non-corporeal entities do become our friends. On "Star Trek: Prodigy," the character of Zero (Angus Imrie) is a Medusan who managed to construct a robot-like vehicle for themselves, allowing them to interact with us flesh-beings without exposing themselves. Sometimes the ineffability of the cosmos works in our favor.

#3445. 10 Shows Like 'Cyberpunk: Edgerunners' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the dramatic conclusion of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners way back in 2022, the show has returned for a new season set in the megalopolis of Night City with a standalone story and a new cast of characters (by necessity).

Though the aesthetic and themes of cyberpunk have their roots in American science fiction of the 1970s and '80s, anime and manga of the '90s and beyond embraced the form and took it to entirely new places—so much so that a Japanese/Polish co-production of an adaptation of a video game from a Polish designer has taken its cues from a couple of decades' worth of great anime and cerebral sci-fi. Which is to say, if you're looking for more heady sci-fi series, these 10 are a good place to start.

An iconic, effortlessly cool genre classic, Cowboy Bebop is one of the undisputed GOATs of anime, blending western, noir, and crime genres and setting the resultant mash to a killer soundtrack of old-school jazz (which serves much the same purpose as Cyberpunk's propulsive electronic grooves). The title's "cowboys" are bounty hunters in a near-future in which humans have been forced to colonize the solar system after Earth became uninhabitable. Different settings, but both shows offer up ragtag crews with highly dubious fates. Former hitman Spike Spiegel leads his crew on one nearly disastrous mission after another, their standalone adventures all building to a thoroughly memorable climax. Stream Cowboy Bebop on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

This one's set in 22nd-century Japan, with a slick Blade Runner-esque aesthetic and a setup reminiscent of Minority Report. Here, technology exists to measure intentions, so crimes can be stopped before they’ve occurred, at which point the “criminals” are placed into psychological treatment (à la A Clockwork Orange)—or subject to summary execution because their threat potential is too high. That ability to predict behavior bleeds over into every aspect of life: careers and even relationships are determined in large part by the same systems that sniff out criminal intent. Obviously, this is all perfectly fine, and there’s no potential for abuse or miscalculation whatsoever...though there are a couple of warning signs. The first involves a new Enforcer who becomes a potential murderer himself when he miscalculates the extent of a criminal’s potential to do wrong, and, even more significantly, the existence of a criminal mastermind who is somehow invisible to the tech, even as his criminal actions grow more and more elaborate. Stream Psycho-Pass on Prime Video and Crunchyroll.

Created by Tim Miller and with director David Fincher as an executive producer, this animated anthology series is a grab bag of wildly diverse offerings: Each episode is produced by a different international studio, with the only link between them being one of the three words in the show's title. One episode deals with robotic gladiator fights in dystopian London, another finds us under the threat of sentient yogurt, yet another finds an ambitious cat learning to make use of a family's robot helper. Its format dictates that no two episodes are going to have the same premise, but it shares with Cyberpunk an edgy sensibility and stories set in an apocalyptic future, albeit with a dark sense of humor—its four seasons offer up a mix of tech, sex, violence, and gorgeous animation. Stream Love, Death & Robots on Netflix.

One of several completely standalone spinoffs of the wildly influential 1995 film (itself based on the beloved manga series), Stand Alone Complex requires no prior knowledge. The style is largely the draw, as the series luxuriates in its fictional Nihama City setting, a world unto itself in a future Japan in which cybernetic people hack directly into the internet. Our sympathies are more with the authorities—in this case, Public Security Section 9, a cybercrime and antiterrorism police unit—than the cyber criminals, but the show approaches some of the same themes as Edgerunners with legit punk style. Stream Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex on Tubi and The Criterion Channel.

In this adaptation of the Richard K. Morgan cyberpunk classic of the same name, Joel Kinnaman and Anthony Mackie (yes, both of them) star as Takeshi "Tak" Kovacs. In this future megacity setting, human consciousness can be transferred between bodies. The tech is widely available, but only the wealthy can afford the backups and protections that make it a form of virtual immortality. Kovacs is a former soldier turned mercenary, revived from a backup after 200 years by Laurens Bancroft (James Purefoy), one of the wealthiest men alive. His motives for bringing the man back are shrouded in mystery, but he's giving Tak a chance to solve a very cold case: his own murder. Stream Altered Carbon on Netflix.

Another popular (and Emmy-winning) game adaptation, Arcane is based on League of Legends, a top-down actioner involving online opponents shooting lasers across a map. It doesn't sound like fodder for a show this impressive, but here we are. The League of Legends lore forms the backdrop for the show, but the pull is in the narrative involving two sisters caught up in the growing conflict between a utopian city and its oppressed underclass, without whom it couldn’t exist. The painted animation style is truly something special—not a stylistic match for Cyberpunk, but the two shows both go far above and beyond to create striking visual worlds. Stream Arcane on Netflix.

Vash the Stampede is a hunted outcast with a dark history that slowly comes to light over the course of the series. He’s got a reputation as a human wrecking ball, bringing destruction wherever he goes, and seemingly just for fun—but in reality he’s far more respectful of life than his pursuers. Still, cities evacuate at the mere possibility of his arrival, and a huge bounty sits on his head (no matter that the bounty hunters do far more damage than Vash). He and his friends—actually a couple of insurance agents—find themselves in a series of misadventures on the planet Gunsmoke, building to a final showdown that caps the series with finality. Visually, it’s probably one of the defining ‘90s shōnen-style action series, with elegantly choreographed gunfights that never get old. Tonally similar, Trigun also shares with Cyberpunk 2 the work of legendary composer Tsuneo Imahori, his music being crucial to both shows. Stream Trigun on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Another from animation studio Trigger, Darling in the Franxx leans heavily into the mecha sub-genre, set in a post-apocalypse where children are bred and indoctrinated into piloting the title's massive Franxx to defend the remnants of humanity. Adults are pretty much immortal, so the kids simply don't have any other utility. Two of these teens begin to develop romantic feelings for each other, potentially complicating their usefulness to society and leading to an explosive, bittersweet finale. Stream Darling in the Franxx on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

What starts out as a relatively straightforward action show about space bounty hunters (the title's “Killjoys”) develops surprising depth over the course of its five seasons. As officially sanctioned Killjoys, the trio at the show’s heart (Hannah John-Kamen, Aaron Ashmore, and Luke Macfarlane) are bound to remain politically neutral at any cost. Initially, that’s a way to get them right into the heat of a fight, but as they develop ties of friendship and family in an exploited community, they come to understand the high cost of unchecked wealth and greed, and the ways in which neutrality always benefits the oppressors. The show’s creators make exceptionally good use of a limited budget and offer up some impressive queer rep along the way, a rarity in pop sci-fi. Stream Killjoys on Tubi or buy it from Prime Video and Apple TV.

Another great cyberpunk metropolis: here it's Kansai, an increasingly lawless city run by elite criminals known as Akudama. An ordinary girl, quite inadvertently, becomes caught up in a major planned heist and is forced to fake credentials as a master swindler in order to stay alive. Like Cyberpunk, the show tackles anti-authoritarian themes among a diverse crew of outsiders. Stream Akudama Drive on Cunrchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

#3444. 6 Upcoming Sci-Fi Movies, Ranked by Hype

The next wave of sci-fi TV is looking out of this world

Science fiction has always been one of the most exhilarating genres to experience on the big screen, and today we’re entering another massive era for theatrical spectacle. Studios like Warner Bros., Disney, and Legendary have given filmmakers, VFX artists, and visionary directors the canvas to explore everything from humanity's distant future to planets in galaxies far, far away. Fortunately, the next few years of sci-fi cinema look just as — if not more — promising.

As studios double down on high-stakes bets, pouring absurd budgets into sprawling worlds and complex narratives like Dune: Part Three and Avengers: Doomsday, speculative fiction remains Hollywood’s ultimate proving ground for event-sized storytelling. To see what’s most exciting on the near horizon, here are the biggest upcoming sci-fi movies ranked by hype.

It’s always a gamble betting on a mid-budget sci-fi concept in a release calendar dominated by legacy IP, even with Keanu Reeves at the center of it. Directed by Deadpool’s Tim Miller, Shiver has been pitched as Edge of Tomorrow meets The Shallows. Reeves plays an as-yet unnamed smuggler who gets trapped in a deadly time loop in the middle of the shark-infested Caribbean Sea after a job goes sideways.

Even in the age of original sci-fi spectacles like Everything Everywhere All at Once and Severance, the lack of any built-in franchise awareness or even a massive marketing blitz behind it makes Shiver sit outside almost everyone’s hype level at the moment, especially in the face of such massive juggernauts on the horizon. Still, watching Miller pair R-rated action choreography with a high-concept time-loop premise in the same vein as Looper, all while letting Reeves carry the story, makes Shiver one of the more fascinating wildcards on the slate, especially if you’re a John Wick fan.

At this point, Legendary's MonsterVerse has settled comfortably into its wild identity, built primarily on ridiculous kaiju matchups. Following the events of Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire, the next installment looks ready to take things past the stratosphere, both literally and figuratively. Director Grant Sputore, who takes over for Adam Wingard this go-around, is gearing up to steer the franchise into cosmic territory. Even with the limited amount of story details, it’s clear SpaceGodzilla will emerge as the franchise's next big bad, which would mark a significant escalation for the sixth film in the series.

The MonsterVerse isn’t exactly the most cerebral science fiction franchise around, and nowhere close as jaw-dropping as Minus Zero, but it has become one of Hollywood's most dependable sources of blockbuster entertainment. You can’t deny there’s something undeniably exciting about seeing kaiju go toe-to-toe, wreaking havoc across some of the world’s most beautiful cities. The idea of a threat from the stars crashing into the MonsterVerse makes Godzilla x Kong: Supernova particularly intriguing, though not quite Star Wars-level intriguing.

It’s not an overstatement to say Star Wars is in rough shape right now. Following the poor reception of The Mandalorian and Grogu, the franchise is in dire need of structural reinvention before one of cinema’s most beloved sci-fi properties falls into full-blown creative obsolescence. At least Star Wars: Starfighter looks like a promising breath of fresh air, bypassing the Skywalker Saga to jump five years past The Rise of Skywalker.

Set to hit theaters on the 50th anniversary weekend of the original 1977 film, Shawn Levy’s standalone entry stars Ryan Gosling as a cynical rogue pilot alongside Mia Goth, Amy Adams, and Matt Smith. The story sees Gosling's character taking a young Jedi child under his wing, giving the film a chance to explore a more personal mentor-student dynamic set against a galactic adventure. In the wake of countless Disney Plus spin-offs that never quite stuck the landing, Levy has his work cut out for him, especially with the film carrying the weight of the much-maligned sequel trilogy with it.

After spending nearly three decades stuck in development hell, The Incredibles director is finally bringing his long-gestating passion project to the silver screen. Set in an alternate retro-futuristic megacity as imagined from 1939, the animated sci-fi noir follows Raymond Gunn (Sam Rockwell), the last human private investigator as he is pulled into a murder conspiracy involving extraterrestrial visitors and multimedia superstar Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson).

Director Brad Bird has tapped a laundry list of additional stars to back the voice ensemble, from Alan Tudyk to Michelle Rodriguez, and it looks like the exact kind of stylized swing mainstream animation rarely takes anymore. It already reminds me of Satoshi Kon’s unfinished final project, Dreaming Machine, which was also set in a retro-futuristic society like Ray Gunn’s Metropia. Watching Bird blend hard-boiled detective fiction with mid-century pulp sci-fi is an exciting prospect, and you won’t have to wait long to see it. Ray Gunn releases in theaters on December 4 ahead of its debut on Netflix later that same month.

Denis Villeneuve has already pulled off what filmmakers thought was impossible by turning Frank Herbert’s dense prose into twin modern sci-fi classics. Dune: Part Three is poised to ring in even more hype and acclaim as it pulls in new players and villains into the overarching conflict. Adapting Dune Messiah, the third installment picks up with Paul Atreides (Timothée Chalamet) sitting on the Golden Lion Throne, forced to reckon with the fanatical fallout of his holy war across the imperium.

Jason Momoa returns as the ghola Hayt, a resurrected clone of fallen Atreides swordmaster Duncan Idaho, and is joined by Robert Pattinson as the shape-shifting conspirator Scytale. Villeneuve's closing chapter on Dune is undoubtedly one of the most ambitious and exciting sci-fi events of the year, but it lands on the same day as Marvel’s Avengers suit up to take on one of their toughest foes yet.

Opening on the same "Dunesday" weekend, the Russo brothers’ return to Marvel isn’t pure hard sci-fi in the traditional sense, yet its multiversal stakes make it the loudest pop-culture collision on the calendar. Built around reality-bending incursions and a crossover that pulls the Avengers, The Fantastic Four, and the Fox-era X-Men into one universe-shattering event, Avengers: Doomsday is easily one of the most anticipated comic book blockbusters in years. Bringing Robert Downey Jr. back into the fold as Victor Von Doom is a swerve unlike any other, but one that will prove the most exciting to witness as he collides with Marvel’s pantheon of heroes on-screen later this year.

The multiversal saga has had more than its fair share of missteps, leaving plenty of skeptics wondering if Marvel can actually recapture its Infinity War and Endgame momentum. Love it or hate it, nothing else on the release schedule commands a bigger mainstream footprint than watching Marvel’s architects try to pull off the biggest crossover event Hollywood has seen yet. And, in the wake of that surprise VisionQuest post-credit scene, the hype is at a fever pitch.

#3443. Anne Hathaway's 2024 Romance Movie Is A Must-Watch For Colleen Hoover Fans

We're in a golden age of romance movies based on popular books, over which presides queen Colleen Hoover. There have been four movies based on Colleen Hoover novels and they've thus far ranged from sort of okay to entirely forgettable. But there's no denying it can be fun to settle down with a film you know is going to be absolute nonsense and just turn off your brain while two hot people fall in love and do it and stuff. Unfortunately, once you've watched the four Hoover films, you're stuck with the books until the author decides which of her stories to adapt next. In the meantime, may I direct your attention to a romance starring Anne Hathaway and Nicholas Galitzine, which at least tries to be more than an excuse for more hot people doing it scenes.

"The Idea of You" sees Hathaway falling for He-Man in a romantic comedy that, wouldn't you know it, is based on a book — because Hollywood will seemingly only green-light love stories if they've been pre-approved by BookTok. This one adapts actress turned author Robinne Lee's 2017 novel of the same name, in which she tackled the notion of women losing their desirability post-40. The movie similarly explores this idea via Hathaway and Galitzine's age gap relationship, and did so successfully for the most part.

Hathaway, of course, starred in the latest Hoover adaptation, the dead-on-arrival "Verity," which was helmed by "The Idea of You" director Michael Showalter. Sadly, for those expecting a fairly straightforward romance, the "Devil Wears Prada" star spent a good chunk of the movie sitting motionless and glaring at Dakota Johnson while she stole her husband. "The Idea of You," however, was a much better Showalter x Hathaway collab, and it's available to stream right now on Prime Video.

With its older-woman-falls-for-boy-band-singer narrative, you'd be forgiven for thinking "The Idea of You" is a movie that started as fanfiction. But in a 2024 TIME article, Robinne Lee pushed back against interpretations of her book being Harry Styles fanfiction and explained the real impetus for her story. "I was learning the hard way that in Hollywood, after 40, women are much less desirable," she wrote. "The assumption was that we ceased to be sexual beings and were thus less valuable. I was eager to prove the industry—and our culture at large—wrong, in my own little way." Lee, who criticized those who dubbed her book "fluff" or "fanfiction," saw her story as being about "a woman's midlife sexual awakening," and strove to ensure it was both "tantalizing and complex."

Much of that is preserved in the 2024 film adaptation, which Michael Showalter co-wrote with Jennifer Westfeldt. Anne Hathaway plays single mother and art gallery owner Solène Marchand, who accompanies her teenage daughter to Coachella. There, she meets Hayes Campbell (Nicholas Galitzine), the lead singer of boy band August Moon and all round handsome English gent. Despite there being several years between the two, Solène and Hayes share an instant connection and embark on a passionate love affair. But the latter's popstar status invites scrutiny, and as you might expect given Lee's explanation of her novel, most of it is an excuse to attack the 40-year-old Solène for being with a younger man and generally hurl misogynistic abuse.

Can the pair's relationship survive? You'll have to watch "The Idea of You" on Prime Video to find out — which, if you're reeling from the absolute nonsense that was "Verity," is well worth doing.

"The Idea of You" premiered at the 2024 South by Southwest film festival before going straight to Amazon Prime Video in May of that year. While that direct-to-streaming trajectory might typically indicate a less than stellar romantic comedy, "The Idea of You" actually earned some impressive reviews — a testament to Robinne Lee's efforts to go beyond your typical romantic fiction fare as well as Michael Showalter and Jennifer Westfeldt's ability to preserve that effort in their adaptation.

On Rotten Tomatoes, the film holds a very respectable 81% "certified fresh" critic score — a damn sight better than the 32% "Verity" managed to eke out. /Film's Ryan Scott was certainly impressed, writing in his "The Idea of You" review, "this is the genre at its best." Otherwise, reviewers were won over by Anne Hathaway and Nicholas Galitzine's chemistry and performances. That's to be expected in Hathaway's case. The actor is usually the best thing about any movie she's in, and while there are arguably more compelling modern Hathaway performances — her chilling 2023 thriller that flew completely under the radar, "Eileen," being one example — she does a fine job in "The Idea of You," conveying all the vulnerability and strength of the Solène Marchand in Lee's original novel.

Galitzine, meanwhile, is also perfectly charming if a bit too impressed with himself. The man is no stranger to romance stories, either, having starred alongside Netflix's romance queen Sofia Carson in 2022's "Purple Hearts" (watch that if you want a more straightforward romantic drama). Otherwise, "The Idea of You" is a great palette cleanser for recovering "Verity" viewers but should also go down well with Colleen Hoover fans craving a bit more romance from their Hathaway-led entertainment.

#3442. Ridley Scott's 44-Year-Old Blade Runner Mystery Won't Be Answered In New 2099 Spinoff

Blade Runner 2099 will keep one lingering question a mystery.

Since Ridley Scott adapted the sci-fi thriller in 1982, Blade Runner has become a cult classic and remains one of the most underrated movies from that era. However, the classic didn't develop into a franchise until 35 years later, when Denis Villeneuve directed the critically acclaimed sequel, Blade Runner 2049. Now, the universe is expanding with the first television sequel Blade Runner 2099, set to premiere on Prime Video this month.

With so much rich lore expanding through sequels and spinoffs, one of the most debated mysteries is whether Harrison Ford's protagonist, Rick Deckard, is a replicant. Unfortunately, it appears that the question will remain unresolved even with Prime Video's new series. In a recent issue of Empire Magazine (via The Direct), Blade Runner 2099 showrunner Silka Luisa confirmed that the script doesn't mention Deckard at all, saying, "Why would you ask?" That lack of reference means that the series won't address his humanity.

Furthermore, she also argued that the lack of clarity about who is human or a replicant is built into the world's lore, exclaiming: "Not knowing is part of what makes the world so disorienting."

The upcoming 2099 series will take place 80 years after Scott's original movie and 50 years after the sequel. While the two epic movies saw Ford and Ryan Gosling's protagonists hunting down rogue replicants, the show turns the tables, as replicants become the ruling class after winning the war against humans. Nevertheless, the story is similar to Blade Runner's search for rogue replicants. This time, the main players are a Replicant Blade Runner, Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), and her partner, Cora (Hunter Schafer), a human posing as a replicant.

Luisa's recent comments track with updates about the show's connection to the movies. Despite being in the Blade Runner universe, the showrunner previously said watching the two movies wasn't required, and that Ford won't appear in the series. In September 2026, she told Collider that she structured the show so that "you would understand because of the way the story evolves." The 50-year time jump from Blade Runner 2049 may be the key reason to avoid mentioning Deckard and keep the show standalone since he may be long dead.

Unfortunately, that also means the question of Deckard's humanity will continue to linger as a cold case. Although Philip K. Dick's novel, Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, made it clear that the protagonist was human, Scott introduced more ambiguity about his humanity in the film.

In fact, the legendary filmmaker has argued that Deckard is indeed a replicant, with the unicorn dream sequence and Gaff's original origami serving as proof. Meanwhile, Ford countered that notion, intending for his character to be human to provide the emotional resonance as he develops romantic feelings for the replicant Rachael (Sean Young).

Blade Runner 2049 ended with Gosling's K helping Deckard reunite with his daughter after faking his death, and the sequel never took a direct position on his humanity. Now, that ambiguity will linger, allowing the debate to persist even after the 2099 series drops.

The remaining main cast includes Dimitri Abold and Lewis Gribben, while Tom Bruke, Daniel Rigby, Johnny Harris, and Amy Lennox have recurring roles. Scott is an executive producer. Luisa also confirmed that Blade Runner 2099 won't have a season 2 because it has a contained beginning, middle, and end.

Blade Runner 2099 will drop all eight episodes on November 25, 2026, on Prime Video.

#3441. Leonard Nimoy Loved This Star Trek Episode That Allowed Him To Show Off A Different Side Of Spock

What was Leonard Nimoy's favorite "Star Trek" episode? It's almost a trick question. Human beings are constantly changing and fickle creatures; the answer to our favorite anything can change depending on our moods. Nimoy, who played Spock for almost 50 years, couldn't be expected to give one consistent answer for that long.

But there are a few episodes that Nimoy consistently named among his favorites, including in his 1975 autobiography "I Am Not Spock." One of them was "This Side of Paradise," co-written by D. C. Fontana and Nathan Butler and one of the best Spock episodes of "Star Trek." The Enterprise visits colony world Omicron Ceti III, home to a plant species that secretes spores that take root in humanoid hosts. Once they do, the hosts remain in a state of perfect bliss, but they also lose all their ambition. (The story is a likely reference to the Lotus-Eaters in "The Odyssey.")

Spock is one of the infected. His stone face cracks into rubble as he becomes joyful, happily expressive, and even rekindles a romance with local botanist Leila Kalomi (Jill Ireland). Nimoy wrote in "I Am Not Spock" that he enjoyed the episode for showing Spock in a mood we almost never saw him — not coldly logical, sarcastic, or struggling to control his emotions, but genuinely carefree.

"This is a very special episode for me for obvious reasons and particularly because, where Spock was so totally adult in most of his attitudes and reactions throughout the series, this episode provided a chance to expose the complete child within. We saw him loving, picnicking, romping, and literally swinging playfully in the trees. It was a total exposure of internal Spock that so many people have always suspected was there."

Watching "This Side of Paradise" now, it might remind you of the Apple TV series "Pluribus," where all of humanity is turned into a blissful hive mind (collectively "The Others"). In "This Side of Paradise," strong negative emotions literally destroy the spores, which is also a weakness of the Others in "Pluribus."

In "This Side of Paradise," though, there's no identity theft. The spores let Spock be his innermost self. Compare other times we see Spock's emotions come out, like in "The Naked Time" where he cries over having never told his mother he loved her, or "Journey to Babel" where said mother, Amanda (Jane Wyatt), recounts how Spock used to cry because other Vulcan children bullied him. As only a half-Vulcan, Spock is especially self-conscious about living up to his people's teachings about logic.

When the spores hit him, those anxieties melt away. Note how Leila says to him he has "no need to hide [his] inner face anymore" and Spock says "I can love you," as if finally allowing himself something he'd previously denied.

Nimoy described other "Star Trek" episodes as favorites such as "Devil in the Dark," where the Enterprise crew visit a mining colony to find a creature killing the inhabitants. The culprit, a Horta (resembling a pile of living molten lava), is sentient and Spock telepathically communicates with it, discovering it was only acting to protect its offspring. Nimoy praised that one as a "wonderful episode about the fear of the unknown," and "Devil in the Dark" is known to be a favorite of William Shatner's, too.

"Devil in the Dark" and "This Side of Paradise" are very different episodes, but both ones anchored by Spock. Little surprise that Leonard Nimoy loved them.

#3440. This Christian Bale Western Drama Flopped In Theaters But Is Worth Revisiting

For a long time it seemed as though audiences might see Clint Eastwood and John Wayne team up in what could have been the greatest Western ever made. That long-gestating, never-realized project was set to be called "Hostiles" and was supposed to be based on a script by Larry Cohen. Alas, the Duke remained entirely against collaborating with a spiritual successor so opposed to his traditionalist roots, and the film was never made. In 2017, however, we did get a movie called "Hostiles" which had similarly languished as a semi-finished script for years. This film had nothing to do with the planned Eastwood/Wayne vehicle, but it did focus on two seemingly opposed parties who find common ground as their harrowing story plays out on the plains of the Old West.

"Hostiles" stars Christian Bale as a United States Army cavalry officer forced to escort a Cheyenne war chief across the dangerous terrain of 1892 America. It's written and directed by Scott Cooper who most recently oversaw Jeremy Allen White's haunted performance in "Springsteen: Deliver Me from Nowhere." Prior to that, Cooper worked with Bale on the 2013 crime drama "Out of the Furnace" and in 2015 he directed "Black Mass," the Johnny Depp-led crime drama based on real life mobster Whitey Bulger.

"Hostiles" came directly after "Black Mass" in Cooper's filmography, and saw him re-team with Bale for a film that was well received by critics despite being a box office disappointment. Today, the film barely gets a mention. But it should, as Cooper and Bale managed to deliver a taut Western drama that was worthy of far more attention than it got from mass audiences.

In 2017, Christian Bale led the weary and grim "Hostiles," a film that very nearly made our best dark Westerns list. Set in 1892, it follows Bale's Army Captain Joseph Blocker, who's nearing retirement and looking forward to leaving his military years behind him. But President Benjamin Harrison has one more job for Blocker. Before he's allowed to retire, he must escort a cancer-stricken Cheyenne war chief named Yellow Hawk (Wes Studi) and his family from Fort Berringer, New Mexico to his tribal lands in Montana. Bale's Army Captain initially refuses on the grounds that he and Yellow Hawk are old enemies. But he's coerced into accepting the job and sets out on the perilous journey.

Along the way he meets widow Rosalee Quaid (Rosamund Pike), who joins the group on a trek that becomes increasingly dangerous. As such, despite their differences, Blocker, Yellow Hawk, and their cohorts must come together to survive a harsh and unforgiving landscape.

As Deadline noted in 2018, "Hostiles" is based on an old manuscript from Donald E. Stewart. The screenwriter, who passed away in 1999, penned the Oscar-Winning 1982 biographical thriller "Missing" and the 1990s Jack Ryan films: "The Hunt for Red October," "Patriot Games," and "Clear and Present Danger." During the '80s, Stewart also wrote a version of what became "Hostiles," which came to Cooper by way of Stewart's widow. It seems she came across the manuscript while packing to move house, and having been impressed by "Out of the Furnace," sent it to Scott Cooper in the hope he could finally realize her late husband's vision.

Upon reading Donald E. Stewart's "Hostiles" manuscript, Scott Cooper decided to expand upon what he called the "kernel of an idea about a man who, in Christian Bale's character, has been indoctrinated by the United States government from a very young age essentially to fight and to kill." Thus began the process of finally bringing "Hostiles" to the big screen. Sadly, when it finally did hit theaters, the movie grossed just $35.7 million on what Deadline claims was a $39 million budget (The Hollywood Reporter put the budget at $50 million).

On the plus side, "Hostiles" did earn a respectable 71% Rotten Tomatoes score. It isn't the finest score, but not only did the film make /Film's best Westerns of the 21st Century list, RT isn't the most nuanced indicator of how critics actually feel about the movies they review. In other words, whether "Hostiles" is, in fact, one of the best Westerns of this century depends on who you ask. Richard Whittaker of the Austin Chronicle, for instance, found "Hostiles" to be "timeless yet contemporary," and praised the film for "diving headlong into the ongoing and often horrific impact of the United States' policies and attitudes to indigenous culture." Dan Jolin of Empire, meanwhile, called Christian Bale's performance "astounding." On the other hand, the San Francisco Chronicle's Mick LaSalle was unimpressed with the film's "dull characters," an "almost-endless tedium" and its "nihilistic violence."

The only way to know for sure where you stand on this mostly overlooked Bale-led Western is to check it out for yourself. Unfortunately, the film isn't streaming anywhere at the time of writing, but can be rented for a reasonable price from the usual digital platforms.

#3439. Five Smartwatch Heart Rate Zone Hacks Every Runner Should Know

If you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio. Legend has it that easy, conversational effort cardio—also known as cardio that takes your heart rate into "Zone 2"—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine to faster race times and even a longer life.

To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout. The catch is that Zone 2 is easy to get wrong, especially since no one can agree on what it actually means.  Your smartwatch can show you your heart rate, but many recreational runners will still drift into a “gray zone” that's too fast to be truly easy, and too slow to give them a real workout. If you're struggling to hit Zone 2 consistently, there are a few smartwatch hacks that can help.

Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue. A 9:30 mile might be Zone 2 on a flat, cool day and Zone 4 on a hot, hilly one.

Dig into your watch's activity settings (on Garmin, it's Activity > Data Screens; on Apple Watch, the Workout app's metrics layout; on Coros, Polar, and Suunto, similar menus) and put live heart rate zone front and center, ideally as a zone number or colored gauge rather than just a raw bpm figure (though this assumes these zones are accurate—more on that below).

Create an alert when your heart rate goes above or below a target range, delivered as a vibration pattern, a beep, or both. Set the alert for the upper boundary of Zone 2, and you've essentially hired a mini coach who taps you on the wrist whenever you get overzealous. Whenever you hear or feel that buzz, you’ll know you need to ease into a slower jog until your heart rate settles.

Instead of free-running and checking your numbers afterward, build structured workouts that carry the targets for you. In Garmin Connect, TrainingPeaks, Apple's Custom Workout feature, Coros Training Hub, or similar platforms, you can create sessions like "10-minute warm-up in Zone 1, 40 minutes in Zone 2, 5-minute cooldown" and sync them straight to your watch.

During the run, your watch displays the current step, the target range, and whether you're above, below, or in the pocket. Many will automatically advance between intervals and alert you when it's time to shift gears.

Heart rate-based intervals, like 4 x 4 minutes in Zone 4 with Zone 1 recovery, where you don't have to do mental math or check the clock.

Progressive long runs that start in Zone 2 and finish in Zone 3.

Hill repeats, where pace is meaningless but effort matters.

Most watches calculate default zones using a generic formula like 220 minus your age, which can be off by 10 to 20 beats for any given individual. If your zones are wrong, your Zone 2 training isn't Zone 2 training.

Here’s how to fix your watch’s heart rate zones:

Find your true max heart rate. The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded.

Use lactate threshold heart rate instead. Many watches can estimate this automatically after a few hard efforts, and zones built from threshold tend to be more personalized than ones built from max.

Customize the boundaries. Dive into the heart rate zone settings and input your own numbers. Some runners prefer the "MAF" method (180 minus age, with adjustments) for aerobic base building, and most watches let you set that as a custom range.

Recheck every few months. Fitness changes, and so do your zones.

A screen crowded with cadence, vertical oscillation, ground contact time, running power, and lap pace is a recipe for second-guessing.

Create a dedicated Zone 2 data screen with just two or three fields: current heart rate zone, elapsed time, and maybe distance. Turn off auto-scroll so it doesn't flip to a screen full of numbers you don't need. If your watch supports multiple activity profiles, make a separate "Easy Run" profile with this stripped-down layout and keep a different profile for tempo days and races.

A chest strap (or a forearm or upper-arm optical band) is generally more accurate and responsive than the wrist-based sensor on your watch. For heart rate training, where a few beats can mean the difference between Zone 2 and Zone 3, I recommend buying one. This COOSPO heart rate monitor is one of my favorites, and it's only $31.99.

The bottom line: Your smartwatch can make heart rate training far easier, but only if you set it up to support you rather than overwhelm you.
