#3438. 10 Best Western Movie Gunfights Of All Time, Ranked

While Westerns boast breathtakingly rustic vistas and memorably rugged main characters, chances are, we're there to see some sharpshooting gunplay. Many Western movies that everyone should watch at least once are anchored by a riveting action set piece between frontier gunfighters. These sequences range from drawn-out battles throughout harsh landscapes and dusty towns to quick-draw showdowns over in a single burst of gunfire. We're looking back at personal favorite gunfights in the history of Western movies, each earning a spot in cinematic history.

Silver screen legends like John Wayne and Clint Eastwood immortalized themselves through the gunfight scenes in Westerns they starred in. In many cases, the single most iconic scene in a given Western is its gunslinging action sequence. After all, the Wild West archetype is one revolving around its laconic gunfighters, not its bucolic communities on the fringes of civilization.

With those qualities in mind, these are the best Western movie gunfights of all time ranked, epitomizing the genre's gunslinging appeal.

So much of the classic 1953 Western "Shane" is the build-up to its titular protagonist finally showing everyone what he's got. Played by Alan Ladd, the character is a drifter with a mysterious past who comes to work on a farm on the frontier. When these homesteads are targeted by an unscrupulous land baron, Shane's lethal skills quickly come in handy. This comes to a quick-draw climax as Shane kills the murderous crook along with his sadistic hired gun Jack Wilson (Jack Palance), though Shane himself is wounded.

Ladd's Shane is the ultimate gunslinger archetype, though he really only gets one gunfight in the entire movie. Fortunately, "Shane" makes this sequence count, with this violent inevitability expertly staged and crafted. To heighten the mood, much of this climax is filmed in a shadowy saloon as Shane overcomes the obvious trap that he knowingly walks into. Fans still debate over 70 years later if Shane survived this gunfight, which is a testament to how memorable the sequence and its ambiguous aftermath are.

Even though it became a Western that flopped at the box office, the 2007 remake of "3:10 to Yuma" does its 1957 predecessor proud. That said, the difference between the two movies are most acutely felt in how they each end. The 2007 remake features farmer Dan Evans (Christian Bale) escorting outlaw Ben Wade (Russell Crowe) to a train station, with Ben begrudgingly going along for the last run. What follows is a running gunfight against those trying to stop Dan, who still finds the time to convince Ben to cooperate.

The last few minutes of the "3:10 to Yuma" remake are its most exciting, while filmmaker James Mangold still delivers on its main character arcs. Any sense of triumph is quickly undercut by the movie's tragic conclusion, differentiating it from both its short story source material and the 1957 film. The movie handles that fake-out marvelously while not mitigating the excitement that came before during this desperate run. Easily one of the greatest Western movies of the 2000s, "3:10 to Yuma" saves its best for last.

For as breezy as the overall movie is, the most well-known scenes in "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid" are its most relentlessly intense. Though the duo being pursued by a posse across the Wild West for their train robberies stands out, the movie's ending is arguably its most famous sequence. Having relocated to Bolivia to resume their criminal activities, Butch (Paul Newman) and the Sundance Kid (Robert Redford) are ambushed by the authorities and take shelter in a nearby building. Charging outside, Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid go out in a blaze of glory, with the movie ending on a freeze-frame as the pair are gunned down.

The alternate ending of "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid" thankfully wasn't used, which would've actually shown its likable duo gruesomely killed. Instead, the scene leaves the carnage to the audience's imagination, rather than treading the same territory as the ending of "Bonnie & Clyde." That freeze-frame approach works well for the overall movie, giving the story its inevitable ending but without dwelling on the violence, staying in line with its general tone. The only gunfight on this list which doesn't show its decisive salvo on-screen, "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid" focuses on its title characters' legend rather than its tragedy.

John Wayne led a lot of different Western movie gunfights, from classic quick-draws in "The War Wagon" to shadowy shootings in "The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance." But the Wayne-starring gunfight that stands out from the rest of his work is his climactic confrontation in "True Grit." Wayne plays U.S. Marshal Rooster Cogburn in the 1969 movie, finally catching up with a crew of outlaws he had been pursuing for the entire film. After being insulted by the gang's leader Ned Pepper (Robert Duvall), an incensed Cogburn charges them alone with a gun in each hand and his horse's reins in his teeth.

John Wayne considered "True Grit" to be his first decent role in 20 years, and his one-man charge cements his character's place in his legacy. The action sequence isn't just the movie at its most rousing, and it shows a more ornery side to Wayne's usual frontier archetype. Expertly twirling his rifle in one hand to chamber a new round, just as he did in "Stagecoach" three decades prior, Wayne hasn't lost a step. Putting a furiously gun-toting Wayne back in the saddle, "True Grit" proved this old dog still had some new tricks.

Over a decade later, "Django Unchained" is still Quentin Tarantino's biggest movie, at least from a commercial standpoint. The final act of the 2012 movie takes place in Candyland, a notoriously brutal plantation run by the cruel slave owner Calvin Candie (Leonardo DiCaprio). Subjected by Calvin's nightmarish hospitality in an effort to rescue Brunhilda (Kerry Washington), the enslaved wife of Django (Jamie Foxx), King Schultz (Christoph Waltz) kills Calvin. This kickstarts a particularly blood-soaked gunfight, as Schultz is killed and Django battles gunmen around the plantation, until he is eventually forced to surrender.

The sanguine shootout may not be the final showdown in "Django Unchained," but it's a scene that we wish would never end. After the smug cruelty that Django and Schultz endure in Candyland, the action sequence feels like a cathartic release as Django exacts comeuppance on his hosts. To heighten the effusive enjoyment of the scene, Tarantino uses "Unchained (The Payback/Untouchable)" by James Brown and Tupac, while making every bullet hit like an artillery shell. The best gunfight that Tarantino has filmed to date, "Django Unchained" has its titular hero bring bloody retribution to its main villain's antebellum lair.

For much of "Unforgiven," the violent backstory of outlaw Will Munny (Clint Eastwood) was only hinted at, with Munny himself focused on being a farmer and single father. After learning that his old friend Ned Logan (Morgan Freeman) was murdered by the sadistic sheriff Little Bill Daggett (Gene Hackman), with his body mockingly displayed, Munny's lethal demeanor resurfaces. Storming into Little Bill's saloon, Munny shoots him and several of his associates, maintaining a clear-eyed, if furious, focus. After finishing off Little Bill, Munny threatens everyone to properly bury Logan or experience his wrath again before departing from the rainy frontier town for good.

The "Unforgiven" ending reveals that some legends are better left to fade away, and Munny is every inch the killer that he was reputed to be. Moreover, Munny inadvertently demonstrates Little Bill's own insight against him, staying calm and collected during the chaos of the gunfight, allowing him to take down all his enemies. Keeping in tone with the rest of the revisionist Western nature of the movie, this burst of violence isn't particularly flashy or stylized. But that makes the carnage all the more grounded and with understated menace as Eastwood delivers his definitive word on the genre that made him a star.

The most famous shootout in real Wild West history was the gunfight at the O.K. Corral in 1881 between the Cowboy outlaw gang and lawmen led by Wyatt Earp. Though this fateful showdown has been dramatized plenty of times in Western movies, the most entertaining depiction is in "Tombstone." Roughly serving as the centerpiece of the movie, the scene only lasts less than a minute, like the historical event. Several of the outlaws are killed in the exchange, while both of Wyatt's brothers are wounded before inciting the wrath of the other gang members.

"Tombstone" presents its historical figures in a stylized and colorful light, helping make it one of the best Western movies of the 1990s. Comparatively, the gunfight at the O.K. Corral is played relatively straight, which helps it stand out from the rest of the movie. The action is quick, brutal, and consequential, setting in motion the back half of the movie's stakes. Certainly one of the best gunfights in a relatively modern Western movie, "Tombstone" knows a lot is riding on its marquee confrontation and delivers accordingly.

The single most recognizable shot in Sergio Leone's "Once Upon a Time in the West" is the sight of three gunmen confronting Harmonica (Charles Bronson) at a train station. The scene opens the film, playing out largely with diegetic noise as the three gunfighters await the incoming train with their target. This sets the stage for Harmonica's arrival, earning his nickname from his first appearance with a screeching melody played from his mouth organ. Unfazed that he's outnumbered three-to-one, Harmonica takes his position against his three enemies and guns them all down singlehandedly though wounded in the skirmish.

"Once Upon a Time in the West" is bookended with genre-defining gunfights, but the opening sequence is the superior of the two. Leone's masterful positioning his actors in frame and suspense building until the inevitable draw finally punctuates that crescendo with a single exchange of gunfire. With Leone, it was all about finding ways to fuel that tension before letting it finally go off like a pressure cooker, a lesson that has visibly influenced Quentin Tarantino. "Once Upon a Time in the West" is among Charles Bronson's best movies and seeing him anchor the movie's opening gunfight sets the mood for Leone's requiem to the genre.

If "Once Upon a Time in the West" is best known for its opening, the following year's "The Wild Bunch" is best known for its ending. The movie follows a group of aging American outlaws in the early 20th century, led by Pike Bishop (William Holden), who flee to Mexico after a botched bank heist. The ensemble get caught up in the revolution south of the border, culminating in the quartet making their last stand against the full might of the Mexican army. Gathering around a machine gun emplacement, the group are eventually overwhelmed and killed but not before massacring scores of soldiers.

The gruesome to "The Wild Bunch" was reportedly as brutal to film as it was to watch, heightening the verisimilitude of the sequence. In a matter of seconds, this situation escalates out of control, full of fire and fury as Pike and his associates stand in the face of oblivion. There's no mistaking that these four men are marching quietly to their deaths, but as the scene reveals, they're going out on their own terms and they're not going alone. More than just the tale of four old outlaws, "The Wild Bunch" signals that the Wild West era didn't die out peacefully but with a violent fire in its guts.

Of course a Clint Eastwood Western was going to top this list, and of course it was going to be "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly." Virtually every Sergio Leone Western, like "Once Upon a Time in the West," has a standout shootout sequence, but the greatest is in his 1966 epic. The movie reaches its crescendo when it brings its titular trio together in a sprawling cemetery as they search for a hidden stash of loot. With the three gunslingers at odds, the characters have a tense staredown before Blondie (Eastwood) guns down Angel Eyes (Lee Van Cleef).

Powered by a stirring score by Ennio Morricone, the climax is one of the most effectively staged sequences Leone has ever directed. The intercutting of close-ups between the three main characters before being punctuated by a single burst of gunfire with mounting suspense all the while is masterfully done. The moment also provides Blondie with another opportunity to pull a fast one on Tuco (Eli Wallach), secretly unloading his pistol for the duel. The quick-draw gunfight that epitomizes Leone's meticulous style, "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly" ends on a truly iconic note.

#3437. The Office's Downfall Can Be Traced Back To One Moment

In 2005, two TV shows premiered as mid-season replacements, which isn't usually a great sign for said series' potential longevity. One was "Grey's Anatomy" on ABC, which became one of the longest-running TV shows in history. The other? "The Office," an adaptation of Ricky Gervais' British series of the same name that became one of the biggest hits in the entire history of NBC.

With Steve Carell leading the way as the well-meaning but unbelievably buffoonish Michael Scott (the regional manager of the Scranton branch of paper company Dunder-Mifflin), the American version of "The Office" made it past a somewhat rocky first season and became a small-screen staple, launching the careers of Carell and co-stars like John Krasinski, B.J. Novak, and Mindy Kaling. (It also, arguably, led to an uptick in small-screen mockumentaries like its successors "Modern Family," "Parks and Recreation," and "Abbott Elementary.") After running for nine massively successful seasons, "The Office" wrapped up its run in 2013 with a finale that actually stuck the landing ... but the road to the finish was rough.

You can argue all you want about how to pinpoint the downfall of "The Office," but I won't entertain any debate. The answer is that "The Office" hit a major point of no return in Season 7 when Carell left the show, which led to Michael Scott moving away from Scranton and decamping to Colorado. Despite its best efforts to continue relatively uninterrupted, the series just didn't functionally work without Michael Scott.

It's perfectly understandable that Steve Carell wanted to leave "The Office" behind after spending so long playing one character. (He's a pretty talented guy, after all.) Still, the show should have just ... ended. Even the lead-up to Michael's exit was, all things considered, sort of bleak. This is conjecture on my part, but it really felt like, in Season 6 episodes like "Scott's Tots" and "Koi Pond," the show was leaning into Michael's worst impulses and making him straight-up unlikable instead of silly but well-meaning.

The reason for Michael's departure, however, is undeniably sweet. After human resources representative Holly Flax (Amy Ryan) makes her debut appearance in the Season 4 finale "Goodbye Toby," she and Michael ultimately fall in love before she gets moved back to her original Dunder-Mifflin branch in Nashua due to higher-ups fretting about the pair's relationship. Then, in Season 7, she returns to Scranton, and while Holly and Michael have been broken up for some time when she finds herself back in northeastern Pennsylvania, they get back together ... but their happy ending is threatened when family troubles mean that Holly needs to move back to Colorado.

Thankfully, by this point in the series, Michael is back to being essentially likable again, so he does the right thing: He proposes to Holly and tells his colleagues he's moving with her. His final episode, "Goodbye Michael," is incredibly moving, especially the moment where Pam Beesly-Halpert (Jenna Fischer) says goodbye to Michael in the airport. Yet, the show loses its footing forever as he departs, and it never recovers. Why? Well, the string of potential replacements for Michael is lackluster at best and egregiously unfunny at worst.

One of the many crimes committed in the final two seasons of "The Office" is that the show managed to make English treasure and comedy legend Catherine Tate actively exhausting, but I'm getting ahead of myself. First, "The Office" pulls out the stops by bringing in Steve Carell's "Anchorman" cohort Will Ferrell (the proverbial comedic big gun) as Deangelo Vickers, a deeply confusing and unfunny new manager who's written off after getting a brain injury during a pickup basketball game. From there, Creed Bratton's erratic "Creed Bratton" briefly becomes the manager (and it goes just as well as any "Office" fan would expect), and while James Spader's unfathomably bizarre Robert California has his moments as one of Creed's successors, he doesn't work, either.

Ultimately, Tate's Nellie Bertram and Ed Helms' Andy Bernard are the people who run the Scranton branch most consistently in Michael's absence, and not only are they both terrible at the job, neither of them recreates the magic that only Carell could bring to the series. Instead, Tate's Nellie is, at varying times, exceedingly ridiculous or shrewd (it depends on the episode you're watching), whereas Andy is so expendable that "The Office" briefly writes him off. (This was done to free up Helms to go film "The Hangover Part III" at the time.) Moreover, everyone eventually gets simplified to the point of parody (i.e. Flanderized, to use a popular "Simpsons"-inspired term), so much so that Andy, himself an Ivy League graduate, becomes borderline illiterate. Put simply, it's a mess.

Yes, "The Office" has a great series finale, but the journey to getting there was rough without Michael Scott. Decide for yourself: The show is currently streaming on Peacock.

#3436. Netflix's Award-winning Dark Sci-fi Series is Officially Returning

Netflix's dystopian sci-fi show is in production

Get ready for more dystopian science fiction because an eighth season of TV series Black Mirror is in production for Netflix. Variety reports that the show began filming this summer, but has no confirmed release date. Series creator Charlie Brooker is back, and he will write and executive produce the series alongside Bisha K. Ali.

“Black Mirror will return, and hopefully it’ll be more Black Mirror than ever,” Brooker said in an interview with Netflix’s Tudum when the series was renewed this January. “I can confirm that Black Mirror will return, just in time for reality to catch up with it. So, that’s exciting. That chunk of my brain has already been activated and is whirring away,” he added.

Black Mirror is an anthology sci-fi series that began in 2011 on the British network Channel 4 before moving to Netflix. The show largely focuses on near-future dystopian scenarios, tapping into contemporary anxieties about our relationship with technology; "black mirror" refers to phone and computer screens. The series currently spans 33 episodes and a special across seven seasons. There’s also the experimental interactive film Black Mirror: Bandersnatch (which was admittedly more interesting in theory than practice).

Over the years, the show has divided critics, with some praising its trenchant observations on modern society while others find its messaging ham-fisted and numbingly cynical. The series' anthology format certainly adds to these divided opinions, since it is easy to hold both views at once: some episodes are definitely better than others.

Black Mirror has won multiple times at the Emmys, and “San Junipero,” “USS Callister,” and (somehow) Black Mirror: Bandersnatch took home the Outstanding Television Movie award for consecutive years from 2017 to 2019. Since then, some argue the series has declined with its fifth and sixth seasons. Considering that the phrase “It’s like we’re living in a Black Mirror episode” has become increasingly common, it will be interesting to see if the series can stay ahead of the times.

The first seven seasons of Black Mirror are now streaming on Netflix.

#3435. Robert Downey Jr.'s 90s Supernatural Fantasy Flop Is Worth Revisiting

It's no exaggeration to say that Ron Underwood's 1993 fantasy comedy film "Heart and Souls" boasts one of Robert Downey Jr.'s best performances. He wasn't nominated for an Oscar (although he surely deserved to be), but at least he won a Saturn Award for Best Actor for his work on it. Yet, because it flopped at the box office, it's rarely ranked among Downey's best movies of all time.

Downey stars in "Heart and Souls" as Thomas Reilly, an arrogant yuppie who is possessed by a pack of friendly ghosts that have been following him since birth. Thus, over the course of the movie, Downey takes on the speech patterns and affectations of his ghostly co-stars (Kyra Sedgwick, Tom Sizemore, Alfre Woodard, and Charles Grodin), and he does so with utter aplomb. The result is a film that's funny, profound, and sentimental in equal measure. It has the mood and structure of a high-concept Hollywood comedy, but with a toe rooted in the warmth of something like "It's a Wonderful Life." Plus, its view of the afterlife is pretty light and fun and makes sense in a secular way.

The world of ghosts plays by its own rules in "Heart and Souls," but it's not oblique or difficult. Here, the living and the dead are cosmically bound, like sometimes-invisible family members contracted to make wrongs right and assuage regrets. It's a positive and touching movie with its messages tucked in between hilarious bouts of Downey zaniness. Ultimately, Thomas learns to be less selfish and far more understanding to his girlfriend, Anne, played by Elisabeth Shue. See what I mean about the amazing cast?

"Heart and Souls" opens in 1959 and introduces us to our ghost characters while they're still alive, each of them boarding the same ill-fated bus. Julia (Kyra Sedgwick) is hoping to find her boyfriend, whose marriage proposal she regrets rejecting. Penny (Alfre Woodard) has to work a late shift away from her sons. Milo (Tom Sizemore) is a small-time crook who conned some valuable stamps from a local kid and regrets it. And Harrison (Charles Grodin) is a singer who just fled an audition due to overwhelming stage fright.

Sadly, their bus driver, Hal (David Paymer), gets distracted and crashes the vehicle, killing everyone on board in front of a car carrying a woman in labor. The four passengers, now ghosts, then witness a young Thomas being born. Over time, the ghosts realize they're physically bound to Thomas (meaning, they get dragged along if he walks away) and grow up with him. However, because they're invisible to everyone but him, Thomas' parents assume he's mentally unwell. So, the ghosts eventually decide to become invisible to Thomas to protect his mental health.

Fast-forward to the present, and the ghosts are unexpectedly visited by the now-deceased Hal. He tells them that Thomas is their "earthly vessel" and they should've been spending their time using him to right the wrongs in their lives so they can finally enter the afterlife. Now, they have to solve their biggest regrets in the next few days or risk oblivion.

Thomas, meanwhile, has become a heartless foreclosure banker who believes he had schizophrenia as a child, causing him to see his childhood "friends." But after the ghosts reappear to him, he eventually accepts that, yes, they are real, and he agrees to help them solve their earthly problems and ascend.

I maintain that "Heart and Souls" is one of the best films of its year. And, to reiterate, Robert Downey Jr. gives an Oscar-worthy performance in it. However, he wouldn't win his Oscar until "Oppenheimer" decades later, having only just been nominated for an Academy Award for the first time right before "Heart and Souls" came out for his turn as Charlie Chaplin in Richard Attenborough's biopic "Chaplin."

Overall, critics were mixed on "Heart and Souls." Most reviews tended to praise the performances from the movie's gaggle of stars, as seen in Michael Wilmington's review for the Los Angeles Times. He noted that "Heart and Souls" was about the spiritual crisis of modern humanity, "buried under several tons of Hollywood slick." But, he added, you should trust the film's actors. To quote him directly:

"There's one great opportunity for virtuoso fun here: the chance handed Downey to impersonate the mannerisms of his co-stars whenever one takes over his body. With [...] delicate, precise mimicry [...] he slips delightfully into [Alfre] Woodard's feline assurance, [Tom] Sizemore's swagger, [Kyra] Sedgwick's sexiness or [Charles] Grodin's repressions. The character he's playing — the same kind of languid, self-obsessed, inwardly anxious hedonist he played throughout the '80s — isn't deep, but Downey digs something comic out of his superficiality."

If that sounds fun or intriguing, it can serve as your "in" to "Heart and Souls." You may discover a new gem.

#3433. ’12 12 12′ Review: Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan’s Ticking-Clock Heist Thriller Runs on Broken Time

Every episode of “12 12 12” opens with the same explanation of its title: Citing the fictitious law enforcement manual, “Principles of Crime, FBI Research Center, 4th Edition,” Anthony Mackie explains, “A high asset robbery, professionally conceived, is 12 months in planning, 12 hours in execution. A bank robber who’s not caught within 12 days is not caught at all.” Then the screen splits horizontally to reveal images from the 12 months of preparation, the 12 hours of execution, and the 12 days when thief extraordinaire Paul Galvin (Jamie Dornan) does his best to elude Mackie’s obsessed FBI agent Jack Strickland. And then, we’re off to the races. Related Stories ‘The Good Daughter’ Review: Rose Byrne Sizzles in Peacock’s Brutal Trauma-Drama About Crime-Solving Sisters ‘American Doctor’ and ‘You Can See Everything’ Lead 2027 Cinema Eye Honors Film Nominations

The heist genre, in theory, seems ripe for this kind of temporal manipulation. A game of wits between cops and criminals typically involves plenty of twists, many of which pull the rug out by flashing back to show where, when, and how it was placed so stealthily underfoot. Also working in “12 12 12’s” favor is the genre’s familiarity: There will be “getting the team together” montages, there will be unexpected hiccups in the days and hours during the robbery, there will be chest-thumping meetings between our confident cop and the equally confident con artist. Throw in the complex heist itself and the tense escape soon after, and there appear to be enough recognizable pieces that jumbling them up shouldn’t prove too confusing.

And “12 12 12” isn’t confusing. It is, however, convoluted. Taking a serpentine route through well-trodden territory does more to undermine our enjoyment of an otherwise well-mounted chase than it does to liven things up. Heists are inherently exciting. They’re exciting in conception (when master thieves can wow us with their slick plans), they’re exciting to see carried out (when the shit hits the fan and even the most astute architects have to think on their feet), and they’re exciting to get away with (when safety is within reach, but it could be snatched away at any moment). Anticipation, suspense, and anxiety work to form a natural arc, and disrupting that arc over and over, every hour for eight hours, in service of a few extra twists — and to extend what’s obviously a movie-length story across eight hours — simply isn’t worth it.

On that note, let me get this minor but essential point out of the way now, quickly and clearly: Jamie Dornan needs more weird roles, not more conventional ones. We saw what he can do in “Barb and Star Go to Vista Del Mar” (a modern comedy classic). Let the man cook — or sing or dance or all three at once! He can do it! Honestly, I believe he can do anything. (Remember the bee movie?! No, not that bee movie — the other one.)

Anyway, here his character’s only unique attribute is his brilliant… planning. He’s got a mind for details, and he uses it to map out every possible contingency before embarking on his elaborate heists. Caught in a bind with his dumbass brother (Jack Kesy, doing his best Travis Kelce impression), Bobby lays it out in aptly blunt terms: “Paul, you’re the fucking plan guy, so plan me a plan.”

But the only plans Paul wants to make these days are for his family: He’s happy working on fishing boats off the coast of France and coming home to his wife, Severine (Agathe Rousselle), in their little apartment above a bar. He’s bonded with his father-in-law, Serge (José Garcia), who’s the Marxist papa Paul never had, and he’s got a kid on the way.

Unfortunately, Bobby can’t stop being Bobby and winds up indebted to the wrong people; people who don’t just want their money back, but who want more money to make up for the inconvenience. And since Bobby already owes more money than either brother could ever pay back, Paul has to take on one last job to free his brother — and himself — from their lives of crime.

Too bad that puts him back on Jack’s radar or, I should say, squarely on Jack’s radar, since Jack is nursing a (secret) grudge against Paul from years earlier. Ever since, he’s been obsessed with catching the one criminal who’s eluded his grasp. He wants revenge, he wants “respect,” he wants to win — “12 12 12” throws out a number of motivations for Jack early on that clearly don’t paint the full picture. They’re placeholder reasons until the show deems it time to dig into what’s really driving him to move to Zurich, hole up in a shitty police station, and wait for Paul to try to steal something.

Mackie, who’s reunited with his “Falcon and the Winter Soldier” director Kari Skogland, gives great determined face, and Dornan is the softest, sweetest guy on the FBI’s most-wanted list. Thankfully, co-creators Dudi Appleton and Jim Keeble don’t ask their lead characters to betray their core identities amid all the twists and turns, shading Jack as more of an antagonist (all-consumed and, thus, single-minded to a fault) and Paul as more of the protagonist. (He doesn’t want to steal, but now that he must, he’s going to do it the right way.) That helps keep our rooting interests in line, which goes a long way toward a satisfying emotional payoff, even when the momentum ebbs and flows with every flash-forward, -back, and -sideways.

With slick locations and clever-enough problem-solving, “12 12 12” should satisfy die-hard heist fans (but not “Die Hard’s” heist fans). It just takes a circuitous route to scratching that itch, and that’s almost as aggravating as not scratching it at all.

“12 12 12” premieres Friday, November 13 on Apple TV with two episodes. New episodes will be released weekly through the finale (Episode 8) on December 25.

#3432. Why Walter Koenig Held His Tongue To Keep His Star Trek II: The Wrath Of Khan Role

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

"Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan" gives Pavel Chekov (the late Walter Koenig) one of his meatier arcs in any of the "Star Trek" films. In his new assignment as first officer of the USS Reliant, Chekov and his captain, Terrell (Paul Winfield), scout planets as a testing site for the Genesis device. But what they think is planet Ceti Alpha VI is actually the barren Ceti Alpha V, where the Enterprise left Khan Noonien Singh (Ricardo Montalbán), the 20th century's most infamous genetically engineered warlord, and his followers at the end of the episode "Space Seed."

Chekov and Terrell are captured and brainwashed via Ceti eels implanted in their ears. Khan and his people thus seize the Reliant, and boom, we have our movie. The sequence on Ceti Alpha V is predicated on Khan and Chekov recognizing each other. When Chekov and Terrell come across Khan and co.'s makeshift home, Chekov recognizes the name "Botany Bay" (the name of the sleeper ship where the Enterprise found Khan in "Space Seed"). Once the pair are captured, Khan recognizes Chekov and proclaims "I never forget a face."

Chekov also speaks to and of Khan as if he witnessed the events of "Space Seed." Except, technically, he didn't. "Space Seed" was made in "Star Trek" Season 1, and Koenig/Chekov only joined the cast in Season 2. Ergo, he obviously never appeared in "Space Seed" and shared no screentime with Khan. Oops!

Over 40 years later, Trekkies still note the inconsistency and rationalize it. Koenig, for his part, has said he recognized the error when he read the script, but chose to stay silent to preserve Chekov's role. Considering how often "Star Trek" overlooked Chekov, it's hard to blame him.

"Wrath of Khan" writer Harve Bennett wasn't a "Star Trek" fan when he took the job. That worked for the best. "Wrath of Khan" is widely credited for revitalizing "Star Trek" and part of that is because Bennett and director Nicholas Meyer brought fresh eyes. To that end, they couldn't expect everyone who would go see "Wrath of Khan" had previously seen "Space Seed." So, the movie doesn't rely on the episode outside of its big picture story details, which are easily explained via some dialogue in Khan's first scene. (I saw "Wrath of Khan" before "Space Seed" as a kid, and I followed the former just fine.)

But Chekov knowing Khan is the kind of detail that evidently slipped by Bennett. Koenig, who was asked to read the script and give it a "Trekkie read," had a vested interest in not pointing out the mistake. As Koenig put it when interviewed in "The Fifty-Year Mission: The First 25 Years" by Edward Gross and Mark A. Altman: "I was faced with the ethical dilemma of mentioning it to Bennett or letting it go. I chose survival as opposed to ethics."

Chekov is the only member of the "Star Trek" main cast who shares physical screentime with Khan in the movie. (Khan and Kirk only ever talk via viewscreens and communicators.) It's also Khan's first appearance in the movie, as well as the scene from "Wrath of Khan" that I rewatch the most in isolation. Montalbán's performance, savoring every line, is just spectacular. I can see why Koenig would, as an actor, want the chance to be in a scene as strong as that one, and he holds his own balancing Chekov's courage and fear.

For Koenig's part, his cheeky theory to explain away this inconsistency was that Chekov once made Khan wait an uncomfortable amount of time to use the Enterprise's restroom. "Chekov was on the Enterprise, just offscreen" has become the go-to fanon answer. The novel "To Reign in Hell: The Exile of Khan Noonien Singh" by Greg Cox legitimizes that; Chekov is said to have led a failed effort to retake the Enterprise from Khan, and is part of the detachment that helps Khan and his people get settled on Ceti Alpha V.

Despite the continuity gap with "Space Seed," Chekov was the best pick among the main characters as the one captured by Khan. Amusingly, this is precisely because he's the most ancillary one. The Enterprise can function without him in a way it wouldn't without Spock (Leonard Nimoy) or Dr. McCoy (DeForest Kelley).

While Koenig evidently feared that they would swap Chekov's part out in the script, the only other main character who could work would be Uhura (Nichelle Nichols), which would add some icky subtext to Khan violating her body with the Ceti eels, or Sulu (George Takei). With Sulu, you run into the same problem because he wasn't in "Space Seed" either! While Sulu/Takei was part of the show in Season 1, he was absent for that particular episode. If it had been Sulu who landed on Ceti Alpha V with Terrell and met Khan, you might be getting forum posts highlighting that inconsistency today.

Walter Koenig may have created a small problem in "Wrath of Khan" by staying silent here, but he helped fix a much bigger one, too, by suggesting moving Spock's death to the end of the film.

#3431. 50-Episode Sci-Fi Masterpiece Boasts One Of The Greatest Performances In TV History

It is a no-brainer that a sci-fi show is only as good as the performances of its cast. A sci-fi show can boast everything from high production value to compelling conceptual foundations. However, if its ideas are not driven by grounded performances and rootable characters, it is almost always bound to fail.

Fortunately, one 50-episode sci-fi thriller perfectly understands this and delivers one of the greatest performances in TV history. Created by Graeme Manson and John Fawcette, Orphan Black has an incredibly compelling opening hook. It begins with a scene where a character, Sarah, witnesses the death of her own doppelgänger. This prompts her to assume her identity.

With what follows, Orphan Black turns into a harrowing exploration of identity as it unfolds a grand conspiracy involving human cloning. From a thematic and conceptual standpoint alone, Orphan Black is brilliantly written. The show is packed with enough twists and turns and narrative highs and lows to keep viewers glued to their screens.

However, the Canadian sci-fi show's true appeal lies in the phenomenal performance of its lead, Tatiana Maslany. Throughout the show's runtime, she plays multiple characters and ensures that each has a distinct identity. If it wasn't for her, the near-perfect sci-fi show probably would not have been half as successful.

Tatiana Maslany plays a total of 17 clones in Orphan Black. Instead of purely relying on their distinct physical appearances to highlight their differences, Maslany fully embraces their mannerisms and personalities. She immerses herself so deeply into every clone's identity that a viewer can take one look at even a still frame from the series to tell who she is playing.

For instance, when she plays Helena, everything from her demeanor to her expressions turn feral and predatory. Meanwhile, she seems more warm when she appears as Cosima. Alison is another memorable clone from the series because Maslany perfectly projects her clipped hand gestures. In some of the best story beats from the show, Maslany also plays meta clones.

Instead of portraying a specific cloned variant, she captures how one cloned character in Orphan Black is pretending to be another. In this feat of meta-acting, she intentionally allows some nervousness and hesitance to bleed in. This ensures that viewers know they are looking at an impersonator.

Every time actors play multiple characters in the same movie or show, it is hard not to notice overlaps in some baseline mannerisms.

Maslanay's performance, in contrast, is exceptional because almost every clone seems to have a completely distinct identity. As a viewer, it becomes hard not to routinely forget that you are watching the same actor play so many different roles. With every clone's story, Orphan Black also switches genres. Such wild swings in tone could have easily turned the series into a disjointed mess.

However, it is Tatiana Maslanay's performance that single-handedly holds the show's tonal shifts together. Orphan Black's story makes massive pivots where it is a suburban black comedy in some story beats while a sci-fi family drama in another. Each pivot feels like a compelling journey in the overarching story because Maslanay carries every character with ease.

This explains why Tatiana Maslanay even won a Primetime Emmy Award for her performance in Orphan Black and the show is still considered a timeless sci-fi masterpiece.

Orphan Black follows a streetwise hustler who becomes entangled in a complex conspiracy after witnessing the suicide of a woman who bears an uncanny resemblance to her. As she assumes the deceased's identity, she uncovers a secret that places her life in jeopardy.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3430. Apple Won't Make a Small Phone so This Company Is Stepping In

Big smartphones have long been the norm. It seems many, if not most, of us prefer our smartphones to be akin to tiny tablets. Even Apple's smallest iPhone isn't that small, with a 6.1-inch display. (Compare that to the 5.4-inch iPhone mini it used to sell.) But just because a lot of us like it that way doesn't mean all of us do.

Despite what companies like Apple would lead you to believe, there are plenty of people out there who want their smartphones to be smaller. For some, the iPhone mini was perfect, featuring a design that most could use comfortably with one hand. While the sales might not have been steady enough for Apple to continue producing the mini line, anecdotally, I know quite a few people who would happily keep using iPhones this small, if only Apple would make more of them. Perhaps you know people like this too; maybe you're one of them.

While the rumor mill does not suggest that Apple plans to make a new iPhone mini, that doesn't mean the dream of the tiny smartphone is dead. Enter "Enough Phone," a new device with a humble goal: to create a "small, modern smartphone that's enough."

Enough Phone really does seem small. The company says its upcoming device is 133mm by 64mm, and less than 12mm thick. That's the equivalent of 5.24 inches by 2.52 inches, and less than 0.47 inches thick. It's remarkably similar to the iPhone 13 mini, at 5.18 by 2.53 inches, and 0.3 inches thick. While the Enough Phone might be a tad larger overall, and perhaps noticeably thicker, it's still reminiscent of that "mini" footprint.

The Enough Phone's 5.3-inch display isn't particularly modern, however. While we don't know the display type, we do know that it has a resolution of 1520 x 720, which may look less sharp to anyone coming from the 2340 x 1080 resolution of the iPhone 13 mini. I'd wager that most people interested in a device like this aren't looking for an ultra-sharp OLED display anyway, but it's worth noting here.

As for the Enough Phone's other specs, the company says it plans to pack in a 2.4GHz MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip with 8GB of RAM, 128GB of built-in storage, though you can expand that with a microSD card (something you don't see on many smartphones these days). The current plan is to ship with a single 50MP Sony IMX766 rear camera, and a 32MP selfie cam, which would be amongst the highest-resolution front-facing cameras on any smartphone. It supports 5G, Wi-Fi 6, and eSIM, with the option to use a physical SIM as well.

Enough is also aiming to make its smartphone more repairable than the competition. While smartphone OEMs have made slight improvements to repairability in recent years, few phones are made to be opened up by the user, and their components replaced. While Enough Phone isn't fully modular, it is designed with easy-to-open screws, and comes with a fully replaceable 3,500 mAh battery. Combined with promised software support through 2032, Enough says this device "should last you into the next decade."

Now, all of these specs are targets, as the phone is currently in the prototype stage. Enough says that final details may change "slightly" during testing. I would at least hope that the dimensions, particularly the screen size, remain the same by launch. What will likely stay the same, however, are the ringtones: Enough says they hired composer Brian Squillance of LAANDS to produce the jingles for its phone, which is a neat touch.

Unfortunately for Apple fans, however, Enough Phone isn't an iPhone. That said, it doesn't have to be an Android phone, either. While you can buy the phone with Android 17 installed, you can also choose to run OdysseyOS, a minimalist "de-Googled" operating system made by SLEKE. Enough says OdysseyOS is meant for "intentional phone use," which might appeal to anyone looking for a phone that's "dumb" as well as small.

Of course, neither operating system is iOS. Unfortunately for Apple users, the only true iPhone options here are to continue using an old iPhone mini, which Apple does still support, or to opt for an iPhone 17e, the smallest iPhone the company currently makes. It's pretty easy to find a used and refurbished iPhone 13 mini for reasonable price; but while they can still run the latest version of iOS, you won't be able to take advantage of all of Apple's newest features. Plus, while there's no telling how long Apple plans to support the 13 line for, it won't support it forever—by iOS 28 or iOS 29, your phone might lose support entirely.

If the promise of a modern mini smartphone entices you, you can back the Enough Phone on Kickstarter today. While the company's $399 "Super Early Bird" reward is already sold out, as of this article, the "Early Bird" reward is still up. That reward costs $449, and includes a glass screen protector pre-installed, a protective case, a USB-C cable, a USB-C to 3.5mm headphone adapter, a hex screwdriver, and green "Founders' Edition" backplate screws. Enough says that the retail price for its phone will be $599 after the campaign, so you can save $150 by backing the phone today—if you're serious about small phones. The Enough Phone is slated for a May 2027 launch.

#3429. Stephen King Named This Alfred Hitchcock Thriller As One Of His Favorite Scary Movies

Back in 2017, IndieWire amassed a list of Stephen King's favorite scary movies based on the titles he had either previously recommended on social media or written about in his 1981 non-fiction book "Danse Macabre." Among the many, many films included were Ridley Scott's "Alien," Mario Bava's "Black Sunday," Brian De Palma's "Carrie" (itself based on King's own litany of feminine rage), and George A. Romero's "Dawn of the Dead."

Somewhat surprisingly, Alfred Hitchcock's 1972 serial killer "Frenzy" made the cut as well. "Frenzy" was Hitchcock's penultimate film and is famously the only one of Hitchcock's movies to receive an R rating in the United States. Indeed, one might be startled to see actual on-screen nudity in a film from The Master of Suspense. The murders in "Frenzy" are notably brutal, too, and the movie, quite shockingly, contains scenes of sexual assault. This was clearly an attempt by Hitchcock to push the envelope, and one can only speculate if he was drawn to the film's twisted serial killer mentality, the sweatiness of the overall picture, or its sheer amount of on-screen violence.

"Frenzy" tells the story of Richard Blaney (John Finch), a sad-sack and impoverished London-based former military man who is accused of sexually assaulting his ex-wife, Brenda (Barbara Leigh-Hunt), and using a necktie to strangle her to death. However, the necktie is connected to a string of other murders that have been committed all over the city, as the real killer is Richard's creepy friend Bob Rusk (Barry Foster).

As with so many other Alfred Hitchcock movies, the main character in "Frenzy" becomes a falsely accused man on the run (see also: "The Wrong Man," "Stage Fright," "The 39 Steps," "Young and Innocent," "North By Northwest," "Saboteur," "I Confess"), and he has to elude capture to clear his name. Along the way, Richard ends up finding an ally and lover in his former co-worker Babs (Anna Massey) ... although, with Rusk still engaged in his murderous shenanigans, that doesn't bode well for her.

Hitchcock films excel at making audiences unwittingly root for the bad guy (see "Dial M for Murder" and "Psycho" for two better-known examples), and "Frenzy" includes a sequence where Rusk has to retrieve a personal item of his from a victim whose body he has already disposed of. Because of this, viewers are forced to watch as he struggles with the tension of having to retrieve the incriminating evidence, and while we might not feel sympathy for Rusk, we do become involved in his plight. (It's one of the most noteworthy scenes in Hitchcock's filmography.) You can see, then, why Richard turns to Rusk for help at one point, not knowing that his friend is the murderer.

The final act of "Frenzy" gets a little involved and maybe spins a little too far off with its trials and prison sentences, but know that the ultimate conclusion is very satisfying. It's a tonally unique movie as well, feeling very loose and 1970s-y. And where many of Hitchcock's previous films felt mannered and polite despite involving murder and fetishes, "Frenzy" is comparatively casual, focusing more on Rusk's overcooked murderous mindset and the sexual element of his killing spree.

What many cineastes saw as the sexual subtext of Alfred Hitchcock's previous movies becomes text in "Frenzy." By the 1970s, the filmmaker could afford to be a little more frank. The murder scenes, more so than in any other Hitchcock movie, "Psycho" included, are brutal and unsettling. There's even one particularly memorable shot in "Frenzy" of one of Rusk's victims, freshly dead, with her eyes wide and her tongue lolling out, that will remain in your nightmares for quite some time. This is not the balletic, aesthetic, obfuscated violence of Hitchcock's earlier movies. This is disturbing.

Many critics responded very positively to "Frenzy" at the time. Roger Ebert gave the film four stars (out of four), writing that it was both a departure for Hitchcock and a return to form. As he put it:

"This is the kind of thriller Hitchcock was making in the 1940s, filled with macabre details, incongruous humor, and the desperation of a man convicted of a crime he didn't commit. The only 1970s details are the violence and the nudity (both approached with a certain grisly abandon that has us imagining 'Psycho' without the shower curtain). It's almost as if Hitchcock, at seventy-three, was consciously attempting to do once again what he did better than anyone else."

Ebert added that "Frenzy" possesses a nice macabre sense of humor, another feature Hitchcock's fans appreciate from the Master. Vincent Canby, writing for the New York Times, listed "Frenzy" as one of the 10 best films of its year, and it was a hit at the box office to boot. (There's a reason we here at /Film once listed it as one of Hitchcock's 20 best movies.) Clearly, Hitchcock hadn't lost his talent for snagging audiences.

#3428. In Shana Feste’s Films, Gender-Flipping Cinema’s ‘Tradition of Celebrating Damaged Men’ Is Its Own Reward

Shana Feste knows her filmography might be a bit tough to pin down. Some directors like to stick to a certain genre. Not Feste. Some only like to work with certain stars. Not Feste. Others enter a franchise and never look back. Not Feste.

But over the course of nearly two decades behind the camera, Feste has carved out a particular sweet spot, regardless of the genre or the cast or the wider world her stories fit inside: She likes complicated women. Not unlikable women, but messy women, contradictory women, women who get things done their own way. It’s a signature unto itself.

“My filmmaking, my history, people have not really known what to do with me. I’m making a comedy, I’m making a horror film, I’m making a genre thriller,” Feste told IndieWire during a recent interview. “But I do find that they’re all starting to build into each other, especially the trajectory from ‘Country Strong’ to ‘Run Sweetheart Run’ to ‘Heartland.’ I’ve always been drawn to women who don’t behave correctly. I’ve always been interested in women who don’t grieve correctly, who mother incorrectly, who love incorrectly. I just want women to have the freedom to behave in this contradictory, destructive, funny, selfish way and be given the same freedom that male characters are given.” Related Stories Box Office: ‘Club Kid’ Scores Best Limited Expansion of the Year as Younger Audiences Embrace Jordan Firstman’s Oscar Hopeful Box Office: ‘Ebenezer’ Opens to Modest $19 Million, Showing Johnny Depp Is Still a Draw for the Right Price

Another shared characteristic between Feste’s complicated women: They may be messy or unexpected, but they tend to get shit done. In her new film “Heartland,” getting shit done is at the center of the story, as the Nashville-set drama follows Jessica Chastain as Misty Jones, a former country-singing superstar who left the business after her designation as the, ahem, “cunt of country” became too much to bear. She’s thrust back into that world after her niece, rising star Charlie Heart (Carter Faith), goes missing. Misty, being Misty, takes it upon herself to get to the bottom of an increasingly dark and twisted mystery, no matter what it takes.

“I am a mom of three, 51, and I’m like, ‘Let’s write about some women who get shit done,’” she said. “I find a lot of those women exist. I’m living in the South now that I see those women every day and am inspired by them. We have this long-established cinematic tradition of celebrating damaged men. But when women behave similarly, they could be labeled as hysterical or dramatic or that word, unlikable. I want to prove that wrong.”

For the (complicated, messy, extremely capable) character of Misty, Feste said, she initially tapped into her longtime love of film noir. She always gravitated toward the Humphrey Bogart types, she said, but wondered what might happen if they gave those sorts of roles to women. That also fed into the dark underbelly of the Nashville scene that the film interrogates, a perfectly noir-ish idea.

“It could have been any city, but specifically this dark underbelly had to do with the music world,” Feste said. “Sadly, it was a common experience for a lot of artists that I spoke with. It was an experience that I’ve experienced in our industry, and it was all too relevant. When we were making the movie, a lot of conversation around Diddy was happening. He had just been arrested, and things were coming into light. We thought, oh wow, this is such a topical moment. And I’m like, it’s always topical, sadly. Whether we’re Epstein, Diddy, Weinstein, this is always going to be in the world, sadly.”

But Feste is also someone who loves this world and wants to celebrate what’s good and true about it. “Country Strong” was about making it — and maybe even making it again — even at great personal cost. “Heartland” just ratchets that sensibility up.

“I wanted to lean into the secrets and the dark corners and the underbelly, but I also will always celebrate the artistry and the storytelling of country music,” she said. “Misty says one line that really speaks so much to me about what the film is: ‘You don’t deserve country music.’ It takes a lot to deserve country music in my eyes. Country music is like the apex of storytelling. So to point out someone who doesn’t deserve country music, I mean, that’s a big insult for me.”

Feste started writing “Heartland” around four years ago, mostly because she was really missing the world of country music that framed her 2010 music drama “Country Strong.” “My father died about eight years ago, and I found myself listening to a lot of country music when he died,” she said. “In the years after he died, going back to the music that he loved, that he used to play for me in the car when we were driving on road trips, I realized that when you’re a writer, you don’t know quite why you write something until years later. And I realized, oh, I’m really missing my father.”

She was also eager to reteam with her “Country Strong” collaborators Jenno Topping and Randall Poster, two people who Feste said have believed in her the most over the course of her career. (Topping and Poster both produced “Heartland,” with Poster also serving as music supervisor, as he did on “Country Strong.”) “When I’m having my darkest days about, I don’t know, me and what I create and my career, knowing that they believe in me has always been such a huge lift,” Feste said. “So having them help me tell this story was just monumental. It was being with someone that you knew had your back the entire time.”

If “Heartland” sees Misty feeling ill at ease in the very spaces that used to celebrate her talent, Feste had the opposite experience. Six films into her directing career, she said “Heartland” let her approach her work in an entirely new way. And it felt good.

“What was really valuable with this experience is that I felt completely comfortable saying, ‘I don’t know,’ and I don’t know if I’ve ever felt that way,” she said. “Certainly not with my first few films, feeling like as a woman, I had to know every answer from every head of department immediately. It was only working with this group of filmmakers, Jenno and Randy and [production designer] Naomi [Shohan], some of my heads of production, that I knew that they saw my vulnerability not as a weakness, but as a strength. I was able to say, ‘I don’t know, what do you think?’ That’s where a very new form of collaboration happened that I haven’t experienced in my career, and with Jessica as well.”

Casting Chastain was an easy call for Feste. She wanted someone who could sing and who was admired in this space, but Chastain’s way of working and approach to on-set life gave Feste more to work with than she could have dreamed.

“I always want my films, especially when we’re shooting a movie that takes place in Nashville, to feel authentic, and I knew Jessica already had a huge buy-in from this audience. The South, they love her from ‘George & Tammy,’” Feste said. “And Jessica can sing, and that is another qualifier. Whenever I’m making any kind of movie with music, I want the actors to be able to sing their own material. But I think most of all, Jessica is one of the biggest champions of other women that I’ve ever met.”

It was freeing for Feste to say “I don’t know,” but Chastain also made it clear that she was there to support Feste’s vision and leadership.

“There were certain times on set where it would get a little loud or kind of disorderly, and people would be talking and having opinions, and no matter what, she’d be like, ‘Shana, sorry, I couldn’t hear you,’ and it was like this just gentle reminder, ‘This is who is leading the ship right now for me,’” the filmmaker recalled. “It was done in the classiest, most polite way.”

That approach turned the collaboration into more of a partnership. When Chastain had an idea, Feste was eager to listen. Even a decade ago, she said, that might not have been so easy for her.

“If I had been the director that I was 10 years ago, it would’ve scared me to death, because Jessica is not afraid to come into a scene and say, ‘OK, wait, that might not be serving us. Let’s throw that idea out of the window. What if we did this?,’” Feste said. “As a director, I’m planning, and every shot is in my head, and I’ve done the work, and I’ve done the homework, and I’m the A student. And to be able to relinquish control and admit when my idea wasn’t the best idea and she’s coming in with a stronger idea because she is Jessica Chastain? She has done the work. She has made this character so rich. This wasn’t a scary experience. It was actually going to elevate the scene and make it work even better.”

It was always the plan for Feste’s stars to also sing their songs to add to the film’s deeper authenticity. “When I’m watching movies that feature performing artists, and there’s so much hype, and they’re playing this celebrated musical performer, and then they come on, and we hear them sing and we’re like, have they been re-voiced? It’s just kind of mediocre? You just kind of lose your authenticity. You lose the ownership of the movie,” she said.

Casting Jennifer Nettles was something of a no-brainer for Feste, and so was actually directing the country superstar. “I didn’t know how to direct someone how to move on stage. That is something that’s not in my repertoire of directing. I can direct someone talking about their divorce in a bedroom, but how to command a stage and move your body? That is something that she learned over 20 years of experience being a superstar,” she said. “Most of the time I said, ‘Just speak to the audience like you are at the Opry, like you’ve done a thousand times. Make it your own.’ She did so much heavy lifting for me.”

So too did Carter Faith. In early discussions about the five characters in the film who are musical artists, Feste said she and Poster were constantly trying to figure out who they would sound like in the real world. Was Misty an Emmylou Harris? A Miranda Lambert? And who was young rising star Charlie Heart? Was she a Taylor Swift type? Poster had an easy answer: She sounds like this actual rising star, Carter Faith. And when it became clear that Faith was able to and interested in auditioning for the role? Serendipity.

“She was like a breath of fresh air,” Feste said. “I remember asking her, ‘Carter, what do you think you have in common with Charlie?’ And she said, ‘Well, we both have boy names.’ My heart exploded. It was the most non-Hollywood endearing response. Then I heard her story of how she was eating red beans and rice, crashing on couches, calling all of these places on Lower Broadway just to get an audition to be the performer at 10:00 AM on a Monday morning. She is someone who really moved to Nashville the day she graduated from high school to make it. She was Charlie. So much of her experience was exactly what the character was going through. So it was only the question of, are you brave enough to access all that trauma of how you got here? And she was absolutely, she said yes, and she trusted me, and it makes me emotional thinking about it because that’s an incredible trust to have.”

Faith also wrote the lyrics to the song that plays at the end of the film, which Feste sees as “dialogue that I could never write.” All the songs in the film and on its soundtrack, including the ones Feste simply imagined as titles first, like “Texas Land,” or that her stars like John Hawkes wrote or that Poster commissioned, add to the film’s incredible authentic feeling and sound. “Working with musical performances in film, it is so additive because it just takes the storytelling to another level. It’s beyond the dialogue. It’s beyond physical blocking. It tells story in this just purely emotional, raw, beautiful way,” she said.

Next up: In true Feste fashion, she’s working on or thinking about a variety of other projects next, including the next chapter of the “Dirty Diana” story, which she first cooked up during lockdown, a TV series about a Southern family, and her “dream project,” which is about Texas bank robbers. Mostly, she said, “I really want to continue working in this space. I want to continue telling stories about messy, complicated, vulnerable Southern women. I think that’s my bread and butter.”

#3427. I’m a Deals Writer, and These Are My Top 10 Tech Deals This Week

As Lifehacker's deals writer, I'm always looking for the best bargains on TVs, speakers, laptops, and other tech. Now that it's Friday, I've gathered together this week's sales highlights, all of which I've vetted using my favorite price-tracking tools to make sure they are actually good deals.

This week, you can already feel the early Black Friday deals heating up with price cuts on the M5 MacBook Air, Bose speakers and headphones, a Samsung OLED TV, and more.

The MacBook Air with the M5 chip comes in both 13-inch and 15-inch sizes, and if you're interested in either, it's a good time to buy: Amazon is selling both right now at a $200 discount. That brings the 13-inch MacBook Air to $1,099.99 (down from $1,299) and the 15-inch MacBook Air to $1,299 (originally $1,499), reaching their lowest prices since the June price hikes.

The WH-1000XM5 headphones were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6s. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (originally $399.99). These are still incredible headphones in 2026, and with a $200 discount, they are a steal.

Bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones are down to $199 from $359, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet. Weighing around 8.1 ounces, they’re among the lightest premium noise-canceling headphones, with generously padded earcups and a cushioned headband that spreads pressure without gripping too tightly. They’re also easy to pack for travel, as the earcups fold and swivel for storage in the included hard-shell carrying case.

The Bose SoundLink Plus hasn’t been on the market for long, but it’s already earned strong reviews—CNET labeled it “the Goldilocks of Bose Bluetooth speakers,” and it’s down to $179 (originally $269). This is a great opportunity to snatch a quality portable speaker with a big discount.

Amazon has cut the price of its latest Fire TV Stick 4K, dropping it to $24.99 from $59.99 and bringing it to its lowest price ever. At this price, it's an affordable way to bring 4K streaming to an older television or give a sluggish smart TV a performance upgrade.

The Sony WH-CH730N are $128 (originally $179), the lowest price they've ever been. They use the same Sony Connect app as the premium headphones; as a result, you get a 10-band slider on the EQ menu, a battery care feature that extends the longevity of your battery life, 50 hours of juice, ANC, Ambient Sound (transparency mode), Multipoint to connect to two devices at once, and Bluetooth 6.0.

I got the Roborock Qrevo CurvX because it seemed like the perfect robot vacuum for me, as I have a dog, a mix of different floor types, and a gym with a workout mat, and it excels at handling them all. Amazon currently has it for $749.99 (originally $1,499.99), a 50% discount, and the lowest price it has ever been.

Samsung’s HW-Q600F soundbar is down to $379.97 at Amazon from $499.99, a $110 discount that brings it to its lowest price ever. This 2025 model sits in the middle of Samsung’s Q-Series lineup and pairs a sleek, angular bar with a subwoofer in a 3.1.2 setup. Dolby Atmos also brings a modest sense of height, and effects track cleanly from left to right. You get a graphic equalizer and sound presets for adjusting the audio to your preferences through the included remote.

The Ultimate Ears Miniroll is down to $49.99 (originally $79.99), the second-lowest it has sold for so far. It’s a small, flat, puck-shaped Bluetooth speaker that weighs just over half a pound, with a removable rubber strap you can attach to a backpack, bike handlebar, or shower caddy. Despite its size, the Miniroll can get surprisingly loud—which PCMag confirms in its review—and at moderate volume, it has enough sound for a kitchen or backyard without sounding thin. As for its battery life, you get about 12 hours of playback before it needs a charge over USB-C, while its IP67 rating protects it from dust and a brief dunk in water.

If you're looking for a premium model, Samsung’s 65-inch S90H OLED TV is down to $1,397.99 from $2,697.99 at launch, saving you over $1,000. The sale price is easier to justify when you consider that this is a new 2026 model. If the 65-inch model does not suit your space, Samsung also sells the S90H in 42-, 48-, 55-, 77-, and 83-inch versions, and those sizes are discounted as well.

#3426. 5 Funniest 'Peanuts' Comics About Dogs

Starring Schroeder! (I kid, they’re all with Snoopy)

Broadly speaking, there are three types of Peanuts comics. There are the funny ones, the sweet ones, and ones that are both funny and sweet. (And, let’s be honest, there are a good number of boring ones too.) But, very generally speaking, those are the three types of good Peanuts comics: funny, sweet, and the ones that do both of those things.

I bring this up because my goal here is to find the five funniest Peanuts comics about dogs. Not like, just Peanuts comics “starring Snoopy,” even though all of them do, but comic strips that are actually about dogs and the nature of dogs in general, if that makes sense. So that means no Flying Ace or Joe Cool stuff. I love those, but I wanted to define this one pretty narrowly about “dogs” (which, I guess, is still pretty broad).

I also wanted to just go for the funny ones. These aren’t the sweet “go hug your dog” Peanuts comics, or even the sweet/funny ones that check all the boxes for Snoopy fans. I was determined to just find funny, dog-themed Peanuts comics which illustrate Charles Schulz’s impressive abilities as a joke-writer.

Dogs do live a pretty enviable life. They have no jobs, people bring them food for free, and simple pleasures like stick-throwing are entirely fulfilling. A lot of people wish life was that simple for them — I know I do. Here, Snoopy addresses those feelings of jealousy many humans have towards dogs and basically says “Yeah, being a dog is pretty great.”

From Jan. 6, 1952, this is the first-ever Sunday strip of Peanuts. The comic had begun in 1950, running six days a week with its regular, four-panel daily strips, but its growing popularity brought it to Sundays.

In these early ones, Snoopy didn't really have all of his more human-like personality traits that would become his signature. Instead, he was just a regular, adorable old dog, which is evidenced here when Snoopy does something that it’s hard to imagine him doing: biting Charlie Brown. It comes during a game of tag where a bunch of kids are running around, tagging each other. One of the kids tags Snoopy, then we see Charlie Brown shout “Ow!”

Then we see Charlie Brown with the back of his shorts missing, with an angry expression as Snoopy looks on innocently. Meanwhile, a kid named Patty — this is the original Patty, not Peppermint Patty — tells Charlie Brown, “Don’t get mad, Charlie Brown…. That’s just his way of tagging!”

What I love about this one is it seems like it could be about something deeper. Snoopy is experiencing some serious malaise, feeling like his life has no meaning at all. And because we all love Snoopy, it makes us all empathize with him and worry about him. Snoopy often acts like more of a human than a dog, and in this comic strip, he seems like he is a super-depressed human. And then, after multiple panels that make Snoopy look like he’s going through a mid-dog-years crisis, Charlie Brown arrives with a full bowl of food. All of a sudden, Snoopy snaps out of it and his life has meaning again. Snoopy may act like a man, but he’s all-dog.

I love how mad Snoopy is in this one. He’s such a happy dog that we rarely see him in a bad mood, which is why this one is so funny and feels like he’s being a real dog here. Dogs hate to see their food bowls empty, and it’s hilarious to see Snoopy play that very dog-like emotion.

Is this one too sweet? It is really funny, but I fear I’m breaking my own stupid rules here. I just couldn’t resist this one. I mean, it is about “dogs” and quite literally the “nature of dogs,” with Lucy talking about the reason for a distinctive dog behavior. Yet the sleepy Snoopy on top of Linus’ head is super cute. I guess it’s impossible to entirely separate the humor of Peanuts from its inherent sweetness.

#3425. If You Liked Colleen Hoover's Verity, Watch Dakota Johnson's Acclaimed 2025 Movie Next

If you liked seeing Dakota Johnson starring in a twisted psychosexual drama like "Verity," which is based on the novel by Colleen Hoover, you might want to check out the more adult romantic drama "Materialists," Celine Song's acidic essay on modern dating from 2025. /Film's Bill Bria said in his review of "Materialists" that it was structured like a typical rom-com, but more heartfelt, full of yearning and depth.

More than anything, though, "Materialists" deals with a deeply cynical approach to romance, just as the title would lead you to believe. It's about how modern matchmaking has become a painfully specialized industry because modern adults have become all too fixated on the superficial qualities — and the earning power — of their potential mates. Johnson plays a cold-hearted matchmaker-for-the-rich named Lucy who has trouble weaning her male clients off of the idea of dating younger women exclusively. The movie itself seems to wince whenever one of Lucy's clients says they desire a woman who is "fit"; those characters might as well be yelling "no fat chicks."

Over the course of the film, Lucy finds herself torn between two potential boyfriends who have both appeared — or reappeared — in her life. On the one hand, she can pursue Harry (Pedro Pascal), an unbearably handsome, unfathomably rich, and suitably tall man who ticks all the boxes on the average dating profile requirement list. On the other hand, she has reconnected with her ex-boyfriend John (Chris Evans), a struggling actor who was always disorganized and never wealthy, but who loved her deeply. Does Lucy choose a life of poverty undergirded by true love, or does she follow her more cutthroat, materialistic instincts, and pursue the wealthy man who can give her a life of luxury?

For long portions of "Materialists," Lucy's choice seems obvious. Harry may not have the same kind of passion as John, but he is definitely interested in Lucy, and he is happy to share his wealth. There is a coldness, however, to his well-moneyed lifestyle, and something vaguely transactional about his love affair. She also becomes startled when she learns a secret about Harry that we won't spoil here. She begins to question if her attraction to him is genuine, or if it just checks the right boxes on a typical dating profile.

As "Materialists" unspools, however, it begins to skew away from the acidic nature of its opening act and begins strolling toward a drama about romantic truthfulness. Lucy is also thrown for a loop when she unwittingly matches one of her long-single clients Sophie (Zoë Winters) with a man who sexually assaults Sophie. Lucy subsequently doubts her every romantic instinct, and a portion of "Materialists" becomes about Lucy trying to reach out to Sophie to make amends. Perhaps she can mitigate her bad romantic instincts by being a genuine friend to this woman.

The ultimate answer is perhaps a little treacly, but Lucy finds herself drawn back to John. The pair had previously broken up over his incapacity for amassing wealth and her frustrations with the boring everyday financial struggles they went through. Now, however, she is beginning to appreciate the nature of human connection, and John looks more and more romantically alluring.

Of course, one could argue that Dakota Johnson, in being torn between Chris Evans and Pedro Pascal, is hardly in an unenviable place. We should all be so lucky to have two devastatingly handsome movie stars equally eager to court us.

"Materialists" was a pretty big hit, making almost $108 million worldwide on a relatively small budget of only $20 million. When the movie hit streaming, "Materialists" became a hit for HBO Max. The film isn't terribly deep in its commentary on the foibles of modern romance and the shallowness therein, but it's at least about something, and it features multiple beautiful people alternately romancing one another. It also, according to our exclusive interview with writer/director Celine Song, was modeled on a film noir, giving the film an alluring, mysterious quality. All those elements put together seemingly were what drew people out in such numbers.

Critics largely liked "Materialists," as evidenced by its 77% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, based on 307 reviews. Angelica Jade Bastién, writing for Vulture, felt that the movie didn't delve deeply enough into its own thesis that modern romance is directly tied to capitalism. Indeed, she wrote that, in its last act, the film "pivots to a more conventional romantic narrative of the kind it had promised to upend, if not outright critique."

Stephanie Zacharek, writing for Time Magazine, was more generous, writing that Celine Song is speaking very much to the moment, analyzing what romance means in an ego-driven and money-driven world of Instagram and an easily reduced sense of personal value. "That's the world 'Materialists' takes place in," Zacharek writes, "and Song sees what's funny and what's terrible about it at once—even as she acknowledges that it's human to yearn for beautiful things, and for comfort. She's chosen the perfect actors for this enterprise."

If you want a romance that mixes acid with some thoughtfulness, check out "Materialists."
