I'm a big fan of the commuting bubble. What is it? Well, it's what I've lovingly called the place I go to when I commute on public transport. As soon as I put on my headphones or dig my earbuds out of my bag, I slip into my own little bubble to focus on work, read a book, or (more often than not) lock in on transport delays and timetables.

And some of my personal favorite earbuds — from CMF by Nothing, Sony and Bose — are on sale for Black Friday. This year, with prices across tech climbing higher and higher it's nice to see some deals on products I can truly recommend.

I use each pair of earbuds for a different instance, whether I need focus or awareness of what's going on around me. Hopefully, they'll be able to help you create a commute bubble of your very own come Monday morning.

The CMF Buds 2a are some of the finest budget earbuds you can buy, at just $29, and even cheaper for Black Friday. The sound quality is impressive and the customizable ANC makes them a winner for daily use. Minor drawbacks, like the plasticky feel and lack of in-ear detection, are typical at this price point, and the overall performance makes them an excellent yet affordable choice — for $19, you really can't go wrong.

My favorite kind of journey is one where I can block out the surrounding noise and focus. Whether it's finishing off some work or getting stuck into my latest book, decent ANC is essential.

With the early Black Friday sales, you don't need to break the bank because you can pick up the CMF by Nothing Buds 2a for just $19 on Amazon — that's less than grabbing lunch at my nearest restaurant!

These buds also have EQ customization in the app, so the sound quality can be altered to suit you. But yes, the best part is the ANC. It's shockingly good, and it blocked out all of the ambient sound around me.

The Bose Ultra Open Earbuds are stylish open-ear earbuds that don’t compromise on audio features. They're very comfortable to wear all day, whether I'm at my desk or in the gym.

When I'm in a situation where I don't know my exact route, or there are cancelations happening because of the weather (more often than not), I need to be totally aware of my surroundings. Open-earbuds are the answer.

For the past few months, I've been keeping the Bose Ultra Open Earbuds in my bag, and they come in handy more often than you'd think. Being able to listen to my music in excellent quality while also paying attention to chatter and announcements around me is incredibly useful.

Bose are at the higher end of the open-earbuds market, but the price point is worth it, especially during Black Friday sales for $40 off on Amazon.

The Sony WH-1000XM6 are the flagship noise-cancelling headphones everyone should have. The 40-hour battery life can take me through most of the week, and the lightweight design makes them comfortable to wear all day long.

This is the ultimate "please don't bother me" option — the Sony WH-1000XM6. These over-ear headphones are the perfect balance between blocking out your surroundings and staying aware.

The noise-cancelling on these cans is some of the best I've used, but you can also switch modes to have the ambient sound loud and clear in your ears. This means that when I'm on a flight, for example, I can tune out the cabin noise and welcome it back in just before landing so I don't miss any announcements.

Out of the three earbuds and headphones on sale, the Sonys are the ones I reach for the most in my collection as they come in handy more regularly, but one of the other options may suit you better.

If you have a DIY enthusiast on your list—or if you just want some new tools for your own projects—Black Friday sales are a good time to snag low prices on quality tools. If you know what to look for, you can get up to 65% off on trusted brands. Here are a few of the best deals out there right now.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set, or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you some money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. Here are a few of the best early Black Friday deals on cordless tool sets.

The Ryobi 6-tool 18-volt combo set is on sale for $199, 33% off its regular price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, a circular saw, a sawzall, an oscillating multi-tool, a work light, a 1.5-amp-hour battery, a 4-amp-hour battery, a charger, and a tool bag. The Ryobi 18-volt drill and driver set is on sale for $99, 34% off its usual price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, two 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a great starter set because it has the first two tools you need for a cordless kit and it comes with batteries so you can expand your set for cheaper as you develop your skills.

The Ryobi 4-tool, 4-volt project set is on sale for $99, 61% off its typical price at Home Depot. This set comes with a rotary tool, a project light, a glue pen, a mini drill, two rechargeable batteries, a charging cable, a set of starter rotary bits, and three glue sticks. This set is handy for DIY projects that require fine detail, like wood carving, craft projects, or framing pictures.

The DeWalt drill and driver combo set is on sale for $149, 38% off its regular price on Amazon. This set includes a drill, an impact driver, 2 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted brand for drills and drivers, and a good start for a cordless DIY tool set.

If you have a cordless tool set already and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something they can use, a single tool deal can be just the thing.

The DeWalt 20-volt compact drill/driver is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 45% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 20-volt, 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. It’s a good first tool for a set.

The Milwaukee 18-volt impact wrench is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 68% off its typical price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. This is a good tool for driving bolts through tough materials and for automotive projects.

The DeWalt 20-volt oscillating multi-tool is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 50% off its regular price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it's ready to use out of the box. #3402. After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

With Cannes entry “Bitter Christmas,” Oscar-winning Spanish auteur Pedro Almodóvar (“Talk to Her”) is back making movies in his native language. Since his debut “Pepi, Luci, Bom and Other Girls Like Mom” in 1980, Almodóvar has written singularly identifiable, heightened, rhythmic, and mellifluous Spanish dialogue.

While Tilda Swinton and Julianne Moore adeptly wrangled his translated English in Golden Lion-winner “The Room Next Door,” which deployed his usual bright Almodóvar colors and exacting mise-en-scène, the director did not enjoy dealing with the unions in New York. “In Spain everything is much more immediate, and also it is my language, it’s my culture,” he told me during the New York Film Festival. While he doesn’t rule out making another English-language movie, it would have to be small-scale. “I don’t find myself, anymore, capable of dealing with a production that is chaotic with a lot of people and a lot of characters.” Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

Now he’s back in Spain in self-referential, meta autofiction mode in full force. The results are exhilarating. “Bitter Christmas” offers a movie within a movie, as writer-director Raúl (Leonardo Sbaraglia) crafts a script that lifts some key story points from his friends’ experiences. Even though Almodóvar considers the movie one of his riskiest, it’s the filmmaker’s biggest hit in Spain since “Volver.”

Almodóvar considers “Bitter Christmas” to be “twins” with Oscar-nominated “Pain and Glory,” which starred his old favorite Antonio Banderas as his alter ego. “‘Pain and Glory’ is more about the physical pain, right?,” he said. “The character [Raul] has had a lot of surgeries, and his fear is about that the fact that he’s not going to be physically able to to handle another another film shoot. Whereas in this film I deal with a different pain, which is the pain of writer’s block, of the blank page, or writing something that doesn’t quite come together for you. The character of Aitana in the film says to Raul, ‘you know we are all losers, you have lost grace.’ And by grace it means inspiration, something that is equally painful to that writer-director as the physical pain was to the writer director in ‘Pain and Glory.'”

Mostly when Almodóvar sits down to write, he’s making things up. He’s gotten into trouble in the past for raiding his friends’ stories. “There is not any law that creates the limits of the autofiction,” he said. “There is no law that’s going to define the limits of what you can appropriate and what you can’t appropriate. But if I’m inspired by the life of someone who’s close to me, who’s going through a difficult time, as a writer, you are selfish, because what propels you is the idea, even if it means going against the relationship. I don’t feel comfortable the two or three times that I did it. This is the limit: not to hurt anyone. But it’s normal that writers are influenced by everything in life you see, you talk to with others, you read, you see movies. So it’s impossible to renounce the influence of the life of others.”

And he’s passionate about making movies. As Raúl says in the film, “This is all there is to my life.” But Almodóvar has never suffered writer’s block. “I inspire myself because this is the profession that I know better than anyone, than any other,” he said. “The only thing that separates me from this alter ego is that I never lived a creative crisis. The experience I have had is more scripts that have taken me a long time to find the solution and to get them to gel together. But I’ve always succeeded ultimately.”

And he only recently discovered panic attacks, which took him by surprise. “I hadn’t previously experienced panic attacks, but now I have,” he said. “At that moment I was unconscious, and it was something awful, awful.”

Needless to say Almodóvar spends most of his days sitting at his desk at the computer. (Hence his legendary bad back.) Mostly he enjoys writing but also feels the clock ticking. “You always feel like time is lacking, right?” he said. “Especially that moment when you get that idea that’s going to become the motor of your story, you feel like there’s no time to breathe, because you want to get it all down as fast as possible. They’re quite intense days as we’re trying to get this. And then once I’ve started the story, my process is to get up in the morning and start writing. Those are some of the most pleasurable days in my life because you know where you’re going. But also, I have to pay attention to everything, because in that moment that you are possessed by the idea, you experience everything in your life filtered through the sensibility of the story that you’re writing.”

Listening to music feeds his creative beast. While he was writing “Talk to Her,” he listened to Caetano Veloso’s “Cucurrucucú Paloma,” a song that he had heard thousands of times, “but then it was like an epiphany. I discovered the song, and you feel it in a different way.” And in “Bitter Christmas,” his two actresses in the movie-within-the-movie listen to “Weeping Woman” from the filmmaker’s longtime muse, Mexican chanteuse Chavela Vargas.

Finally, the filmmaker had fun making himself the bad guy. “This was a new structure for me,” he said. “What I liked about it was that I could talk about myself as a writer-director, but mostly I also enjoyed the part of becoming the villain in a sense of that story. But the spectator does have to pay a lot of attention because if they go to the bathroom for two minutes, they’re going to miss something and be lost.”

In one scene, the filmmaker offers a close-up of the cursor on the computer screen. “Even though the cursor itself is not a very cinematic thing to see,” he said, “it’s his call to creativity, right? It’s the thing that calls him and pulls him in to have to tell his story. So it’s autofiction.”

Going forward, Almodóvar has no plans to put himself at the center of another film. “I promise not to talk about me anymore,” he said. “I was interested since the beginning of my career about the origin of creation and the relation with reality. Inspiration and life together, like the two sides of a coin. This mysterious question that so fascinates me is about not just where does creativity come from, how does it come, when does it come, how does it manifest? I have reached the end of my exploration around this.”

Up next: He’s writing, he said. “This is almost the opposite of this one. The new one will be very different.”

A Sony Pictures Classic release, “Bitter Christmas” is now playing in theaters in New York and Los Angeles. It expands nationally on November 25.

#3401. Forget 'Game of Thrones,' These 10 Fantasy Shows Have Perfect Final Seasons

Game of Thrones is undeniably one of the biggest television and cultural phenomena of the 21stcCentury, and its legacy is likely to be remembered for generations to come. However, the final season was rather divisive. Some fans defend it, while many others have dragged it through the mud, criticizing it for being rushed, nonsensical, and deeply unsatisfying.

It's a thing that happens sometimes: some shows just don't end on a high note, especially in the fantasy genre. On the other hand, there are plenty of fantasy shows out there that do have excellent finales, which is pretty widely agreed on. These finales didn't sow division amongst the fanbase; they satisfied long-time viewers and did everything they were supposed to.

Like it or not, franchise creator George Lucas says that Star Wars is more in line with fantasy than with sci-fi. Star Wars: The Clone Wars was the first animated TV show to be produced within the current canon, and it lasted seven seasons and 12 whole years. Set between the second and third prequel films, the saga follows various Jedi knights, Sith lords, bounty hunters, politicians, and clone troopers across engagements in the galaxy as the Republic faces off against the Separatists.

The sixth season aired much earlier than the seventh, due to Disney acquiring the brand around 2014. However, Disney still made the effort to release the final season during the height of the COVID pandemic, which is exactly what fans needed. The final season was amazing, too, featuring a climactic confrontation and wrapping everything up in a nice little bow, providing a smooth segue into the third film. This final season is one of the finest efforts Disney's Star Wars has undertaken.

The Dragon Prince is an animated series set on the magical continent of Xadia. The land has been divided in half following a catastrophic war, with humans segregated to the West and the Elves to the East. Dividing the two is a massive river of magma, overseen by the king of dragons. However, humans assassinate the dragon king, along with his egg, using dark magic, throwing both realms into chaos. In the West, two human princes team up with an elf when they discover that the dragon king's egg was actually not destroyed at all, which makes them embark on a quest to take it to the elves and remaining dragons.

The animation on this one is absolutely gorgeous and jam-packed with vibrant colours and detailed environments. The Dragon Prince also has a fascinating world, a simple but effective magic system, a grand sense of adventure, and some highly emotional moments. The seventh season wrapped everything up perfectly and proved that the showrunners never lost their mojo throughout its run, not even for a second.

His Dark Materials is the second attempt at adapting the novel trilogy by Philip Pullman, following a disastrous movie effort in 2008, which halted all chances of a sequel. This modern HBO effort was much better and was far more faithful to the book. Playing into themes of the multiverse, magic, and mythological creatures that impressed long-time fans of the original work.

The plot concerns a young girl living in an alternate version of England, who is the key to undermining and dismantling a shadowy corporation that runs much of the known world. She is accompanied by her dæmon, a small shape-shifting creature who serves as a sort of animal companion for her. His Dark Materials is clearly crafted with love, as the showrunners hid a ton of Easter eggs that only book readers will pick up on. The final season was not a cancellation, but rather the point that there was no more source material left to cover: all three books had been adapted. This means its conclusion is well-rounded and complete, as well as utterly amazing.

Shadow and Bone is based on the novels by Leigh Bardugo, which have a sizable fanbase. Unfortunately, it wasn't sizable enough to sustain the multi-million-dollar budget, resulting in the show's cancellation just two seasons in, ending on a cliffhanger, no less. This cancellation was not received well by fans, who actually adored it for how it embodied the atmosphere and humour of the original novels.

Rather than being a Medieval-themed fantasy, which the genre tends to favour, it went a little more steampunk, feeling more like Victorian England, instead. This ensured the show had a distinct identity separate from other fantasy TV shows. It's full of witty writing, heartfelt moments, and a shockingly detailed world for what was originally a YA series. The second and final season cranked things up to 11, doing everything just right, even if it didn't attract the numbers it needed.

Avatar: The Last Airbender is a classic Nicktoon that completely threw out the typical Nickelodeon formula. Instead of being a comedy with zero continuity, it was a distinct, beginning-to-end adventure, although it definitely had its comedic moments. As many know by now, the story is about four nations, each representing the elements of air, fire, earth, and water, which are in turmoil following a widespread invasion from the Fire Nation.

It is prophesied that an Avatar will rise, learn to "bend" all the elements, and bring harmony to the land. With an aesthetic inspired by Japanese anime and Medieval East Asia, the series was acclaimed for its profound moral wisdom, light-hearted humour, and action-packed antics. This show had everything going for it, including an explosive finale that never gets old, no matter how many years have gone by.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

Arcane is an animated series based on the popular MOBA video game League of Legends. The universe of the game has always blended elements of sci-fi, fantasy, and steampunk, and the show tends to follow in its footsteps. Ordinarily, video game adaptations are seen as shameless cash grabs, though Arcane was quite the opposite. It was actually created by some of the game developers and was crafted with such care that it even won multiple Emmys.

Arcane is only two seasons long, but it still became a major television event, with its final season becoming a highly anticipated entry in Netflix's library. Don't be fooled by the two seasons thing, though--it didn't get cancelled, and it was willingly brought to a proper close by the showrunners. This meant the final season wasn't rushed, and was crafted just as carefully as the first, making for an action-packed adventure that was surprisingly moving.

What We Do in the Shadows is a series created by Taika Waititi, based on his 2014 movie of the same name. Filmed in a mockumentary style, the idea is simple: what if a bunch of classic Gothic European vampires were abruptly thrust into 21st Century New York City? The result is every bit as absurd and horrifying as you could possibly imagine.

Concluding after six whole seasons, the horror/fantasy/comedy reached a proper conclusion that left very few, if any, loose ends. As it ended, it retained much of the same flair and quirky humour that made fans fall in love with it in the first place, proving that its final season could be just as good, if not better than its first.

The Twilight Zone is one of the most revolutionary television series ever made. Created by Rod Serling, this anthology series describes itself as featuring ordinary people in extraordinary circumstances. It tends to blur the line between genres, featuring episodes that stray into sci-fi, fantasy, and horror. Some are about aliens or robots, while some feature ghosts or demonic entities. Each episode has its own unique concept, cast, plot twist, and self-contained storyline, so no two episodes are alike.

After five seasons, the show came to an end, yet it felt like it could have gone on forever. Whether the writers were running out of ideas or not, The Twilight Zone maintained its momentum throughout its five-year run, never once dipping in quality or producing anything short of perfection. As such, the final season for this show is just as brilliant as the rest of it.

Kingdom is a South Korean Netflix series based on a webtoon-turned-graphic novel. Set at the end of the Middle Ages, the show features the historic kingdom of Joseon as it is plunged into chaos. This is due to the tyrannical Haewon Cho Clan making a violent bid for the throne by using a mythical resurrection plant, unleashing a zombie horde in the process. Now, the current royalty has to fight with their competitors on top of an army of the undead.

Kingdom received two full seasons plus one feature-length special episode before being soft-cancelled. Even though it's doubtful it will ever come back at this point (which is made even more infuriating by the fact that it ended on a cliffhanger), that doesn't change the fact that each and every episode is flawless. This fantasy/horror is absolutely singular in atmosphere, and brought a whole bunch of interesting concepts to the table. The final season is even better than the first, and is pretty much perfect in every sense of the word.

Based on the novel series by the late Robert Jordan, The Wheel of Time was unceremoniously cancelled right as it hit its stride. The first season was average, the second was good, but not great, and the third was absolutely stellar. This is probably why its abrupt cancellation prompted a massive online fan campaign to try and save it, which is a response that was quite unexpected.

Story-wise, the show is about a chosen one named the Dragon Reborn who is destined to either save the world or destroy it. The show had its own distinct identity, bringing Jordan's fascinating world to life in a way that nobody had seen before, and absolutely nailed the casting. It had such a unique vibe too, one that is completely unmatched by other fantasy shows. It's honestly such a shame that The Wheel of Time never got to see a proper conclusion, but at least its third and final season ensures it went out on a high note.

#3400. Vision's Entire Family Tree Across All Marvel Lore

Without a doubt, the Vision has one of the most complex and strange family trees in all of Marvel Comics lore. Not only does the synthezoid have one family born of magic and one of science, Marvel Comicsbut he also has an impressively unique array of "siblings" as well.

Going beyond the normal rules and limitations of typical organic biology, the Vision has a father who's an evil genocidal robot, a grandfather who accidentally created that robot, two wives with very different origins and backgrounds, and so many more siblings, children, and more "family" members (artificial, magical, and otherwise).

In honor of the MCU's recently concluded VisionQuest series, here is Vision's entire family tree in the comics explained, and how each member relates to the heroic synthezoid.

It all starts with Hank Pym, aka Ant-Man, aka Giant Man, aka Yellowjacket. In the comics, Pym was the creator of the artificial intelligence known as Ultron (not Tony Stark and Bruce Banner like in the MCU). Ultron was formed from Hank Pym's own brain patterns. However, when Ultron went rogue and became a genocidal robot hell-bent on humanity's extinction, one of his most classic schemes involved Vision's creation. As a result, Hank Pym has long been considered Vision's "grandfather" in terms of the lineage in Marvel Comics.

Janet van Dyne, The Wasp, is connected to Vision via her marriage to Hank Pym, making her Vision's grandmother of sorts. This is largely due to Ultron viewing Janet as his own mother. However, that does make Ultron's creation of his robotic wife Jocasta even stranger, seeing as how he used Janet's brain patterns to create his artificial soulmate (though it does help explain Jocasta's name).

Ultron is Vision's creator and the closest thing he has to a father. After rebelling against Hank Pym, Ultron chose to build Vision, a powerful new weapon to use against the Avengers, as seen in 1968's Avengers #57. However, just as Ultron rebelled against his father, Vision also rebelled and joined the Avengers against Ultron, eventually joining Earth's Mightiest Heroes long-term along with other superhero teams over the years.​​​​​​​

Dr. Phineas Horton is another important figure as it relates to Vision's origins and creation, despite not technically being the person who created him. Instead, Horton was the scientist responsible for building the original Synthetic Man, otherwise known as the original Human Torch or Jim Hammond. It was because of Horton's early work that Vision's construction was possible. Likewise, Ultron used spare parts and the template used to create Jim when creating Vision.

Technically, Jim Hammond's Human Torch is the closest thing Vision has to a physical twin or brother. Originally, it was believed that Ultron repurposed Jim's dormant android body to create Vision, which would have made Vision a reincarnation of sorts. However, it was later retconned that Ultron merely used the body template and spare parts from Horon to create Vision, making the synthezoid and his predecessor separate beings who eventually met one another and fought side by side on the West Coast Avengers for a time.​​​​​​​

When creating the Vision, Ultron used the brain patterns of Simon Williams, aka Wonder Man, meaning much of Vision's personality and emotions were inspired by Williams, making the two of them brothers of sorts (and have often referred to each other as such). However, their relationship has at times been complicated, seeing as how Simon also developed the same feelings for Wanda Maximoff's Scarlet Witch, who would become Vision's first wife.​​​​​​​

Victor Mancha is another artificial child of Ultron, which technically makes him Vision's younger brother. Having debuted in the beloved Runaways series, Victor is part human and part machine as a unique cyborg. Like Vision, he rejected Ultron's dark plans for him and became a hero instead, and was largely inspired by Vision himself. However, things got messy after Victor accidentally killed Vision's son, Vin, which in turn led to Vision's second wife, Virginia, murdering Victor (though Victor was eventually brought back to life).​​​​​​​

Like Vision, Jocasta was created by Ultron, which, from one perspective, would make her his sister. However, she was also designed to be Ultron's robotic bride, meaning she can also be considered Vision's stepmother. To make things even more complicated, Jocasta was based on the brain patterns of Janet van Dyne (Vision's "grandmother). However Marvel fans choose to view her familial connection to Vision, she too rejected Ultron and became a hero just like her brother/stepson/grandson.

Alkhema was Ultron's second attempt at creating a robotic companion after Jocasta. Built using the brain patterns of Bobbi Morse aka Mockingbird. While Ultron intended for her to be more obedient, she too became more obedient, though not so fully that Alkhema became a hero like many of Ultron's other created family members.

#3398. ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List

With the end of ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026, the world’s premier annual celebration of cinematography has come to a close. Poland’s largest film festival prides itself on shining the spotlight on directors of photography, saving each film‘s final introduction and the biggest round of applause for the artist who shaped its images. Post-screening Q&As are filled with discussions of lenses, aspect ratios, and shutter speeds as the artists gleefully get technical about the choices that give each film its distinct look.

Inevitably, the festival’s awards focus on cinematography as well. The top prize from the Main Competition is the Golden Frog, which is presented by the jury to the cinematographer of the winning film. The competition was filled with major films that played Cannes, Venice, and Toronto and have Best Cinematography Oscar glory in their sights. Other awards announced throughout the festival honored cinematography work in TV, documentaries, music videos, and short films. The festival also included the FilmLight Colour Awards, led by jury president Sean Price Williams, which highlighted achievements in color grading. Related Stories After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

This year’s Main Competition Golden Frog went to “Fatherland,” Paweł Pawlikowski’s stunning black-and-white portrait of Thomas Mann’s tour of postwar Europe. The award went to cinematographer Łukasz Żal, while Pawlikowski received a special mention for directing. The Golden Frog for Documentary Features was “To Hold a Mountain.”

The Main Competition was headed by Joe Walker, a frequent Denis Villeneuve and Steve McQueen collaborator who edited all three “Dune” movies, “Arrival,” “Sicario,” and “12 Years a Slave.”

The complete list of award winners from ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 can be found below.

Silver Frog Special Mention for Director: May El-Toukhy

Bronze Frog Special Mention for Director: Andrey Zvyagintsev

Golden Frog Special Mention for Directors: Eliza Godlewska and Alan Ruczyński

Golden Frog for Best Director’s Debut: Kaifeng Zhong

Golden Frog for Best Cinematographer’s Debut: Eira Wyn Jones

Golden Frog for Best Documentary Feature: Eva Kraljević

Golden Frog for Best Documentary Short: Maxim Arbugaev and Vladimir Egorov

Golden Frog for Best TV Episode: Maciej Sobieraj

Golden Frog Special Mention for Director: Jan Holoubek

Garmin’s top adventure watches have different strengths

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Fenix 9 Pro is Garmin's flagship watch and offers a more attractive design than the Enduro 4, along with extra features and more choice in the size and display you get.

The Garmin Enduro 4 is cheaper and lighter than the Fenix 9 Pro, and offers better battery life too.

Buying one of the best Garmin watches brings with it some guarantees with regard to the features you can expect, especially at the higher end of the brand’s line-up, where the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro and Garmin Enduro 4 both sit.

These watches offer stellar sports tracking and training analysis, along with the best navigation tools you’ll find on a smartwatch thanks to their offline routable maps. They are also equally accurate with GPS and heart rate, in my experience, and run the same software.

However, after testing the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro and Enduro 4 extensively, there are certainly some key differences between the two in other areas, most notably design and battery life.

If you want more details on either watch, check out my Garmin Fenix 9 Pro review or Garmin Enduro 4 review, but read on for a summary of the differences between them I noticed when testing them individually and at the same time.

The biggest difference between the two watches is price, since the Garmin Enduro 4 costs much less than the Fenix 9 Pro.

You’ll pay $899 for the Enduro 4 right now, while the cheapest Fenix 9 Pro model is $1,099, whether you choose the AMOLED version or the Fenix 9 Pro Solar with a memory-in-pixel (MIP) display like the Enduro.

The key thing that the Fenix 9 Pro offers with its design is choice. It comes in three sizes — 43mm, 47mm and 51mm — and you can pick between an AMOLED or MIP display, and even choose between colors for the bezel and sensor guard.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

In contrast, the Enduro 4 comes in one style and size. It’s a 51mm watch with a MIP display, and it only uses titanium for its bezel, with a mostly plastic case, whereas the Fenix 9 Pro has a full titanium case.

This gives the Fenix 9 Pro a more elegant look, but it also makes it considerably heavier than the Enduro 4. I tested a 51mm Fenix 9 Pro AMOLED, and both it and the Enduro 4 are large watches, but the Enduro 4 counters that a little by being so light.

When it comes to the display, picking between AMOLED and MIP will come down to personal preferences.

I find AMOLED brighter and clearer in almost all conditions, and just as good as MIP in bright sunlight these days, and I prefer using an AMOLED watch in general, but MIP uses less power and is less obvious on the wrist, and the Enduro 4’s display was still clear enough to see at all times.

Both watches have sapphire crystal screens and built-in flashlights, but you get an extra green mode on the Fenix 9 Pro’s flashlight.

You also get a diveproof watch with the Fenix 9 Pro, which can be used to depths of 40m. The Enduro 4 has a high waterproof rating of 10ATM and is fine for swimming, but isn’t a diving watch.

Another addition on the Fenix line is a mic and speaker, which can be used to take voice notes and give voice commands to the watch.

One advantage of the Enduro 4 is that it ships with Garmin's fabric ComfortFit band as standard, which I much prefer to the silicone band on the Fenix 9 Pro. You can buy the ComfortFit band separately, but it will cost $59.

The design differences speak to the approach behind the two watches. The Enduro 4 is built to be simpler and lighter, which helps it to be more affordable, but the Fenix 9 Pro is the all-singing, all-dancing option with a variety of models to pick between.

The two watches share very similar sports tracking and training analysis features, and both have proved to be similarly accurate throughout my testing.

There’s only one difference worth flagging in this area, which is that the Fenix 9 Pro is a diveproof watch and has Garmin’s scuba, apnea and snorkel sports modes.

One of the biggest features you get on the Fenix 9 Pro (InReach model) that isn’t available on the Enduro 4 is LTE and satellite connectivity.

This feature requires a subscription but allows you to stay in contact with the world when you’re off the grid or phone-free, through messaging and the ability to send SOS alerts.

Otherwise, both watches share the usual Garmin smart features. They can store music and link to streaming services, make NFC payments through Garmin Pay, and have access to the Connect IQ app store.

Along with being cheaper and lighter, the main advantage of the Enduro 4 is its incredible battery life.

Whatever Fenix 9 Pro you opt for, including the Solar MIP watch, the Enduro 4 will outlast it in both watch and GPS modes, partly because it has a bigger solar ring than the Fenix 9 Pro Solar.

I've compared the 51mm models of the Fenix 9 Pro to the Enduro 4 below. Note that to get the full solar battery life listed, you need to be out and about in sunny conditions for three hours a day on average.

In my use, the Enduro 4 lasted me 16 days on its first charge and is tracking for 17-18 on its second charge, whereas the 51mm Fenix 9 Pro AMOLED lasts me 10-11 days with the screen set to always-on.

This was during the British winter too, when I gave the Enduro 4 almost nothing in terms of a solar charging boost, so you can expect the gap to be wider in sunnier climates.

13.3mm (43mm),13.8mm (47mm), 15.8mm (51mm)

10 days (43 mm), 18 days (47mm), 31 days (51mm) (raise to wake)

18 hours (43mm), 32 hours (47mm), 56 hours (51mm)

The Garmin Fenix 9 Pro line-up offers more features and choice than the Enduro 4, and I prefer the all-titanium design of the Fenix and its brighter AMOLED display.

However, the Enduro 4’s relative simplicity will appeal to many people, as will its lower price, longer battery life, and lighter design.

If you’ve been eyeing the Fenix 9 Pro Solar in particular and don’t really need the connectivity features on the watch, then I think the Enduro 4 is a better value buy. Or even the Garmin Enduro 3, for that matter, since it has a similar design and feature set to the latest model.

#3396. Update Your iPhone to Prevent People From Seeing iMessages They Shouldn't

Has this ever happened to you? You add someone new to an iMessage group chat, and wonder, "Huh, can they see any of the messages from before they were added?" The answer to that question is supposed to be "no." By design, new iMessage group chat members are only privy to texts that arrive after they were added. When they join, it's essentially a blank slate, as if you just created the group for the first time. At least, that's how it's intended to work.

As it turns out, there's a bug with iMessage that may allow new group chat members to see texts from before they were added to the chat. That's a problem, and not just for the iPhone users out there talking smack about people before inviting them to join the group chat. It means iMessage, and Apple's platforms in general, aren't working like they're supposed to be. You don't have to be talking behind people's backs to not want new members seeing existing chats. Maybe you're planning a surprise party for someone, and add them to the group once everyone's in on the plan; maybe the texts in the chat aren't relevant to the current group, and the person joining simply does not need to access them.

That's not all: There exists another security flaw that could allow remote hackers to join an iMessage group and receive new messages. You might add a new user to a group chat and inadvertently invite them to read all existing messages, while at the same time being attacked by a bad actor who can then intercept all future messages. Not good.

Luckily, there's currently a fix for these problems. Apple patched (and revealed) the bugs, along with seven other security flaws, with a series of software updates on Monday for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro. Not all of the updates include patches for these two iMessage flaws—specifically, some of the updates for older Apple devices. But the rest, including iOS 27.2.1, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, macOS 15.8.3, watchOS 27.2.1, and visionOS 27.2.1, include the iMessage patches.

Each update includes its own list of patches, but, for this article, I'll take a look at the nine patches in iOS 27.2.1. You'll find the two iMessage bugs, plus seven other patches, in the list below:

AirPlay: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113968: Apple

App Intents: Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113963: László Várady

Bluetooth: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory. Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management. CVE-2026-113970: Apple

brotli: Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption. Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation. CVE-2026-111497

CoreUtils: Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction. Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks. CVE-2026-113965: Apple

CoreUtils: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation. CVE-2026-113961: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined. Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-113960: an anonymous researcher

Rapportd: Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113969: Apple

For a full accounting of the patches included in the other security updates, check out Apple's official security releases site.

To install Apple's latest security updates, you'll simply need to update your device as you usually do. On iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro, head to Settings > General > Software Update; on Mac, go to System Settings > General > Software Update. Here, follow the on-screen instructions to download and install the latest version of your device's software.

#3395. Box Office: ‘Ebenezer’ Opens to Modest $19 Million, Showing Johnny Depp Is Still a Draw for the Right Price

If Johnny Depp was hoping that “Ebenezer” would mark a glorious return to mainstream movies, he may need to hold out for another vehicle. The Christmas fable, released long before Thanksgiving, let alone the holidays, topped the box office this weekend with $19 million domestically and $42 million globally, a solid but unremarkable debut. It shows that enough moviegoers are able to look past the scandals that led Hollywood to remove Depp from their call sheets for the better part of a decade, but also exposed the limitations of his popular appeal.

The fact is that Depp was always something of a dicey commercial proposition. Put him in a “Pirates of the Caribbean” movie and you were guaranteed to earn $1 billion even if the script sucked and the plot seemed designed at the end of a wine bottle. Team him with Tim Burton, as he was quite successfully with “Sweeney Todd” ($153 million gross, $50 million budget), “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory” ($475.8 million gross, $150 million budget), and “Alice in Wonderland” ($1 billion gross, $200 million budget), and you were likely to have a big hit. Well, unless they were looking to reboot “Dark Shadows.” Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

But the rest of Depp’s track record was spotty. “Public Enemies” ($214.1 million gross, $100 million budget) and “Black Mass” ($100 million gross, $53 million budget) did well considering they were R-rated adult dramas, but struggled to break even because they cost too much to make and Depp commanded his full $20 million salary. Then there were the costly bombs, a litany of duds that includes “Mortdecai” ($47.3 million gross, $60 million budget), “The Lone Ranger” ($260.5 million gross, $250 million budget), “Transcendence” ($103 million gross, $150 million budget), and “Alice Through the Looking Glass” ($300 million gross, $170 million budget), the latter a return to Wonderland sans Burton. Many of these seemed like paycheck gigs rather than an attempt to burnish Depp’s star power. There was a private island to pay for and a pirate-themed wine cave to keep stocked on Depp’s sprawling French estate. But the promise of another Jack Sparrow adventure meant that Hollywood was able to look the other way, confident that there was more plunder to be found by allowing the actor to follow his idiosyncratic muse.

Depp could have kept going like this, but his messy personal life interceded. Depp’s reputation took a hit in 2020 when he became embroiled in a costly, two-continent legal battle against ex-wife Amber Heard, in which he was accused of domestic abuse. He denied the allegations, and later lost a U.K. libel suit against The Sun, when the court found an article calling Depp a “wife beater” was “substantially true.” Depp would go on to defamation trial against Heard in the U.S., after she wrote an op-ed in the Washington Post, calling herself a domestic abuse survivor. By that time, he’d been fired from the “Fantastic Beasts” franchise (it would be canceled after a non-Depp-led installment bombed), and was consigned to appearing in straight-to-streaming schlock or barely seen indies. But it wasn’t just the reputational damage that made major studios skittish about Depp. They had grown tired of his antics. There were reports he would show up late and unprepared, even as his salary demands and requests for perks escalated. That’s fine when your movies are making lots of money, it’s less charming when they are losing it.

So a lot is riding on “Ebenezer.” Depp looked a little uneasy on red carpets promoting the movie and Paramount, which is backing the film, wisely kept him from doing profiles with harder-hitting journalists who might ask him a probing question. He also cut his salary, reportedly receiving a $5 million paycheck to play one of his dream roles — Ebenezer Scrooge, and with it a chance to wear fright makeup and talk in a weird voice. But unlike most of Depp’s recent films, “Ebenezer” is poised to be a modest financial success. The film skewed older, with 59% of its domestic audience over the age of 30, and was slightly more female, as only 48% of ticket buyers were men. Paramount said it over-indexed in the South. One warning sign is that family crowds didn’t turn out in force for the PG-13 movie, comprising just 9% of opening weekend crowds.

However, the $38 million budget is low enough that if the film continues to draw crowds through the holidays and performs well overseas, where it has earned $23 million, it will turn a profit. But that points to a new reality — Depp is a sound bet, for the right price. Maybe that was a lesson that studios should have taken long ago. Depp’s taste is rococo, but Hollywood kept treating every one of his outings like potential blockbusters when a little more caution was warranted.

Next up for Depp is “Day Drinker,” an action thriller that seems to play into the star’s libertine image. Lionsgate will release the film in March. Will it be the vehicle that puts the 63-year-old Depp back on top, or will it, like “Ebenezer,” confirm that there’s still a smaller, but committed audience for his antics? Budget accordingly.

#3394. Stephen King’s 16-Episode Supernatural Series Rewrites The Rules Of His Greatest Sci-Fi Movie

An ongoing Stephen King series, The Institute, has cleverly re-written the rules that define the author's 44-year-old movie. Based on Stephen King's book of the same name, The Institute premiered on MGM+ in 2025. While it did not achieve the same level of success as HBO's It: Welcome to Derry, it easily ranks among some of the better Stephen King TV shows.

In season 1, The Institute was primarily criticized for being too derivative. It came off as another Stranger Things rip-off instead of etching its own identity. The Institute season 2, however, is gradually turning out to be a fascinating expansion of Stephen King's original book. With each episode, it is not only expanding its source material's lore but also dabbling with many unique high-concept ideas.

After two episodes, The Institute season 2 is primarily driven by the concept of precognition, which is the ability to see the future. Interestingly, The Institute is not the first Stephen King adaptation that centers on precognition. 1983's adaptation of The Dead Zone, too, was driven by the same concept. In The Institute, however, the rules of precognition are significantly different.

In The Dead Zone, Christopher Walken's Johnny Smith does not get random flashes of the near future. He can also not willingly look ahead in time and determine what lies ahead. He has to physically touch a person or an object connected to them to be able to see what the future holds for them. The Institute's Luke, on the other hand, either gets waking flashes of the future or he dreams about them.

The veteran precog characters in The Institute are also able to willingly look far ahead into the future. Luke, too, will eventually have more control over his powers. Johnny Smith's power in The Dead Zone is also portrayed as a random fluke, where a car accident and a five-year coma triggers his power. He is not born with it.

Found an error? Send it info@screenrant.com so it can be corrected.

The Institute's Luke Ellis, in contrast, seems to have always possessed telekinesis and telepathy.

His precognition abilities, too, started emerging after he endured extreme stress and experimentation at the titular Institute. Johnny Smith also seems to be the sole bearer of his "curse." While precognition is treated as a rare ability in The Institute, Luke is not the only one possessing it.

The Dead Zone's title, in itself, stems from the "blind spots" in Johnny Smith's visions of the future. These "blind spots" are projections of the future that do not have a deterministic outcome. Only a choice in the present can make them less shrouded. Projections of the future in The Institute are treated as random flashes that lack context. One has to draw assumptions about them before trying to change the outcome.

Despite the difference in mechanism of their central superpowers, The Institute and The Dead Zone tell a similar story. They are both driven by the "Hitler's Murder Paradox," prompting viewers to question whether one is morally obligated to murder someone who is bound to commit a crime in the future. Stephen King's The Dead Zone captures this moral dilemma from the perspective of one sole protagonist.

He must decide whether sacrificing himself and his life is worth it to serve the perceived greater good that could save the lives of millions.

In The Institute, the ones who run the titular organization attempt to reason with the same moral paradox. They torment children with special abilities and imprison them in a facility to leverage their powers to prevent future disasters. While the higher-ups in the shadow organization defend their actions, characters like Luke argue that the long-term future is not deterministic and any visions of it cannot be reliable.

The Institute's Luke faces the same dilemma as Johnny Smith specifically in season 2's episode 2. Every future threat he attempts to evade somehow leads him to more trouble. Even the act of attempting to save his friend from her imminent doom forces him to let the titular Institute capture his friends again. In both Stephen King stories, precognition is more of a curse than a blessing.

The Institute, released in 2025, follows 14-year-old genius Luke Ellis, who is kidnapped and wakes up at a mysterious facility filled with children possessing unusual abilities. Meanwhile, Tim Jamieson, a former police officer, seeks a fresh start in a nearby town, inevitably intertwining his fate with Luke's.

#3393. HBO's 'Harry Potter' Has the Perfect Opportunity to Fix the Movies' Biggest Mistake

Greer Riddell is a London-based film and television journalist writing about comedy, streaming and the evolving media industry in the UK and USA. She works at Collider, covering the latest in film, television and entertainment through interviews, features, reviews and industry coverage.

Her recent brand collaborations include HBO, Warner Bros., Netflix, Hulu, Sky, Disney+ and DC Studios. She has covered titles including Saturday Night Live UK, Rivals, Scrubs, Stuart Fails to Save the Universe, Ludwig, Supergirl and Stranger Things.

Her recent interviews include Florence Pugh, Mike Faist and Christopher Abbott for Netflix's East of Eden, Taika Waititi and Jenna Ortega for Klara and the Sun.

One of the biggest advantages of HBO's Harry Potter adaptation over the original films is the amount of time it has to explore Hogwarts. A feature film has to prioritize the main storyline, meaning many details about the school's history, traditions, and everyday life were cut from Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone. The upcoming TV series can give these elements more attention, depicting Hogwarts not just as the setting for Harry's adventures but as an established institution with its own curriculum, residents, and history.

HBO has already offered glimpses of how the series will restore details from the books, including changes to Hogwarts' iconography. One example is Ravenclaw's crest design, which returns to the book-accurate eagle mascot and blue and bronze colors. Although these may seem like small details, the houses are central to Hogwarts' identity, and their distinct symbols and traditions help establish the school's history.

There are also several customs from the books that the films had little time to explore. When new students arrive at Hogwarts, for example, the Sorting Hat performs lengthy songs that describe the houses and their histories. The books also establish house points, common rooms, and dormitories as important parts of everyday school life. For many international audiences, particularly those unfamiliar with the British school system, the films made these details seem like magical inventions specific to Hogwarts. In reality, the school is modeled in part on traditional British private schools, with their established customs and institutional histories. The HBO series can make that connection clearer, presenting Hogwarts as a prestigious boarding school with traditions comparable to those of Eton or Wycombe Abbey, rather than treating every aspect of its organization as something exclusive to the wizarding world.

Hogwarts is getting some very familiar ghosts.

The series also has more time to explore Hogwarts' curriculum. The films showed a relatively small number of lessons, focusing on those that contributed to the main storyline. Audiences saw Professor Flitwick, played by Warwick Davis, in two very different costumes, Snape's (Alan Rickman) Potions lessons, and just one flying lesson with Madam Hooch (Zoe Wanamaker), which introduced Harry and the audience to Quidditch. However, the books feature a much wider range of subjects, teachers, and magical skills. An episodic format gives the adaptation room to show more of these classes and follow Harry and his classmates as they develop their abilities throughout the school year.

One omitted teacher who seems to be receiving more attention in the HBO adaptation is History of Magic Professor Binns, played by Richard Durden. Binns died while sitting at his desk but did not realize it, so he continued teaching as a ghost. Most students consider his lessons boring, but History of Magic provides important background on the wizarding world's past and makes Hogwarts seem much more like a real school, as there’s always going to be a class that is universally disliked!

Beyond its traditions and school curriculum, Hogwarts is also home to magical residents and creatures who contribute to its everyday life. The films omitted several of these characters or only gave them passing mentions. Gryffindor's ghost, Nearly Headless Nick, appeared, and Ravenclaw’s Grey Lady was played by Trainspotting’s Kelly Macdonald. However, the books feature several other ghosts associated with the different houses — the Bloody Baron, Slytherin's house ghost, and the Fat Friar, who represents Hufflepuff. According to Variety, the HBO series will feature both, played by Andrew Brooke and Daniel Fearn respectively.

One of the most significant supernatural omissions from the Harry Potter films was Peeves the poltergeist. Unlike Hogwarts' ghosts, Peeves has a physical form and spends his time causing trouble throughout the castle, dropping heavy objects, smashing items, and disrupting lessons. He’s regularly supported by Fred and George Weasley, united in their hatred of the Ministry of Magic official Dolores Umbridge. Peeves was originally intended to appear in the films, with British comedian Rik Mayall (The Young Ones) filming scenes as the character; however, they were cut during editing. The HBO adaptation will finally bring Peeves to life, with comedian Peter Serafinowicz (The Tick) cast in the role. His inclusion, alongside the other Hogwarts ghosts, will give the series more opportunities to show the characters who continue to inhabit the castle outside of term time.

The series can also look beyond The Philosopher's Stone to introduce parts of Hogwarts that become important in the later books. In Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, Hermione discovers the school kitchens and learns about the house-elves responsible for cooking, cleaning and maintaining the castle. This leads her to establish S.P.E.W., the Society for the Promotion of Elfish Welfare, to campaign for house-elves' rights and freedom. The storyline also introduces Winky, Mr. Crouch's former house-elf, who Harry and his friends meet after the Quidditch World Cup. Dobby eventually finds work in the Hogwarts kitchens, too. Including this subplot would show another part of how Hogwarts operates beyond the students and teachers. The house-elves carry out much of the work that keeps the school running, and their presence introduces wider questions about the wizarding world's social structure. It would also give Hermione's full personality room to develop, rather than cutting her screen time to prioritize Harry alone.

By including more of these details, HBO's Harry Potter can establish Hogwarts as an institution with its own ecosystem independent of Harry's adventures. The school existed long before Harry arrived and will continue long after he leaves. Its teachers, students, ghosts, house-elves, and traditions all contribute to its identity, and the upcoming series can finally depict Harry as only one part of Hogwarts' much larger legacy.

HBO's Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone is scheduled to premiere on December 25, with streaming available on HBO Max.

#3392. This AirPods Feature Fixed My Biggest Problem With Listening to Podcasts to Fall Asleep

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

There's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to disassociate from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

In the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

The AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.

#3391. Box Office: ‘Club Kid’ Scores Best Limited Expansion of the Year as Younger Audiences Embrace Jordan Firstman’s Oscar Hopeful

Jordan Firstman’s “Club Kid” was the belle of Cannes. Critics raved about Firstman’s feature directorial debut, as well as his sensitive performance as a party promoter turned unlikely dad, and A24 swept in to buy the film for $17 million after a bidding war. But plenty of movies have been embraced at film festivals only to face rejection when they hit the wider world. Would “Club Kid” be another “Dope” or “Begin Again”?

Well, based on a very limited sample size, “Club Kid” seems to be performing just fine, thank you very much. Those raves and A24’s imprimatur of cool are paying off as the film enjoyed the best limited expansion of the year this weekend, grossing $756,060 across 27 screens. That translates into an impressive $28,002 per-screen average. Since opening in six screens on Nov. 6, “Club Kid” has earned nearly $1.5 million. But this very New York story has mostly played in major cities and liberal bastions like the Big Apple, Chicago, Austin, San Francisco, and Los Angeles. Will audiences across the country embrace the story of a drug-taking, sex-positive gay man and his adorable 10-year-old accidental son? We’ll find out on Thanksgiving when it goes wide. In order for “Club Kid” to be a financial success, it will need to more than double the $17 million that A24 shelled out for the rights, because theaters keep half the ticket sales. Searchlight’s “Wild Horse Nine,” which is seen as a near lock for a Best Picture nod, earned $4.6 million domestically in its second weekend. The film about two CIA agents up to no good in Chile has earned $28 million globally. Then there’s “La Bola Negra,” a multigenerational gay epic from Netflix. It’s earned $3.5 million domestically over five weeks in theaters. And “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” which is generating Oscar buzz for John Turturro, picked up $322,830 to bring its domestic haul to $4.7 million after four weeks in theaters.

“Wicker,” with its story of a fisherwoman who becomes romantically entangled with a wicker man, may be too weird to generate a much love from Academy voters, but it has done well for its distributor, Black Bear, earning $1.5 million in North America last weekend. Its global total stands at $36.7 million after four weeks of release.

As for “Club Kid,” A24 thinks its trajectory mirrors that of other recent arthouse hits, with ticket sales pacing alongside those of “Moonlight” ($67 million gross) and “Anora” ($59.3 million gross) at this point in its expansion. Exit scores are among the best in the studio’s history and the film is connecting with young audiences as 80% of ticket buyers were under the age of 35. Next weekend will be another test for “Club Kid” as it expands to 200 screens across the top 50 markets. If it keeps drawing crowds, Firstman and A24 will have a lot to celebrate.

Fall is in full swing, and if your yard looks anything like mine, you’re probably busy clearing scattered leaves while tending to a tired lawn.

What makes it look so worn down are probably the sparse, empty spots across the yard — which leaves me asking: is it too late to plant grass seed in November?

Luckily, I called on some lawn experts to shed some light on this and offer their advice on achieving a lush, resilient lawn even in this colder season.

So before you get ready to sow, here is what you need to consider before grabbing your seed packet and getting started.

While November is typically not the right month to sow grass seed, this can also depend on your regional climate, local soil temperatures, and grass seed type.

For instance, with cool-season grasses (such as Kentucky bluegrass, perennial ryegrass, tall fescue), you should only overseed once the temperatures drop below 50 degrees Fahrenheit.

“It’s not necessarily too late — but it is more of a riskier time to do so,” advises Chris Bonnett, founder of GardeningExpress. “If you are planting grass seed this month, timing is everything, and it will depend on what the weather is like where you are.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

“The soil temperature is the most important thing, as the seeds will need a mild environment to germinate, and you'll need the soil temperatures to be consistently around 46.4 °F to 50 °F or above for germination.”

"If you are planting grass seed this month, timing is everything, and it will depend on what the weather is like"

On the other hand, warm-season varieties like Bermuda grass, zoysiagrass, centipedegrass, and Bahiagrass begin going dormant as the weather cools down. As a result, planting them during cold spells reduces their chances of growing. This is especially the case during colder snaps and the risk of frost.

"Seed should be planted at least 6 weeks before the area's first hard frost, so it has time to germinate and build some root growth before winter dormancy sets in," advises Matthew Koch, Ph.D., research and development at ScottsMiracle-Gro.

"Seed should be planted at least 6 weeks before the area's first hard frost

"Regions that experience a milder fall, also known as the Transition Zone (roughly Kansas through the Mid-Atlantic, including areas extending toward the Carolinas), might be able to have one final feeding before winter, but it is entirely dependent on the local climate, growing conditions, and grass type."

However, if the soil is too cold, experts suggest waiting until warmer weather begins during springtime. “I’d recommend waiting until the spring, adds Bonnett.

"There’s no benefit in rushing to sow grass seed if it’s not going to have the right conditions to germinate and establish well.”

So if temperatures haven’t yet dropped, what is the best method for overseeding a lawn? To give your lawn an optimal head start in establishing healthy grass, experts suggest sowing a fast-germinating seed mix.

“If the conditions are mild enough, choose a fast-germinating grass seed mix such as one containing perennial ryegrass,” adds Bonnett. “This will help give your lawn the best chance of establishing.”

Of course, preparation is essential, so start by eliminating weeds, clearing leaves, and leveling the ground with a rake before you start seeding.

“Scatter the seed evenly and gently rake it into the top layer of the soil. Keep the area slightly moist but avoid overwatering, especially in November when rainfall is more frequent. If the ground is already wet or waterlogged, avoid planting.”

For more top tips, check out how to overseed your lawn in fall for the best results in spring.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

#3388. VisionQuest's Lauren Morais Addresses The MCU's Potential Debut Of Villain Team After Finale

Lauren Morais, who brought Marvel's Lisa Molinari to life in VisionQuest, breaks down her future with the MCU after the finale of the Disney+ series.

WARNING: This interview contains MAJOR spoilers from VisionQuest season 1, episode 8, "Forever."The Marvel Cinematic Universe continues a key theme through one of its most beloved trilogies.

While WandaVision may have begun as one of the many new shows to debut in the MCU timeline after the launch of Disney+, the Elizabeth Olsen and Paul Bettany-starring adventure became the start of a popular era in the franchise. Not only did it lead to the Agatha All Along spinoff, but also one final project that brought everything full circle.

As viewers got to see VisionQuest, which picked up on the events of the 2021 series, bring the long-time hero back, it also served as a massive payoff for the Maximoff twins, with Tommy's story being properly explored. While his brother was off with Agatha Harkness, the Phase 6 drama showed how his life became a bit different, once his soul was placed in Thomas Shepherd.

I was honored to speak with Lauren Morais, who became one of the latest additions to the MCU franchise, as she plays Marvel's Lisa Molinari, a player from the comics who has gone from villain to hero throughout her time in the lore. Throughout the interview, the Welsh star opened up about bringing Lisa's history to life in live-action, and what may be in store for the character after the finale.

As she landed the role of Lisa, Morais broke down her audition process, which, similar to a lot of other Marvel projects, was kept heavily under wraps. The actress also opened up about the kind of research she did once boarding the show.

Lauren Morais: Well, when I first auditioned, I had no idea who she was. It was just a fake name, fake everything, so I had no idea it was Lisa until my last audition, which [was] my third or fourth audition, so that was fun! Then I read the comics, and I dove into her, and I thought she was such a complicated but such a strong woman, which [is the type of] characters that I love to play. But I really loved the aspect of her being an artist and questioning superheroes, and becoming a villain with the Young Masters, itself. I thought it was a real treat to be able to play this character.

Rearrange the movies into the correct US release order.

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

One of the key factors in Lisa's arc in VisionQuest is the deep dynamic she shares with Tommy. However, unlike other TV shows and films where a female character's whole purpose becomes only about serving the male character, the series really explores how Lisa is Tommy's whole world prior to him reconnecting with Vision, while letting her shine outside of their relationship.

When asked if that was something that she enjoyed portraying throughout the season, Morais explained how she cares for Tommy, and how she was able to use her own experience to guide him:

Lauren Morais: "It was so fun to develop that and see that in the script. You meet them both on the bus, and he's about to have a panic attack, and she talks him through it, and she talks through her own survival modes of it, and she got him into the scamming and the pickpocket life, and I thought that was a nice juxtaposition to maybe what we've seen before, but I think all in all, they just really look after each other, and I love that.

Like you said, it's not like Lisa's hanging on to him. It's more like we share a similar past of orphanhood and not belonging, so we're going to stick with each other and look after each other because there's this weird, random connection that instant that you can't really explain. But it's there, and I'm ready to go through this wild journey of finding out that your dad's like a robot. What Lisa thinks, she's still figuring it out, as you can see. But she accepts it because she accepts Tommy in any form he is."

The MCU did a variation of Lisa's Coat of Arms, but with a more grounded approach. While it's not fully Tiboro's Coat from the comics, Morais was excited to see the VisionQuest series honor it in its own way, as she shared how she learned that they were taking this direction with it.

Lauren Morais: "I saw it when I was reading the scripts, it was in one of the stages, like the directions, Lisa has this blazer and has fake arms, and she's pickpocketing. And I thought that was such a fun taste for the audience of Lisa, and also it made sense with her character of being a pickpocket and surviving on the streets.

I thought that was very, very clever, and also as an actor, it was so funny on set, having those arms and that blazer, going to shake people's hands. I gave some people a high five, and some people on the crew hadn't seen the script, so they were very confused when I suddenly had four arms. And I was like, "I'm in Marvel now, I have four arms. This is how it goes, guys!"

As Lisa and Tommy take off with Paladin in the end, Morais was asked if that was perhaps leading to the MCU's Young Masters, or perhaps a variation of the darker team from the comics, as the group is traditionally a group of villains. In terms of what the future has in store for Lisa, she is hoping to see more for her character after the finale:

Lauren Morais: That's up to the Marvel gods, but I think what I would personally love to explore is Lisa's villainy and the Young Masters and her relationship with Tommy going forward. I think that would be so exciting, and taking bits from the comics, and also seeing what she can do with the drone and the forearms and with DUM-E and U. That's what I would love to explore is her and her powers and what she's going to do with them. Is she gonna go for the superhero vibe or the villain vibe? I don't know, but I want to see that.

VisionQuest episode 8 sees the Maximoff brothers finally reunited, as Joe Locke's Billy returned and shared the screen with Ruardih Mollica's Tommy. When asked if there was a version of finale where Lisa and Wiccan got to interact more, Morais responded with the following:

Lauren Morais: I think those are conversations that, when I was thinking about that, is what Tommy and Lisa would have. When they go to the motel, and she's doing the drowning. To me, that was all encompassed in that moment. And as we build up to the finale, those [are] definitely things that Tommy and Lisa have considered. But also, as you can see, I think it was episode four, Tommy says about Vision being his dad, and she just kind of accepts it. She's kind. She trusts Tommy with her whole heart that I think as long as Tommy thinks what he's doing is right, and she'll go with him anywhere. She'll defend him, and if he's in trouble, she knows who to call.

ScreenRant: It seemed like everyone around them was just accusing him of being crazy. But she just kind of accepted it.

Lauren Morais: I think she's gone through so much herself, and she has so much innate trust in him. She's like, 'Yeah, of course, whatever. I'll be by your side because we have each other. We only have each other in this crazy world,' and I don't think she'll [ever] abandon [Tommy] because [they have] gone [a lot.] They've done the [pick-]pocketing, they've been living together in this crazy world without much family - [but] they have each other, I think she's an easygoing girl as well.

While the VisionQuest show is really the end of this trilogy, there could always be more spinoffs, as Bettany's drama was another offshoot. When sharing that the MCU has hopefully not seen the last of Lisa, Morais stressed how she had the best time:

Lauren Morais: "Oh, thank you! I mean, that would be so fun. I've had the best time, the absolute best time, and it's been so cool to see the fan reactions and the theories and people picking up the Easter eggs, oh, it's been a joy."

ScreenRant: "How much have you been paying attention to the theories online? Have you been following any conversations online that you're kind of, 'Oh, some of them are right, some of them are wrong!'"

Lauren Morais: "Definitely, who the Client is. I think that's so fun. There's been so many different theories and theories that I didn't see coming. I've been really enjoying that. Yeah, who the mysterious Client is. I've had friends in my own life ask me, and I was like, "No, you have to watch."

VisionQuest is available for streaming on Disney+.
