#3386. 'Tracker' Is Finally Giving Colter What He Needs After 2 Seasons | Review

It's wild to think that after three seasons on the road, Tracker Season 4 is the first time we see Colter Shaw (Justin Hartley) united with the entire cast. Seriously. Even in the first season, Colter's former handlers never appeared on-screen alongside our favorite rewardist, and the one time Colter met up with one of them in Season 2, his former tech expert was still further east in the Windy City. But now that the rest of the cast has consolidated to Denver, "Blind Spot" offers Colter the opportunity to share some screen time with everyone currently on his roster — and it's about time.

At a nice home somewhere in Denver, Colorado, a man we later learn is named Emelio Chavez (J. Anthony Pena) leaves his wife, Marie (Mercedes Colon), indoors to meet two guys named Hector Cruz (Rafael Cabrera) and Freddie (Mike Miller) in his garage. They speak briefly about a car before Chavez invites his buddies inside for some dessert his wife made — of course, they're only welcome after they dispose of a dead body wrapped in a sheet on the floor. The next day at Reenie Greene's (Fiona Rene) law office, Colter arrives and reunites with his lawyer in the flesh. It's been a while since they've seen each other, and nothing is said about her date with Russell (Jensen Ackles), so those hoping for answers will be disappointed. Colter also meets Mel Day (Cassady McClincy Zhang) for the first time, who awkwardly steps over herself during the introduction. However, Colter is there to work, and he's soon brought before Reenie's mentor, Judge Gail McGill (Amy Aquino), whose daughter, Erica (Daniela Nieves), appears to be missing. Although they haven’t spoken in years, Gail’s terminal diagnosis has led her to make amends.

Tracker works because the case changes every week and the four people solving it never do. Here is which of them you are, what it says about you, and the case for yours being the best of the four.

You would rather handle it yourself and you are usually capable of doing so. Colter is a survivalist who lives in an Airstream and takes reward money for finding missing people, which is a premise that only works because he is clearly running from something of his own.

You know somebody, and that somebody owes you a favour. Reenie is the lawyer Colter calls when a case needs a door opened legally, and she is the only person on the show who can get further with a phone call than he can on foot.

You are two steps ahead and you rarely mention it. Bobby is the one who finds the thing that unlocks the case, usually from a desk, usually about ninety seconds before anybody realises they needed it.

You turn up, change the temperature of the room, and leave people arguing about you. Russell is Colter's brother, ex-military, and the show has never once let the audience settle on whether he is a help or a problem, which is exactly why he keeps coming back.

Speaking to Gail, she admits that she wasn’t really there for her growing up after Erica's father died. Colter asks about what led to their estrangement, and Gail reveals that it was a combination of her own stubbornness and cutting her daughter off. It's been three years since they've spoken, thus far, but she hopes to rectify that. With no social media or current contacts, there's little to go on, but Gail offers Colter a letter to pass to her daughter if he does find her. “I’m going to do everything I can to find her for you.” Meeting with Randy (Chris Lee), the hacker reveals he’s unable to find literally anything — credit cards included — on Erica. The only thing that may give them an edge is an old photo from a deleted social account that leads them to Mile High Taproom, a local brewery where Erica once worked alongside a friend, Ashley Cox (Carina Conti), who appears in several photos.

Arriving at the brewery, Colter speaks with Ashley, who reveals that she thought Erica just wanted a clean break from life. However, the two have since had a falling out of their own after a dispute regarding a guy Erica had been seeing named Jeb Boyd (Jesse Luken). “I have no idea where they landed,” she tells Colter. This gives Randy some extra material to work with, however, and leads Colter to a towing company Boyd owns across town. When he arrives, the door is ajar, and Boyd has been knocked out on the floor. Upon waking up, he tells Colter that three guys beat him up over a Cadillac that Erica had repossessed the night before. Of course, when they try to call her, they have no luck.

Instead, Colter heads over to Erica's place and looks around. Randy calls to reveal that the car itself belongs to a woman named Paloma Nava, a local churchgoer with a clean record. Poking around inside, Colter doesn’t find much other than the fact that her bed comforter is missing, as is a missing curtain. That leads him to a bullet hole in the window frame and, given that the place smells like bleach, it doesn’t look too good for Erica. That's when he has Randy hack into the neighboring camera, where he sees Erica gunned down and her body taken by several goons. Later, when the cops show up, Detective Zahn (Rolando Boyce) reveals that they believe the man involved is Emelio Chavez, who headlines a mean narcotics operation in town. After being told by the detective to stand down for the time being, Reenie shows up and asks what she should tell Gail — Colter asks for more time. He just wants to find answers for her before they tell her that Erica is dead. For a minute here, it really looks as if Colter has failed, but there's, of course, more to the story.

Just then, Randy calls to reveal that Hector Cruz, Nava’s nephew, would have had access to the Cadillac. He further connects Hector to Chavez by linking him to a construction company owned by the outlaw. Colter believes that they probably have Erica’s body in the car, and so heads out to the last spot where Hector's phone pinged — which just so happens to be one of Chavez’s construction sites. Colter comes upon the goons involved, creates a distraction, and takes him out. Looking around, he finds the breach and bloody materials but not the body itself. Breaking into the office, he holds a gun at Hector and starts firing off both questions and bullets — anything to get answers. Apparently, the body they have in the car is a federal agent named Mark Sutton, an undercover DEA agent who was killed by Chavez. But Hector messed up. Having left the car long enough for Erica to repo it, they took the fight to her. Hector tells him that they took the bodies to the gas fields ten miles north, and he won't have enough time to stop them. As usual, don't tell Colter Shaw the odds.

After taking out the federal agent first, Freddie goes back for Erica's body, only for her to fight back. She survived her gunshot wound and does all she can to escape, though Chavez tackles and strangles her. Barely beating him with a rock, she runs off, still wounded. By the time Colter arrives, however, he finds the scene empty. The car is there (trunk open) and Freddie is dead, but Chavez and Erica are missing. When Colter sees the bloody handprint on the car and a trail leading away from the scene, he realizes that Erica is alive. Unfortunately, he's not the only one following her trail toward the nearby power plant. Although she flags down some help, Chavez kills the worker before he can do anything but slow him down, which signals Colter to their location.

With Chavez on her tail, Erica escapes into the plant and hides. Chavez's other men show up, and they invade the plant, looking everywhere for their loose end. Fortunately, Colter arrives in the nick of time to help, dressing Erica's wound and leading her toward the roof. When Chavez and his men enter, he takes out one of the guys and a firefight ensues. Colter beats down Chavez in a one-on-one fight, but before he can take him out to the police, Erica shoots and kills her captor. When Zahn and the rest of the reinforcements arrive, the detective thanks Colter for his help, though notes that the prints on the gun that killed the drug lord have been wiped clean.

That night, Colter visits Erica in her hospital room, who has been reading over her mother's letter. After everything, she decides that she wants to see her mother after all, prompting Gail to walk in. The pair have a heartfelt reunion as Erica finally forgives her mother, and Colter slips out to let them reconcile. Back at Reenie's office, Colter enjoys a few drinks with Reenie, Randy, and Mel. For the first time, the Tracker cast is all together, but, as per usual, Colter does his best to skip out before things get too personal — this was the same technique he used to get out of spending time with Reenie and Randy's cousin Bobby (Eric Graise) back in Season 1's "Chicago."

But before he can perform his Irish goodbye, Colter is cornered by Mel, who asks him to look into what happened to her mother. She still has questions about how exactly her mother died, and Colter agrees to take a look. It's a bit strange that Reenie hasn't brought up what she found to Colter before, but the reward seeker will no doubt be clued in soon enough. “It was nice meeting you,” he says, taking off without looking back. Far be it from Tracker to allow Colter to bond with his allies...

Colter Shaw reunites with the Tracker cast for a one-off episode with some sudden twists.

There’s not long to wait until Percy Jackson returns for another mythological adventure, with season 3 of “Percy Jackson and the Olympians” arriving on Disney+ on November 20. Based on Rick Riordan’s third novel, the new instalment sees Walker Scobell’s Percy embark on a dangerous quest after Annabeth Chase (Leah Sava Jeffries) is captured by the forces of Kronos.

With Grover (Aryan Simhadri) by his side, Percy must rescue his friend, free a goddess in chains and confront a prophecy that could spell disaster for Olympus. There are plenty of familiar faces returning, alongside exciting newcomers including Nico and Bianca di Angelo, while Thalia Grace (Tamara Smart) looks set to play an increasingly important role. But before we dive back into Camp Half-Blood, here are five things worth remembering from the first two seasons.

Fair warning: I’ll be spoiling major events from seasons 1 and 2. So, without further ado, here are five things you should remember before “Percy Jackson” season 3.

Thalia Grace’s return at the end of season 2 comes with a major twist that changes everything heading into season 3. In the original books, Zeus turned his daughter into a pine tree to save her life after monsters mortally wounded her. However, the series reveals that he actually imprisoned her as punishment after she refused to obey him and become his weapon in the coming war.

When Clarisse (Dior Goodjohn) uses the Golden Fleece to heal Camp Half-Blood’s protective borders, Thalia returns to human form. The revelation also raises questions about who the demigods can trust. Chiron (Glynn Turman) and the camp’s leaders had hidden the truth about Thalia from Percy, Annabeth and Grover for years. Her hatred of Zeus could also bring her closer to Luke Castellan (Charlie Bushnell) and Kronos, although where her loyalties ultimately lie remains unclear.

Most importantly, Thalia’s return complicates the Great Prophecy. As Zeus’s daughter, she’s another child of the Big Three who could fulfil the prediction, meaning Percy might not be the only demigod capable of deciding Olympus’s fate.

Thalia’s return wasn’t just a side effect of healing Camp Half-Blood. It also gave Kronos another way to threaten Olympus. The Great Prophecy states that a child of one of the “Big Three” gods (Zeus, Poseidon or Hades) who reaches the age of 16 will decide whether Olympus survives or falls.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Before Thalia returned, Percy was the main demigod connected to the prophecy. Now, Zeus’s daughter could also fulfil it, making the situation much more complicated. The two immediately clash after Thalia wakes up, setting up a potential rivalry between them.

Her return also gives Kronos another opportunity to turn a powerful demigod against the gods. Thalia has plenty of reasons to hate Zeus, which could make her vulnerable to his influence. As season 3 approaches, both Percy and Thalia could play a major role in deciding the fate of Olympus.

After the battle at Thalia’s tree, Percy briefly sees his father, Poseidon (Toby Stephens), in a vision while unconscious. Poseidon tells him that the war against Kronos has officially begun and asks Percy’s Cyclops half-brother, Tyson (Daniel Diemer), to help make weapons in the underwater forges.

Tyson happily accepts, finally feeling like he has a place alongside his father. However, his departure leaves Percy facing the growing threat on his own. While Tyson gets a chance to help the gods prepare for war, Percy must return to Camp Half-Blood and deal with the dangers ahead.

The moment also shows that the conflict with Kronos is much bigger than the fight at camp. With Tyson helping build weapons beneath the sea, season 3 could explore more of the underwater world and Poseidon’s role in the coming war.

Luke Castellan has become an increasingly dangerous threat by the end of season 2. Although Clarisse successfully retrieves the Golden Fleece for Camp Half-Blood, Luke’s forces still achieve something important: Thalia is brought back to life, giving Kronos another powerful demigod who could join his side.

The attack also exposes how poorly Camp Half-Blood is being run. After King Tantalus (Timothy Simons) is killed during the siege, Dionysus (Jason Mantzoukas) reluctantly takes charge again but does little to organize the campers. Instead, Percy steps up and gives an inspiring speech, encouraging everyone to defend their home.

This also helps explain why Luke has turned against the Olympian gods. He believes they mistreat their children and care more about their own power than the demigods’ lives. With Zeus’s treatment of Thalia only adding to that argument, Luke has plenty of ammunition to convince others to join Kronos. Heading into season 3, he’s still a major threat to Percy and everyone at Camp Half-Blood.

Season 3 adapts “The Titan’s Curse,” which sees Annabeth Chase captured by Kronos’ forces. Her disappearance sets Percy on another dangerous quest to rescue his friend, but it also puts his biggest weakness to the test: his loyalty to the people he loves.

Percy has always been willing to put himself in danger to protect his friends, even when it means ignoring warnings or going against the gods. With Annabeth’s life at stake, that side of him is likely to become even more important in season 3.

The trailer also shows Percy carrying the weight of the sky, a burden traditionally associated with the Titan Atlas. It’s another example of how far he’s willing to go to protect the people closest to him. As the Great Prophecy draws closer, Percy will have to balance his feelings for Annabeth and his friends with the fate of Olympus.

"Percy Jackson and the Olympians" season 3 premieres with two episodes on Disney Plus on November 20. After that, new episodes arrive weekly on Fridays.

#3384. 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.

#3383. Game Of Thrones Officially Brings Back Tywin Lannister In The Lion's Reign

Game of Thrones might have jumped the shark somewhat during its final season, but there's still plenty of love for the fantasy franchise, if you are able to quash those memories and leave them in the past. The best evidence for that is just how many other adaptations there are out there right now, giving fans plenty of options, regardless of what medium they tend to inhabit.

Game of Thrones: War for Westeros is a great example, launching in 2027 and giving players the chance to lead any of the show's major factions in their ultimate quest for the Iron Throne. There are also ongoing adaptations that continue to release regular updates, including one which is about to thrust one of the book's most calculated characters back to the fore.

Game of Thrones is full of all kinds of scheming characters, from those who are loyal to nobody, like Littlefinger, to those who are simply trying to make it through life in as good a shape as possible (a la Tyrion). Arguably the figure who is most successful in their machinations, though, is the Lannister patriarch Tywin, who leads arguably the most powerful family in Westeros at the time of the books.

He's about to serve as a central figure in the latest set of events for Game of Thrones: Legends, the mobile puzzle role-playing game by Zynga that is available for both iOS and Android. The game essentially tasks players with color-matching gems in order to defeat opponents.

The latest event is Kingsroad: The Lion’s Reign, which is set to run from November 9, at 3:00 a.m. ET to December 7, at 2:00 a.m. ET. Set around the very important Kingsroad and Goldroad, there are a bunch of Daily and Weekly Quests to complete for rewards that you would otherwise struggle to accrue in the usual gameplay loop.

In breaking down both the events, the developer shared the following insight:

"Kingsroad: Complete Daily and Weekly Goals to earn Kingsroad points, and progress along the Kingsroad for rewards! Earn 300 points on each of your five Daily Goals, and 800 points for each Weekly goal to reach new Tiers every day. This season’s Kingsroad rewards include Common Champion Shards for the Lannister Spearman, Summoning Tokens, and more! Beyond Tier 50, you can claim a bonus chest of rewards for every 700 points!

"Goldroad: This season’s Goldroad rewards include 15 Legendary Champion Shards for Tywin Lannister (The Hand). Upgrade to Elite Goldroad Pass to earn Exalted Tokens, Legendary Gear, Splendid, Grand, and Forge Summon Tokens, Valyrian Essence, Skill Books, and other bonuses on top of the Kingsroad rewards. Progress through the Tiers to earn more rewards for unlocking and powering up Champions!"

It's worth noting that the Elite Goldroad Pass will cost real world money, though it absolutely isn't necessary to play the game in its current state.

Outside of that, fans of George RR Martin's universe can look forward to the final season of House of the Dragon in 2028, as well as the second season of the excellent Knight of the Seven Kingdoms next year. Don't count on that Game of Thrones Season 8 reshoot any time soon though.

#3382. iPadOS 27.3 adds new iPad setting I instantly turned on

iPadOS 27.3 is currently available in beta, and it introduces a new iPad setting for app windowing that I instantly turned on. Here are the details.

I use the iPad Pro as my primary computer, and for the most part have found Apple’s software changes in iPadOS 26 and 27 to be great upgrades.

But with the powerful new windowing capabilities, there have definitely been some quirks that need refining. One of them involves resizing windows with the traffic light controls in the top-left corner.

For example, in iPadOS 27 the controls move locations and even disappear depending on the size of the window. It can be pretty frustrating.

I need to just get better about learning keyboard shortcuts for window controls. But in the meantime, iPadOS 27.3 adds a new optional setting that I instantly turned on and have been loving.

Inside Settings ⇾ Multitasking & Gestures, if you have ‘Windowed Apps’ enabled you’ll see a new option below it: ‘Double-tap Top of Window to Zoom’

If you use your iPad mostly with touch input, or simply haven’t used keyboard shortcuts enough to remember them, this new setting is a great way to quickly resize windows.

When the setting is enabled, two taps (or a double-click with the trackpad) will zoom the window to take up the full screen. Then you can double-tap again to revert it to its previous size.

I generally keep my app windows in specific size setups, but regularly find myself wanting to go fullscreen temporarily. The new setting provides a convenient way to do that quickly without needing the traffic light controls or my keyboard, and is a welcome refinement to iPadOS windowing.

Will you enable this new iPadOS 27.3 setting? Why or why not? Let us know in the comments.

Denzel and Davis both throw heat in 'Fences'

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Verdict: This period drama is a well-executed adaptation of August Wilson's award-winning 1985 play of the same name. Unfortunately, it notably feels like you're watching a play; it struggles to make the case for why it's a dramatic work of cinema as opposed to a theatrical revival. But as Denzel Washington and Viola Davis start pitching a perfect game, you stop nitpicking and let the performances take over.

Where to watch: Stream "Fences" for free on Tubi or YouTube

"Fences" was a movie I circled on my calendar as I made my way through this year-long Denzel Watchathon. This is considered a seminal work in the legendary actor's career. It's his third directorial effort in his filmography and by far the best. It also earned him his seventh Oscar nomination as an actor (his second of three he'd earn in the 2010s alone).

Once you watch it, it's no surprise why this performance makes the highlight reel. This movie is essentially crafted to serve his character, except for the few scenes where it's designed to highlight Viola Davis. She plays Denzel's on-screen wife in this period drama film, and I'd argue it's her performance that's the more impressive of the two.

Unfortunately, if I have to nitpick, this strength is also the movie's biggest weakness. "Fences" is adapted from August Wilson's 1985 play of the same name. That play was a roaring success, earning Wilson both a Pulitzer and a Tony Award in 1987. Watching this film adaptation, one wouldn't be shocked if Denzel and Wilson (who also wrote the screenplay for this movie) didn't change a thing from the Broadway version. The entire time, it feels unmistakably like you're watching a play.

This isn't inherently a bad thing; I often like movies adapted from plays, and to be clear, I thought this film was excellent. But unlike, say, "A Few Good Men," I failed to see what was added to the performances, to the story, etc., by turning Wilson's play into a cinematic experience. If you had simply had this same cast act out the play on a stage and filmed it on a Sony Handycam, it'd probably be just as good.

If you want to watch this movie before you read on, I have good news! It's currently streaming for free on Tubi, one of the best free streaming services we've tested. You can also stream it for free on YouTube (with ads).

Malcolm has been with the Streaming team at Tom's Guide since 2023, reviewing dozens of movies each year so you don't have to watch the bad ones.

Here are some of the other Denzel Washington movies I've covered to date in my Denzel Watchathon:

Read more: Every Denzel Watchathon movie so far

The sixth installment in August Wilson's 10-part "Pittsburgh Cycle," "Fences," centers around Troy. Portrayed by Denzel Washington in this adaptation, he's a middle-aged man working as a sanitation worker. He appears to be an ordinary working-class Pittsburgher, albeit sans Yinzer accent. But as the story unfolds, it's quickly apparent that Troy wasn't always destined for an ordinary life.

Troy, as revealed by his longtime friend, Bono (Stephen McKinley Henderson), was at one point one of the best baseball players in America. But he had the bad luck of being a Black player in the years before Jackie Robinson broke the color barrier in Major League Baseball. So while his Negro League career earned him plaudits and adulation, it didn't exactly bring in the cash. And you can only dine on praise for so long before reality sets in.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Complicating things is ... well, everything else. His marriage to Rose (Viola Davis) appears healthy, but early on in the movie there are hints this isn't the case. It's clear that money can be a pain point for Troy, who now has less of it than ever because he's no longer collecting part of his brother's (Mykelti Williamson) disability check from the Army. When Troy's 34-year-old son, Lyons (Russell Hornsby), comes asking for money, it's clear that Troy thinks he'll never see that money again, and that he doesn't have enough cash to waste. Even on family.

But it's not Lyons's relationship with his father at the core of "Fences." Instead, the film focuses on Troy's relationship with his other son, Cory. He's 17 years old and the only child produced by Troy and Rose's marriage. His relationship with his dad is somewhat rocky and complicated by the fact that colleges are recruiting Cory for football. Troy, a former pro athlete who now makes a living hauling trash, wants Cory to avoid sports entirely for fear that it will lead him down the same path Troy went down.

Davis is more subtle in her performance. She's not given a ton to do at first, but then she's given some devastating news in a later scene, and it allows her to steal the scene. From that moment on, she steals the entire movie.

Despite all this focus on Troy and his sons, it's Viola Davis who steals the movie as Rose. Denzel is supposed to be excellent in this movie. He's given incredible lines. He's the main character. Every character exists in this story to be a reflection of his impact on their lives or to highlight a trial and tribulation Troy has had to deal with. There's a scene early on where Cory asks why Troy doesn't like him, and Denzel just cooks, as the Gen Z youths would say. In fact, if you've seen a scene from this movie on TikTok, it's probably this scene of Denzel as Troy taking his son down a peg.

Davis is more subtle in her performance. She's not given a ton to do at first, but then she's given some devastating news in a later scene, and it allows her to steal the scene. From that moment on, she steals the entire movie.

In that aforementioned scene, she's not openly weeping, sobbing, or screaming at the top of her lungs, all of which would be perfectly reasonable responses given the news she just received. However, she manages to do a feat of physical acting where snot just runs from her nostrils. It's the clear aftermath of a moment of grief, underlying the fact that she's not nearly as composed as she's forcing herself to appear on the outside.

When I say that Davis steals this movie and doesn't let go, I mean it. She was the lone Oscar winner for "Fences," deservedly taking home the Oscar for Best Supporting Actress. It might be the first movie since "The Manchurian Candidate" where I felt that an actress took the spotlight from Denzel and there was simply nothing he could do about it.

But again, Denzel is great in this movie. He earns an Oscar nomination; the movie itself earns a Best Picture nomination, in no small part due to his performance and direction. It's a tough watch at times. Because it feels like a play but lacks the intimate, almost physical connection between thespian and theatergoer, it can also lose your interest on occasion.

That all is quickly brushed aside, though, as the film reaches its climax. The performances at the center of this movie are the definition of must-watch. And now that it's currently available to stream at home for free, you really have no excuse not to check it out if you haven't already.

#3379. 'Game of Thrones' Meets Jack Reacher in Alexander Skarsgård's Near-Perfect Action Epic

Conor Sheeran is a Movies and TV features writer for Collider. He has a deep passion for cinema and watches everything from the biggest blockbusters to the smallest indies. While he specializes in movies and television, he has also written about politics, culture, and sports throughout his career. Based in New York City, Conor is also a massive fan of the New York Jets, Mets, and Knicks. He is still waiting for any of those teams to bring home a championship in his lifetime. A member of the National Writers Union and the International Federation of Journalists, Conor is a strong proponent of press freedom and collective action.

Few movies of the past decade have been as ambitious and as meticulous in their approach to life and combat as Robert Eggers' The Northman. Released in 2022, the Viking revenge epic combines the violence and political intrigue of Game of Thrones with the "man on a mission" brutality of Reacher, fusing what makes those shows great while improving where they may fall short. Led by a career-defining performance by Alexander Skarsgård, The Northman is a bloody and haunting journey through betrayal and Norse mythology that deserves more recognition than it initially garnered upon release.

Although the film received widespread critical praise, especially for Skarsgård's performance, it never caught on in theaters and struggled to earn back its production budget. Filmed for between $70 and $90 million, it earned just $75 million at the box office, so while it's not considered a bomb, it had enough commercial appeal to leave some feeling disappointed. However, like many hidden gems and cult classics, The Northman's reputation has only grown in the years since release, particularly among viewers searching for the historical, adult-oriented action spectacle Hollywood has become reluctant to produce. With its stunning cinematogaphy, ferocious battle sequences, and emotional story of revenge, Eggers' Viking tale remains one of the best action movies of the 2020s.

Set in the late ninth century, The Northman follows Amleth (Skarsgård), a young prince whose life is forever changed when his villainous uncle Fjolnir (Claes Bang) murders his father, King Aurvandill (Ethan Hawke), and kidnaps his mother, Queen Gudrun (Nicole Kidman). As the young man manages to escape death, Amleth dedicates his life to avenging his father, rescuing his mother, and killing his uncle.

We shan't be going to the Viking times, thank you.

Years later, Amleth has become a hulking Viking berserker, the living embodiment of vengeance and someone who is willing to murder anyone who gets in the way of his quest for revenge. He soon discovers his uncle's whereabouts and travels back to Iceland to finally accomplish his mission. There, he meets and falls in love with a slave woman named Olga (Anya Taylor-Joy), who helps him in his quest.

Skarsgård is nearly unrecognizable in his performance, delivering a physically imposing portrayal that makes Amleth feel less like a man and more like a force of nature. His sheer brutality recalls the unstoppable presence of Jack Reacher, particularly in the Prime Video series Reacher, starring Alan Ritchson. Both characters possess the intimidating physicality and an almost supernatural ability to overwhelm their enemies, often in the most brutal ways possible.

While Reacher operates by a certain moral code, Amleth is consumed by obsession. Revenge dictates where he goes, what he eats and drinks, and who he interacts with, dominating every decision he makes regardless of the consequences. His unwavering, terrifying determination makes him a monster to his enemies while threatening to destroy everything he holds dear.

Beyond its ferocious action, The Northman's DNA is thoroughly mixed with HBO's classic Game of Thrones. Both focus on the brutality of a medieval setting while blending it with the loyalty and political ambition of the day, and both exist in a world where betrayal can be as devastating as any defeat on a bloody battlefield. Much like dragons and the ancient magic of Game of Thrones, Eggers imbues his world with the supernatural elements of Norse mythology, incorporating witches, draugr, and Valkyries to create a world where the line between history and fantasy becomes increasingly blurred.

However, The Northman does not focus on the maneuvering and scheming for a throne that Game of Thrones does, but instead on the violence that exists behind the scenes in a psychologically complex story about the consequences of revenge. One of the film's greatest strengths is its willingness to challenge what Amleth believes about his family. As with Thrones, family members can sometimes become your worst enemies, which is something Amleth did not expect or prepare for.

While the movie's ambition may have exceeded its success, its lackluster box-office performance was never a reflection of its quality. Viewers who love the ruthless medieval world of Game of Thrones and the bone-crunching brutality of Reacher will certainly find something to enjoy with The Northman. It's an unforgettable combination of genres that proves a movie doesn't need to fit into a box to succeed. Most importantly, it shows that action cinema can be visually spectacular, emotionally devastating, and intellectually ambitious without sacrificing the thrills of a fantasy epic.

Amazon is offering early Black Friday discounts on like-new versions of its 2024 Kindles, with prices starting at $152.99 for the Paperwhite and savings of $27 to $75 across five models that include the color-screen Colorsoft and the pen-equipped Kindle Scribe. All five are a generation behind Amazon's current lineup: The company introduced redesigned Paperwhite and Colorsoft models (plus accessories) in October, with the new Paperwhite now starting at $199.99, and replaced the 2024 Scribe with a third-generation model in December 2025. As for its “like-new” label, it means these are pre-owned devices that Amazon has tested and certified to look and work like new.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite (16GB) is down to $152.99 from $179.99 and covers just about everything most people need for everyday reading, including enough storage for thousands of ebooks. Its seven-inch, 300ppi glare-free display is larger than the previous generation’s 6.8-inch screen, with faster page turns, an adjustable warm light, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life. As PCMag notes in its review, it's a great option for readers who don't need color or handwriting features.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $190.99 from $224.99, making it just $38 more than the like-new Paperwhite (16GB). For that relatively small difference, you're doubling the storage to 32GB and getting wireless charging, an ad-free lock screen, and a front light that automatically adjusts to your surroundings—on top of the same sharp seven-inch display, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life as the standard Paperwhite, as noted by this PCMag review.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft (16GB) is down to $220.99 from $260.99 and offers something the Paperwhite models can’t: a color E-Ink display, which makes it well suited to comics, graphic novels, illustrated books, and travel guides. Its seven-inch screen shows that color content at 150ppi while keeping text at a sharp 300ppi, and you can mark passages in multiple highlight colors to keep your notes organized. That said, colors are noticeably more muted than on a conventional tablet, and battery life tops out at eight weeks, compared with 12 weeks on the Paperwhite.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $243.99 from $287.99, making it just $23 more than the standard like-new Colorsoft. For that modest increase, you're getting twice the storage at 32GB, which is particularly useful for comics, manga, and graphic novels that take up more space than regular ebooks, along with wireless charging, an automatically adjusting front light, and an ad-free lock screen. However, as PCMag notes in its review, the color display produces more subdued tones than a conventional tablet, so the Paperwhite remains the more economical choice if you primarily read novels.

The Like-New Kindle Scribe (16GB) is down to $284.99 from $359.99, the biggest dollar discount in this roundup. Unlike the other Kindles here, it's built for reading and writing, with a 10.2-inch, 300ppi glare-free display and a Premium Pen with an eraser and shortcut button—making it the most versatile option for readers who want an e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

#3376. Ring's New $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company announced a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

The drone camera is one of two products in the company's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the company has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

If you're ready to enter this brave new world of security, you'll have to wait a bit longer: The Ring Drone Camera isn't expected to ship until January 2027, but you can sign up to be alerted when it is available for preorder now.

#3375. New Apple TV 4K remote’s best feature requires a newer iPhone model

A new Apple TV 4K releases this Friday (pre-order here), with an upgraded Siri Remote. But the new remote’s best feature might not work on your iPhone.

If you’re interested in the new Apple TV 4K launching this week, or perhaps you just want to buy the upgraded Siri Remote separately (available here), there’s a key limitation you should know.

Precision Finding on the new Siri Remote requires an iPhone 17 or newer.

The most common problem with the current Siri Remote is that it’s easy to lose. And once you lose it, Apple doesn’t offer many options for finding it. But that’s changing with the 4th gen Siri Remote.

You can use the new Siri Remote with any previous Apple TV 4K or Apple TV HD model. And if you do, you’ll benefit from the remote’s new built-in speaker that can be triggered from the Find My app.

Joining the new speaker, the other main change with this latest Siri Remote is Precision Finding. If you’ve ever used the Find My app to track down a lost AirTag, you’ll probably be familiar with the feature.

Precision Finding lets you get step-by-step, guided directions that take you directly to the lost Siri Remote. It’s a huge upgrade from the old tool for finding the remote—which mostly just told you that it’s in your house somewhere.

But Precision Finding relies on the Bluetooth 6 support found in iPhone 17 and 17 Pro models (not iPhone 17e), iPhone Air, iPhone Duo, and iPhone 18 Pro models.

So if you don’t have one of those iPhones, you’ll still benefit from the built-in speaker that lets you play a sound to find the lost remote, but Precision Finding won’t be available.

You can buy the new Siri Remote for $59 on Amazon.

Will this limitation impact your Siri Remote purchase decision? Let us know in the comments.

#3371. 10 Shows Like 'Minimum Wage' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Spinning off of a popular web series, Netflix's Minimum Wage is currently in the middle of a 28-episode first-season run. If that sounds like a lot of episodes for a show in 2026, keep in mind that they're generally less than 15 minutes each, which is perfect for your overloaded to-watch list—especially when they go down so easily. This cringe workplace mockumentary follows the crew of teenagers running a failing pizza place and making (you guessed it) minimum wage; they're under enormous pressure from their boss (Randall Park) to save the business and their one dumb source of income.

The punchy episodes will leave you plenty of time to explore other streaming shows dealing with the utter ridiculousness of the modern workplace. Here are 10 to get you started.

Workplace comedies usually revolve around white-collar office environments (The Mary Tyler Moore Show, 30 Rock, Parks and Recreation, etc.). Like Minimum Wage, Superstore instead follows the staff of Cloud 9, a generic big-box retailer. The show’s deep bench and diverse cast are largely focused on the jokes, but much of that comedy involves the relatable situation of working a job that demands commitment and a smiley attitude in the face of both entitled customers and obnoxious bosses. It's a different venue and age bracket, but a nutty workplace is a nutty workplace. Stream Superstore on Hulu and Peacock.

We're moving away from the workplace and aging things up a bit, but no worries: the name is a little ironic given that the codependent, co-habitating twenty-somethings of the title are hardly mature. Five friends are cohabiting in the childhood home of Samir (Malik Elassal), and dealing with the uniquely Gen-Z humiliations around dating, work, and even health insurance. Only one member of the group has an actual reasonably good job, while career paths for the others include being a temp, waiter, and a part-time ballet instructor. Stream Adults on Hulu.

This offbeat workplace comedy kicks off with a fabulous premise: Jeong Bok-dong (Kim Byung-chul) was a high-level director in a major corporation until one bad meeting saw him demoted. To president! ...of the company's failing Pegasus Mart offshoot. Bok-dong makes it his mission to get revenge by bankrupting the store, hiring eccentrics to execute eccentric, entirely whackadoo plans and accidentally getting Pegasus noticed by customers, who quickly make it more popular than ever. Think The Producers, but in retail. Stream Pegasus Market on Tubi.

It might sound a little (or a lot) niche, but we’ve seen enough headlines about the working conditions at many video game production houses to understand why a workplace comedy set against such a backdrop would make for a dark and juicy comedy. Charlotte Nicdao and Rob McElhenney are the leads, playing a brilliant workaholic and an unsociable egomaniac, respectively, and the chemistry between them gives the show more than enough spark. There's also a four-episode spin-off called Side Quest. Stream Mythic Quest.

A half-hour comedy-drama with an emphasis on the comedy, Gentefied follows three Mexican-American cousins who have built lives in Los Angeles, only to be faced with a new challenge: the looming gentrification of the neighborhood they helped to build via their family's taco shop. Gentefied has a baked-in sense of place and culture and a lot of heart; the second season is even better than the first. Stream Gentefied on Netflix.

Perhaps there's a bit of counter-programming in this dramedy about a couple of scrappy New York City outsiders, but there's a fundamental goofiness to this show about a couple of nice guys who are great at getting themselves into trouble, and equally good at talking themselves out of it. Bryan Greenberg plays Ben Epstein, a quiet guy with any number of big ideas, while Victor Rasuk plays the outgoing, often shameless Cam Calderon; together they manage a startup clothing business with the benefits of neither money nor experience, amiably hustling their way to success, maybe. Stream How to Make It in America on HBO Max and Netflix.

Debuting at the beginning of the Obama administration before getting a surprise revival just a couple of years ago, Party Down is an acclaimed cult sitcom for the ages—lots of laughs, low ratings, and always worth rediscovering. A group of six (or so) struggling LA actors and writers work as cater waiters for a fancy company, with every episode into a new and wildly absurd situation, even as their aspirations far outstrip their actual lives. Stream Party Down on Prime Video and Netflix.

A legitimate sitcom that just happens to be set in Northern Ireland during the violent Troubles of the 1990s, when clashes between nationalists and unionists frequently resulted in violence. It’s a fascinating contrast, brought to life by a writer and creator (Lisa McGee) who lived it. It’s also laugh-out-loud funny—though it doesn’t make any allowances for audiences unaccustomed to Irish accents, so don’t feel bad if you need subtitles until you get the hang of it. Erin, Orla, Clare, and Michelle are joined by James, the only male student at their Catholic girls' school, dealing with normal growing-up stuff in absurd times. This world is a far cry from that of Minimum Wage, but Lisa McGee's sense of the absurd connects both shows—if the setting is a bit more dramatic, the comedy is just as wonderfully silly. Stream Derry Girls on Netflix.

Not a comedy! But about as good an indication of where we are in the modern global workplace as you're likely to find. Hyuk‑jun is a young guy saddled with debt who signs on for some part-time work at a job agency...at 50x the going rate, no less (should've been a red flag). Each new assignment places him in new and increasingly horrific situations, with increasingly arbitrary-seeming rules. But, hey, in 2026, it's a living. Stream Dead-End Job on Netflix.

It's an office (obviously) and not a pizza joint, but the point here is kinda that white-collar jobs in the 21st century can be at least as soul-killing as working customer service. The Office inherited some of the finer tropes of the workplace comedy (mostly involving tossing together a group of weirdos overly invested in their jobs) while also launching a million mockumentary-style shows, running for nine seasons, and becoming one of the most popular shows of its era. Stream The Office on Peacock.

#3370. 5 Fantasy LitRPG Books Better Than 'Dungeon Crawler Carl'

LitRPG is having a moment, and it’s largely thanks to Dungeon Crawler Carl. While Matt Dinniman's book series isn't the newest entry in the video game-inspired literary genre, it's arguably one of its most recognizable titles. It has attracted 14 million readers and is even getting a live-action TV adaptation on Peacock, produced by Universal Television and Seth MacFarlane's Fuzzy Door.

Dungeon Crawler Carl won readers over with its clueless protagonist, Carl, and his ex-girlfriend's pampered tortoiseshell cat, Princess Donut, as they struggle to survive the depths of the World Dungeon, an 18-level death game reminiscent of Squid Game. While the series is undoubtedly a fan favorite, there are plenty of other books that deserve just as much attention, if not more. From an isekai-inspired adventure to a mother fighting to keep her children alive during an invasion, here are fantasy LitRPG book series that are better than Dungeon Crawler Carl.

Readers who want something with no fluff and all grind will find that The Primal Hunter gets the job done. When the universe suddenly becomes part of a multiverse governed by a mysterious System, introverted business analyst Jake Thayne finds himself trapped in a deadly 63-day survival tutorial alongside his coworkers. Armed with a bow and an unexpected knack for killing, Jake quickly discovers that he's much better at combat than he ever imagined possible.

Dungeon Crawler Carl also has plenty of RPG mechanics, including levels, skills, equipment, quests, and achievements. However, these are tied to a televised dungeon competition, where rewards, audience engagement, and entertainment shape how the game unfolds. The Primal Hunter takes a more traditional MMORPG approach. Its System provides a framework for progression through levels, classes, skills, professions, and stats. Jake develops his own build, improves his abilities, and grows stronger to survive increasingly dangerous encounters.

While there are emotional arcs, The Primal Hunter doesn't spend too much time on them, keeping the storyline entirely focused on Jake's growth and combat mastery. Readers will find him spending most of his time either in wilderness zones or alchemy labs. As the story progresses, he faces higher-tier monsters, cosmic-level challenges, and plenty of new abilities to master. It's straightforward and no-nonsense, without requiring too much emotional commitment, making it perfect for a less demanding read overall.

Carl might have his chonky Princess Donut, but Apocalypse Parenting takes things to another level: its heroes are literally a mother and her three young children. Their chances of surviving the situation seem pretty slim, but never underestimate the sheer power of motherhood. When Earth is selected for an intergalactic game show, Meghan Moretti finds herself in survival mode with her children while her husband is away. Think these monsters will spare them? Think again. Little do they know, her own kids will have to learn how to defend themselves, too.

Taking a more survival-focused, character-driven approach to LitRPG, Apocalypse Parenting follows an ordinary mother doing everything she can to keep her three children alive. Rather than focusing solely on fighting monsters or collecting rewards, its RPG mechanics revolve around practical survival skills. Meghan isn't just looking to become stronger for the next battle; she's thinking about securing drinking water by plugging bathtub drains, managing household resources, and preparing her family for the dangers ahead. These everyday decisions become essential to their survival.

Despite its alien sci-fi premise, the series uses its grounded family focus to create a surprising amount of claustrophobic, A Quiet Place-like tension. There's no grand quest to pursue or ultimate villain to defeat; Meghan's main priority is keeping her home and family intact. And when you're a parent, that kind of pressure hits a little closer to home.

The Wandering Inn is perfect for readers looking for something a little simpler and cozier than the grand adventures LitRPG is often known for. Erin Solstice is an ordinary woman from Earth who somehow finds herself transported to a fantasy world. Rather than searching for a way home, she takes refuge in an abandoned inn and eventually becomes its Innkeeper. Instead of pursuing quests or aspiring to become a hero, she focuses on turning the place into a humble home.

In typical LitRPG fashion, skill progression is often tied to killing monsters, completing quests, or finding treasures. Not in The Wandering Inn. Here, characters level up through everyday activities like cleaning, cooking, and even finding menstrual supplies, which can be surprisingly difficult when the creatures around them are unfamiliar with the concept of periods.

However, don't let its cozy, slice-of-life premise fool you. While Erin serves as the story's anchor, the series introduces hundreds of other perspectives across multiple continents, opening the door to storylines involving military strategy, medical drama, and goblin survival. This creates quite a contrast with the quieter life established at the beginning. Readers should expect plenty of whiplash, with monster attacks and wars threatening to destroy the inn just chapters after Erin has been baking bread or playing chess.

Carl might be snarky in Dungeon Crawler Carl, but Jason has even more bite thanks to his sharp tongue and sarcastic attitude in He Who Fights with Monsters. In an isekai-like twist, Jason Asano's life turns upside down when he wakes up naked in a monster-infested hedge maze, where magic and gods exist alongside video game-like mechanics. After surviving a blood cult, stopping an apocalypse-class monster, and discovering his own magical abilities, Jason eventually joins the Adventurers' Society.

Although Dungeon Crawler Carl also incorporates game-like mechanics, He Who Fights with Monsters offers a much more extensive RPG framework. Its detailed character sheets establish measurable attributes, abilities, and progression requirements, giving the fantasy world a clearly defined structure. More importantly, these mechanics are interconnected. Completing quests, defeating monsters, and collecting resources all contribute to character development, making the RPG system feel like a character in its own right. It's a great choice for readers who enjoy the more technical side of LitRPG.

Storytelling-wise, He Who Fights with Monsters takes a more philosophical approach, which makes sense given that its title comes from a Friedrich Nietzsche quote. What begins as a survival story gradually becomes a journey of self-discovery that explores Nietzsche's monster paradox. Jason must learn to fight corrupt gods and powerful elites, but the real question is whether he can do so without becoming just as monstrous as the enemies he opposes.

Alden Thorn has always wanted to be a superhero, but he's not exactly interested in punching monsters in Super Supportive. He'd rather be the guy keeping everyone else alive. That's not an easy dream in a world where an alien System decides who gets magical abilities and what powers they receive. After becoming one of Earth's Avowed, Alden gets his chance, but he'll have to figure out how to make his unusual support abilities work in a world that often values fighters more than healers.

Unlike Dungeon Crawler Carl, Super Supportive doesn't treat its RPG mechanics like a game people happen to be playing. Much of the fun comes from watching Aldren experiment with his abilities rather than simply chase higher stats. He starts with the Meister of Cudgel class but eventually trades it for Chainer, giving him access to powerful wordchains.

Sleyca also takes her time with Alden's character development, giving readers all the more reason to root for the protagonist. Between school, personal struggles, and training on Anesidora, there's plenty happening outside combat. The story also explores alien cultures, interspecies politics, and Earth's complicated relationship with the Artonans. It's a slower, more character-driven LitRPG, but readers who enjoy watching a protagonist gradually figure out his powers will find plenty to get invested in.

Leaker Aaron Perris has discovered evidence of a new Mac app in the works at Apple called Harbor, which makes it easy to run local AI models across one or more Macs.

The Mac has been getting a lot more popular this year, both because of budget-friendly options like MacBook Neo but also as a tool for running AI models locally on Mac Studio, Mac mini, and more.

#3367. There’s a Good Reason the NYC Marathon Winners Wore These Watches

Over 60,000 runners crossed the finish line at the New York City Marathon last week. When you think of the elites fighting for a spot on the podium, you might expect to see only the priciest, most feature-packed GPS watches money can buy—historically, this meant the most premium Garmin Forerunners. Looking at the wrists of this year's New York City Marathon podium finishers, though,  you’ll see that Garmin—the name most recreational runners reach for by default—was far from the only brand on the course.

Here are the watches I’ve been able to confirm among the top NYC Marathon finishers:

Men's winner, Andreas Almgren: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Men's runner-up, Yemaneberhan Crippa: Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro (sponsored)

Women's runner-up, Jessica McClain: Garmin Forerunner 570 (sponsored)

Women's third place, Hellen Obiri: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Nonbinary winner, Ryan Montgomery: Suunto Race 3S (almost certainly sponsored, since this watch was released last month)

An important disclaimer: I haven't spoken with any of these athletes. What follows is my opinion, based on what I know running watches offer the people who wear them.

"Garmin" has long been the default answer to "what running watch should I buy?" It earned that spot with reliable GPS, excellent software, and a huge ecosystem. And on this podium, it's represented by a Forerunner 570—a great watch, but at a price tag most runners would struggle to justify.

Of course, sponsorships muddy the water, since athletes wear what their sponsors put on their wrists. But that's exactly the point: Other brands are investing in elite runners because they believe their products can stand next to Garmin's, and it looks like they’re making the right bet.

It's fair to ask whether Garmin's grip is loosening. The company has increasingly pushed toward the fanciest watches with the most features at higher and higher price points. The Forerunner 570 starts north of $500. Meanwhile, COROS, Amazfit, and others are proving that a perfectly solid, competitive watch doesn't need to cost that much. Is Garmin still the best running watch overall? For ecosystem, polish, and depth of features, it's still a strong contender. But "best" no longer means "the only serious option," and the gap between Garmin and the field is narrower than it has been in years. Sponsored or not, seeing two Coros Pace 4s and an Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro among the top finishers is worth noting.

You don’t need an expensive watch to be elite—just look at the cheap running watches worn by the men who broke the sub-two-hour barrier at the London Marathon this past spring. Training load scores, recovery metrics, maps, music, and smart notifications are nice, but they're extras. If you're shopping for a watch, spend your money on the basics being done right, and don't feel pressured to pay for features you'll never use. Everything besides your time and pace is icing on the cake.

Whichever brand you choose, focus on these basics in your running watch:

The New York City Marathon podium shows a running-watch market that's a bit more competitive and intriguing than the era of "just buy a Garmin" suggests. Garmin is still excellent, but now we’re seeing proof that Coros, Amazfit, and Suunto are all making watches good enough for the fastest humans on the planet. If they can trust those watches on their biggest days, the rest of us can probably trust them with our Saturday long runs.

#3366. iOS 27.2 adds new features in six iPhone apps, details here

iOS 27.2 recently launched with new features for iPhone users, including improvements across six Apple apps. Here’s what’s new.

One of my favorite additions to Messages this year, Suggested Actions, debuts in iOS 27.2.

Suggested Actions appear underneath messages in a conversation when relevant. They can suggest creating a calendar event or reminder, adding to a note, and more based on the context of the message.

The feature was originally part of the iOS 27 beta this summer, but didn’t make the public build. Now it’s back in iOS 27.2, new and improved. There’s also an option to fine-tune which types of suggestions you’ll see.

Read more: iOS 27.2 adds new Messages feature that’s already a favorite

Every major streaming service has its own profiles feature, letting users on the same account keep their viewing history and recommendations separate. Apple TV has long offered such a feature in tvOS, but now with iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2 it’s coming to iPhone and iPad too.

When you launch the TV app in iOS 27.2, you’ll be greeted by a new profile selection screen. You can easily disable it if you don’t want to see if again. But if you ever share your iPhone with kids, the new profiles feature should come in handy.

Read more: iOS 27.2 gives Apple TV a new profiles feature on iPhone

Dual Capture is one of FaceTime’s best new features in years. Added in iOS 27, on compatible iPhones it lets you keep your front and rear cameras both active at the same time while on a FaceTime call.

iOS 27.2 brings a key upgrade to Dual Capture: it’s now available for Group FaceTime calls.

To use the feature, just hit the flip camera button like usual, and by default on iPhone 17 and newer you’ll stream both camera feeds simultaneously.

Read more: iOS 27.2 makes FaceTime’s best new feature even better

Timed with its new Home products push, Apple adds a pair of new Home app features in iOS 27.2 for compatible smart locks.

‘Lock After Closing’ is a new automation setting that lets you choose how long after a door is closed that it should lock automatically. Previously you could only set a duration based on the time since a door was unlocked, not closed.

‘Door Left Open’ tackles a related, but distinct problem: a door being left open too long. With compatible locks, you can configure the Home app to automatically notify you if a door has been left open for a certain period of time.

Read more: iOS 27.2 has three new changes just added this week

Apple Podcasts keeps getting better, with AI-powered automatic chapters and transcripts some of my favorite features. And in iOS 27.2, Apple has a welcome change to the Up Next queue on the Home tab.

Up Next is now split into two separate queues: New Episodes and Continue Playing.

Without the redesigned Health app, none of the new features appeal to me all that much. But performance improvements, bug fixes, and security fixes are always welcomed. What most of really wants is faster and more reliable Siri AI, along with support for a wider range of personal data, such as PDF documents on the iCloud Drive.

New Episodes contains only the latest episodes from shows you follow, while Continue Playing is a hub for all the episodes you’ve previously started but haven’t yet finished.

Apple’s Games app introduces some small updates in iOS 27.2 as well.

The Home tab now shows you recently downloaded games that you haven’t yet played. Previously, you would only see games with some play activity. And Apple says achievement progress and leaderboard scores have been updated in the Home tab to be easier to track. Finally, the Friends tab “provides context on friend suggestions and shows recent games played on friends’ player pages” per Apple.

Which new iOS 27.2 features are you most excited about? Let us know in the comments.
