#3364. I tested the world’s largest flat super ultrawide monitor that’s like having two 27-inch screens side by side — and it’s a game changer for multitasking

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Innocn E49M1R delivers massive, dual-27-inch screen real estate in a unique flat form factor, backed by punchy Mini-LED backlighting and plenty of ports. The lack of USB-C Power Delivery and edge wash-out from sitting too close hold it back slightly — though if you have a deep desk and run a desktop PC, there’s no monitor quite like it.

Widest, flat super ultrawide monitor available

Deep blacks thanks to Mini-LED backlighting

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The Innocn E49M1R isn’t your standard super ultrawide monitor. Instead of a curved panel like on other popular massive displays, it’s completely flat and gives you the screen real estate of two 27-inch, 1440p monitors running across your desk.

When connected to your PC or Mac, you can have two full-sized browser windows or apps running side by side. This makes the E49M1R an excellent choice for productivity, though with a 165Hz panel, Mini-LED backlighting, and AMD FreeSync Premium, it also provides a very immersive gaming experience — granted you have a PC powerful enough to run games at this monitor’s native resolution.

I’ve been using the E49M1R as my daily driver for a month now, and it’s definitely changed how I work. While I’ve used a standard 21:9 ultrawide display for almost a decade, jumping to 32:9 and all that extra screen space has made a real difference while multitasking. Still, it has its trade-offs. While this monitor offers dual HDMI and DisplayPort connections, it’s missing a USB-C port for a one-cable connection to your laptop. Likewise, due to its VA panel and sheer width, colors can appear washed out at the edges if you’re sitting too close.

My Innocn E49M1R review will help you decide if this is the best monitor for your workflow and your desk, or if it’s worth going with something smaller or slightly curved instead.

2 x HDMI 2.1, 2 x DisplayPort 1.4, 1 x audio out, 2 x USB-A, 1 x USB-B

47.82 × 1.99 × 14.43 inches (without stand), 47.82 × 9.31 × 21.44 inches (with stand)

The Innocn E49M1R is truly one of a kind, as there’s no other flat super ultrawide display this large. It takes up the full width of most desks, but in return, you get an impressively bright picture, plenty of screen real estate, enough input ports to connect four devices at once, and built-in speakers for the complete package.

At 47.82 x 1.99 x 14.43 inches, the E49M1R is the largest monitor I’ve ever unboxed. Just like with a large TV, I’d recommend having someone help you unpack it and install the included metal stand. In addition, you also get a power cord, an HDMI 2.1 cable, and a DisplayPort cable in the box. Unfortunately, there isn’t a USB-B cable included, which you’ll need if you want to take advantage of the E49M1R’s built-in USB hub — more on that later.

Just like with the other Innocn monitors I’ve tested, installing the metal stand is a breeze. It simply snaps into the back of the monitor, and a single thumb screw attaches the arm to its sturdy metal base. If you’d rather use one of the best monitor arms instead of the included stand, there are 100 x 100 VESA mounting holes on the back of the display.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

One thing I really appreciate about the E49M1R is that instead of tucking all the ports on the underside like you often see on other monitors, they’re all positioned on the back. Along with being height-adjustable, the stand features a cutout near the bottom to make routing cables up to the display easier.

Port-wise, you get dual HDMI 2.1 inputs and dual DisplayPort 1.4 connections, alongside an audio jack. There’s also a USB-B upstream port that, when connected to your computer, lets you use the two USB-A ports next to it for wireless dongles or a webcam. This isn’t a KVM (keyboard, video, mouse) switch, though, as you can’t share those peripherals across two separate computers. At the same time, there’s no USB-C port with Power Delivery, which feels like an odd omission on a premium, super ultrawide monitor like the E49M1R.

With the E49M1R unboxed and the stand installed, it was time to get it set up on my desk. Now a word of warning here — if you have a desk that’s 48 inches wide, you likely won’t have room for a full desktop PC, though you could tuck one of the best mini PCs underneath this massive display.

I set the E49M1R up on a desk shelf attached to the back of the Secretlab Magnus Evo, and even though that desk is 60 inches wide, things still felt a bit cramped. Fortunately, I’m in the process of reviewing the GMKtec Evo-X3, which is quite thin and designed to be used vertically.

So what’s it like sitting in front of a massive, 49-inch flat super ultrawide? It was definitely daunting at first, but after a few hours, my eyes and neck adjusted to the larger display. By default, you can position one app or browser window on either side, and this felt a lot like the dual-monitor setup I put together last year — just without a gap between the two screens.

While using the E49M1R with two Chrome windows side by side worked well enough, it wasn’t until I installed Microsoft’s PowerToys utility that I could take full advantage of this monitor. Using PowerToys’ built-in FancyZones window manager, I was able to split this 49-inch display into thirds, keeping a smaller window for video calls in the middle with two larger browser windows on either side for multitasking. This worked great, as I could look straight at the center of the screen while presenting and glance off to the side when I needed to check notes or respond to a quick message.

As someone who’s been using an ultrawide monitor for years, making the jump from 21:9 to 32:9 felt natural. If you’ve been using a standard 16:9 display on its own, though, you might be better off switching to a 21:9 ultrawide first before going all the way up to a super ultrawide — especially with a completely flat one like the E49M1R.

One thing you’ll likely have to deal with when switching to an ultrawide — or even a super ultrawide — monitor is black bars on the sides of most video content. However, when you find a video with the right aspect ratio for your screen, it’s a sight to behold.

To put the E49M1R’s video capabilities to the test, I scoured YouTube for 32:9 trailers until I found one for Godzilla vs. Kong. Seeing King Kong leaping across the landscape and fighting in Hollow Earth was downright awesome, and even though this was a compressed YouTube stream, the picture still looked fantastic on the E49M1R.

Based on our lab tests, you can see that while the E49M1R isn’t as bright as some other premium monitors when displaying content in SDR, it absolutely shines with HDR enabled — hitting a blistering 1,474 nits. It did fairly well with color accuracy, though this is a productivity monitor, and I wouldn’t recommend it for color grading or other heavy graphical work.

While 32:9 videos may be hard to find online, the same can’t be said for games. With a powerful gaming PC, you can fully immerse yourself in the action across the E49M1R’s entire 49-inch display.

Even though it was a tight fit, I managed to get the GMKtec Neo-X1 Pro set up on the side of the E49M1R and play some Red Dead Redemption 2. Riding on my horse across the Wild West as Arthur Morgan felt almost like a dream come true, as I could take in all the scenery thanks to the E49M1R’s wider field of view. I’m sure playing a racing game like Forza Horizon 6 would have been even better, though.

It’s worth noting that while the E49M1R has a 165Hz refresh rate with support for AMD FreeSync Premium, the display definitely lags behind the best gaming monitors when it comes to response time. At 8ms, it’s better suited for slower-paced games, which is why I tested it out with Red Dead Redemption 2 as opposed to a fast-paced, competitive shooter.

All in all, though, you can certainly play games on the E49M1R — even if it’s ultimately better suited for multi-window productivity tasks.

There’s truly no super ultrawide monitor quite like the Innocn E49M1R, thanks to its massive, completely flat display. However, that sheer width can cause colors on either side to look washed out depending on how close you’re sitting, and a USB-C port would have been a welcome addition.

Although this is the first super ultrawide monitor I’ve tested, I’ve actually spent quite a bit of time using two of Innocn’s ultrawide displays: the 40C1U and the 40C1R. While the former is a premium display with a 5K2K resolution and the latter is a more budget-friendly gaming monitor, both feature USB-C with Power Delivery.

Unfortunately, the E49M1R doesn’t. Now, I know some budget laptops would struggle to drive a massive display like this one, but most modern machines can handle it just fine. With Power Delivery built in, you also wouldn’t need to reach for your laptop charger — instead, you could just plug in your Windows laptop or MacBook and get right to work on the E49M1R’s 49-inch screen.

For a monitor with a list price of $999, the lack of a USB-C port is really puzzling, especially since I’ve tested much cheaper displays from Innocn that have one.

Now, whether you prefer a flat or curved ultrawide is something you’ll have to figure out on your own. Personally, I like flat ultrawides since they take up less space on my desk and can easily be wall-mounted or attached to a monitor arm.

With the E49M1R and its VA panel, however, its massive width creates a sort of optical illusion. Even though the picture on either side is just as bright as it is at the center, it doesn’t always appear that way — particularly when you’re sitting very close to the display. For instance, with three Chrome windows side by side, content on the outer two would appear washed out when I turned my head to look at it. However, if I pulled my office chair back a bit, it looked completely normal.

Now, if you’re dead set on having the largest, flattest super ultrawide monitor out there, I’d recommend pairing the E49M1R with a very deep desk. That way, you can position the monitor at the very back edge to mitigate this optical illusion. If you’re short on space, though, and aren’t using one of the best standing desks, you could always wall-mount this display just like you would a TV.

The Innocn E49M1R is truly one of a kind, and it’s a great fit for those who want as much screen real estate as possible without a multi-monitor setup or having to give up desk space for a curved display. That alone would be enough, but its Mini-LED backlighting really makes colors pop and blacks appear deeper, too. You also get plenty of ports alongside a built-in USB hub.

While I would have liked a built-in KVM switch as well, that isn’t necessarily a dealbreaker. Missing a USB-C port with Power Delivery could be a problem if you’re mainly a laptop user — though if you primarily use a desktop computer, this won’t be an issue, even if it still would have been a nice addition.

The Innocn E49M1R delivers and then some for anyone who wants the widest, flattest super ultrawide monitor you can get. At full price, you’re getting plenty of screen space for your buck — just make sure this display isn’t too wide for your setup and that you have a desk big enough to house it first.

#3362. This Actively Exploited Chrome Vulnerability Is Putting Your Browser at Risk

If you've seen an uptick in security updates as of late, you're not alone. AI models have become very good at finding new security vulnerabilities throughout 2026. Researchers and hackers alike are increasingly relying on these models in their individual pursuits: Hackers want to find these flaws to exploit them, while researchers want to block hackers from doing so. Microsoft's latest Patch Tuesday update included more than 1,400 patches; meanwhile, Apple's latest security update fixed two iMessage flaws that let both bad actors and innocent parties alike access texts they shouldn't.

Whether you use a Mac or a PC, you probably browse the web with Chrome, or a Chromium-based browser. As it happens, Google's web browsing platform is the latest to receive an important security update—but it's far from the first important Chrome update of the year.

As reported by The Hacker News, Google released a new update for Chrome on Monday that patches nine security flaws. While all vulnerabilities are important to patch, one in particular is more serious than the rest: CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component.

Use-after-free vulnerabilities happen when the system frees up a memory location, but a program tries to access it anyway. It's a glitch in programming, but it offers bad actors an opportunity to break into your system. At worst, it allows arbitrary code execution, or, in other words, gives hackers the ability to run their own code in the app or system.

That's bad enough on the surface, but, unfortunately, Google confirmed that CVE-2026-125350 has an active exploit in the wild. The company is keeping other details close to the vest, but it's dangerous nonetheless. At least someone, somewhere, has used this flaw against a target, which puts all Chrome users (as well as users of Chromium-based browsers) at risk.

What's more, this isn't Chrome's first active exploit of the year—this is its eighth. The company is playing catch-up with hackers looking to target users of its browser, which makes sense, seeing as Chrome is by far the world's most popular browser.

If you're using Chrome on your computer, you'll want to update it as soon as possible. Make sure you're running at least versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 on Mac or PC, or 157.0.8103.50 on Linux. To check, click the three dots in the top-right corner of your Chrome window, then go to More > Help > About Google Chrome.

Other Chromium-based browsers may not have the update yet, but they are affected by this flaw. If you use browsers like Microsoft Edge, Opera, or Brave, keep an eye on your updates to install any of the latest patches.

#3359. 7 Most Politically Subversive Movies of All Time, Ranked

There are multiple ways in which a film can be subversive, whether it's by twisting the tropes of its genres on their head, deliberately undermining traditional societal norms, or bending genres to surprise audiences. One particular thing that makes several of the most subversive movies in history so great, on the other hand, is that they disrupt and aggressively question dominant political ideologies, the mainstream media, and topics that are usually considered taboo.

It's one thing for a film to be artistically subversive, but films that actively challenge dominant power structures and cultural norms instead of reinforcing them prove that politically subversive cinema can be particularly powerful. Over the years, the big screen has been treated to several such movies, made by artists of the caliber of Stanley Kubrick and Pier Paolo Pasolini.

Infamous for being one of the most heavily censored mainstream horror films in history, Ken Russell's The Devils is about as legendary as the director himself. Based on the fall of 17th-century Catholic priest Urbain Grandier and the possessions of Loudun, it's a film which weaponizes blasphemy and sacrilege to tell a story that is, at its core, far more political than it is religious.

There is certainly plenty of religious commentary in The Devils, but what makes it one of the best horror masterpieces of the '70s is how unapologetic it is in calling out procedural injustice, the centralization of power, and government brainwashing through religious hysteria. It's a must-see NC-17 cult classic that's made all the more politically potent by the fact that it's based on true events.

Charles Chaplin had long refused to get with the times and leave behind the silent cinema that he had completely revolutionized. However, going into the late '30s, he found that the subject matter of The Great Dictator deserved to be such a direct political statement that it couldn't possibly be anything but his first true talkie. Thus, the world was treated to one of the best dark comedy movies of all time.

By the time the film came out — and certainly when Chaplin began developing it in 1938 — many in the Western world still vastly underestimated the horrors that were being committed by Hitler and the Nazis. So, Chaplin did what he did best: he took these very serious topics and ridiculed dictators like Hitler and Mussolini, loudly calling for a stop to their atrocities well before the United States entered World War II.

Sergei Eisenstein is widely regarded as one of the most important and influential filmmakers in history, largely thanks to his contributions to the art of film editing. There is no better way to learn about and understand those contributions than watching Battleship Potemkin, one of the best war thrillers of all time, which dramatizes the 1905 mutiny aboard the eponymous Russian battleship.

Battleship Potemkin is proof that even an official piece of state propaganda can be politically subversive. Indeed, though the film was commissioned by the Soviet government to celebrate the 1905 revolution, it was an explosive piece of international political subversion seeking to undermine the capitalist social order the world over. Later on, even the USSR itself came to consider Eisenstein's avant-garde techniques a bit too rebellious for their taste.

Despite how quiet it seems, Kubrick's Paths of Glory is also one of the most outwardly anti-war movies in history, based on the Souain corporals affair that took place during World War I. Due to the film's critically negative depiction of the French military, the country refused to allow Kubrick to shoot there and even refused to allow the movie to screen there until 1972.

What arguably makes Paths of Glory even more radical and subversive, as far as Kubrick's anti-war movies go, is that instead of laughing at the matter, it's an entirely solemn and serious depiction of it. One of the most hopeless war movies of all time, Paths of Glory exposes the dark underbelly of military leadership in ways that no other film had really dared to depict before. In it, patriotism and military justice are dangerous myths used to manipulate working-class young men into allowing themselves to be used like cannon fodder.

What could possibly be more politically subversive than a movie that has been documented to be used as a training manual by both insurgent and counterinsurgency groups? We are, of course, talking about Gillo Pontecorvo's Italian-Algerian masterpiece The Battle of Algiers, a docudrama shot in a newsreel style about the rebellion against the French government during the Algerian War.

It's one of the best films of the 1960s, crafted with such an unparalleled sense of visceral realism that it really does allow the audience to feel as though they're flies on the wall, watching this conflict from the outside. Without ever sugarcoating the horrific violence of anti-colonial resistance or state counter-terrorism, Pontecorvo forces the viewer to witness all of this brutality with every moral nuance and political layer laid bare for them to closely analyze.

From beginning to end and from top to bottom, Pier Paolo Pasolini's Italian-French political art horror masterpiece Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom is a movie specifically designed to be as subversive, transgressive, and provocative as possible. Loosely adapting Marquis de Sade's The 120 Days of Sodom and setting the story in WWII Italy instead of 18th-century France, the film was released a mere three weeks after Pasolini was killed, making it his final masterpiece.

Saying that you need a strong stomach to get through Salò would be the understatement of the century. Pasolini, a lifelong Marxist and critic of Italian power structures, wanted to make a movie that criticized consumerism, fascism, and systematic abuse. Boy, did he succeed. Salò is quite infamously one of the heaviest movies of the 20th century, so politically aggressive and full of unrelenting, stomach-churning horror that it was outright banned across many countries. In many territories, it still faces bans and censorship to this day.

For precisely the same reasons that arguably make it the single most politically rebellious feature film in history, Herbert J. Biberman's Salt of the Earth was one of the first fully independent movies made outside of the Hollywood studio system. That's because Biberman, as well as screenwriter Michael Wilson and producer Paul Jarrico, were all blacklisted in Hollywood at the time due to their alleged involvement in communist politics.

Salt of the Earth was a direct act of working-class political subversion starring actual striking laborers and their families, created as an explicit celebration of worker solidarity and civil rights right at the peak of McCarthyism and the Red Scare in the United States. As if that weren't enough, it's also one of the greatest American films of the '50s, making it a must-see for all those interested in how complex politically radical cinema can be at its best.

#3358. High-Protein Packaged Foods May Not Be As Healthy As They Look

Of the three major macronutrients—protein, carbs, and fat—protein has the best reputation, and it’s fairly well deserved. We need significant amounts of protein in our diet, and nothing particularly bad happens if we get too much. Dietary protein helps you build muscle, and if you’re trying to lose weight it helps stop you from losing too much muscle along with the fat. It also helps to make meals feel filling. Great! But.

Once the general public gets the idea that something is good for you, the companies that make packaged food start putting it in everything. Or, they make products where the good-for-you thing features prominently on the label, whether or not there is very much inside. So a lot of packaged food now boasts protein on the label. Here’s what you should ask yourself about those foods:

Take a close look here—sometimes a food will boast of a certain amount of protein per package but the package contains two or three servings. Other times, the protein per serving is correct, and we're supposed to be excited to have, say, 7 grams per serving. That's just not very much—and certainly not worth paying extra or choosing a less-delicious food just for those few added grams.

It’s good to know how much protein you need in your diet. If you’re not gaining or losing weight, and not doing very much exercise, a 150-pound person only needs about 54 grams of protein a day. (I've done the math for various body weights here.) If you’re working out a lot, or if you’re trying to gain or lose weight (yep, either way), that same 150-pound person will need more like 81 to 95 grams of protein per day. More is OK, but not necessary.

So if you’re trying to get 90 grams per day, 30 grams per meal is a reasonable amount to shoot for. Coincidentally, 30 grams is the amount of protein that tends to make a meal feel satisfying. You can do the math to figure out whether a protein-added product is going to be helpful in your day’s diet.

I think this is the most important question about protein-added foods. It’s not hard to get protein in a meal; meats, dairy, tofu, beans, and grains all tend to supply plenty. So what is this protein-added thing you’re considering, and are you eating it instead of a traditional meal?

Here’s an example. If I’m heading straight from the gym to run some errands, and I need something to substitute for a meal—yeah, this isn’t great planning, but sometimes it happens—a protein bar with 20 grams of protein is a step in the right direction. Much better than a candy bar, anyway.

But then there are things like this "protein mix" trail mix: 7 grams of protein with 200 calories. A double serving would be 400 calories and only 14 grams of protein. Hardly a great choice if your goal is just to add to your protein intake for the day.

And then there are the chips that my kid, for a time, couldn't stop eating. He loves Doritos and such; on a whim, we bought him some protein chips (yes, these are a real thing). Are they better for him than the equivalent amount of Doritos? Arguably, sort of yes. But then he started arguing that since they have protein, he should be able to eat them in place of dinner. We nixed that, but admit it: Are you having that same argument with yourself, feeling better about a snack food because it contains extra protein? If so, the marketing is working—you’re feeling good about your supposedly healthy choices, even though you’re just eating a bag of chips.

Spotify today expanded customization options for its AI DJ, allowing users to choose between different voices and personalities, as well as control how much the DJ talks between songs. Here are the details.

If you’re not familiar with Spotify’s AI DJ feature, the company describes it as “a personalized mix of music and commentary to help you discover new favorites and connect more deeply with the artists you love,” adding that it takes your listening history into account to “[bring] together your favorite tracks, songs you haven’t heard in years, and new releases to keep things feeling fresh.”

Spotify first introduced the interactive version of DJ in May 2025, and soon expanded its capabilities to Spanish-speaking users. Then, last May, Spotify expanded availability to more than 75 countries, alongside support for French, German, Italian, and Brazilian Portuguese.

Now, as spotted by TechCrunch, Spotify is introducing more customization options, including new voices and personalities, as well as the ability to reduce commentary between songs.

In a new post published on Spotify’s For the Record blog, the company announced today that “Spotify Premium listeners in markets where DJ is available can choose from an expanded selection of DJ voices in English and Spanish,” with seven new English options spanning British, American, Irish, Australian, and Indian accents, along with two new Spanish voices.

Additionally, Spotify now lets users choose whether they want commentary between sets of songs through a toggle that reduces the DJ’s interruptions to brief acknowledgments when starting a session or requesting different music.

#3355. Everything You Should Know About Black Friday 2026 Sales: Early Deals, Dates, and Retailers

As is often the case with major sales these days, retailers are increasingly blurring the lines between early deals and the official start of a sale. Black Friday sales appear to be becoming a month-long event, with early deals appearing in the first week of the month. If you haven't been paying attention, major retailers have already put out their plans and even started churning out deals. But you're still in time to make this upcoming Black Friday sale a great one. Here is everything you need to know to prepare you for the big sale.

Black Friday is always the day after Thanksgiving. This year, Black Friday starts at midnight on Nov. 27. Cyber Monday is the Monday following Black Friday, which starts at midnight on Nov. 30.

The major retailers doing sales are the usual: Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Home Depot, and many others. Currently, Walmart has publicized its plans already and has early deals available. Best Buy is offering one of the largest Black Friday and Cyber Week sales, with multiple events and early deals. Target has a three-day event. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

Unlike Spring or Summer sales, Black Friday doesn't focus on specific categories, which means everything is fair game for discounts. In previous years, we've seen tech, tools, fitness equipment, outdoor supplies and furniture, bedding, video games, kitchen appliances, and more. This is one of the best times to make a list of what you need. You're likely to find what you're looking for discounted, and probably at its lowest price it has ever been. If you'd like to avoid having to do all that work, we always vet all of our deals for you. Just follow our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Prime Day and Black Friday are the two best times of the year to get the best deals on most purchases. Of course, depending on what you're shopping for, you might find other opportunities throughout the year, but in general, Prime Day and Black Friday have the best sales.

#3354. Apple to investigate accident that killed three workers at iPhone parts factory in India

Reuters reports that three contract workers died after inhaling gas during an inspection at a Tata Electronics factory that produces iPhone components in India. Here are the details.

As frequent 9to5Mac readers probably know, Apple’s supply chain in India relies heavily on Tata, which manufactures iPhone components and accounts for a significant share of the country’s iPhone assembly operations.

Since Apple began diversifying its manufacturing operations away from China, India has emerged as a major production hub, with roughly a quarter of the world’s iPhones now manufactured in the country.

Earlier this year, Apple found itself linked to an environmental controversy in India, after the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board investigated allegations that wastewater from a Tata facility had contaminated nearby farmland water.

A few weeks later, however, Tata said the regulator had dropped further action against the facility after the company addressed the concerns raised.

At the time, Tata said it had ordered separate testing related to the facility and that the results supported its position that the plant was operating within the rules.

However, the matter was apparently not fully resolved, as just three days later, Reuters reported that local health officials were still investigating complaints from nearby farmers.

And while there had been no major developments reported about the wastewater investigation since then, Reuters reported today that three contract workers died in an accident at the same Tata facility.

The three contract workers died during maintenance work on an effluent treatment ​plant operated by Nalco Water at the Tata facility, which is located in Hosur in Tamil Nadu, ​district official Dinesh Kumar said, adding that the deaths occurred when the workers inhaled gas while inspecting an external nano-filtration tank.

Reuters added that “Apple’s team is visiting ​the plant to assist in ​the ongoing investigation,” though the company did not respond when reached for comment.

The report added that Tata and Tamil Nadu authorities are also investigating the fatal accident, and noted that “production was not affected as the facility was closed for the Hindu festival of Deepavali this week.”

#3352. CleanupBuddy 2.0 expands beyond the keyboard with new display cleaning features

Developer Gui Rambo updated CleanupBuddy today, expanding its ability to prevent accidental inputs while cleaning your Mac from the keyboard to the touchscreen. Here are the details.

If you’re not familiar with CleanupBuddy, this is a nice little app that locks the keyboard to prevent accidental inputs while the user cleans it up.

Once they’re done cleaning, users can press and hold both Cmd keys to unlock the keyboard, then proceed to grease it up again.

The app also features a fun little animated character that reacts to your cleaning sessions with playful (and sometimes snarky) comments.

Today, CleanupBuddy was updated to version 2.0, with options to dim the display and ignore touch inputs, making it useful for users of both the new touchscreen MacBook Pro and Macs with traditional displays.

You can use the new “Lock Touch Screen” option to block touch input while cleaning a supported touch screen. On Macs without a touch screen, the “Dim Display” option can still be used to darken the display for easier cleaning.

Today’s update also tweaks the in-app character, which now uses on-device Apple Intelligence to generate personalized comments before and after cleaning sessions, based on stats such as time spent cleaning, key presses, and mouse clicks.

Rambo explains that these stats are collected only during cleaning sessions and stored locally on the Mac, and that users can independently turn off both cleanup stats and Apple Intelligence integration in the app’s settings.

Other tweaks in today’s update include temporarily disabling Sticky Keys and its Shift-key shortcut during cleaning sessions, as well as improving the readability of the “Start Cleanup” button when using Liquid Glass.

CleanupBuddy 2.0 is available for $2.99 and is compatible with macOS 14 and later, while the new personalized messages require macOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled and its models ready to use.

#3351. Why Websites Show the Wrong Server Location When You Use a VPN

There are many reasons why someone might use a VPN, but most often, it’s to conceal your real geographic location or prevent websites from tracking your online activity. It can also be a way to get around location-based restrictions that stop you from accessing certain websites or platforms.

When you connect to a VPN server in the United States, websites are supposed to detect that your online traffic is originating from the U.S. That way, you can access online platforms that use IP filters to block non-U.S. traffic or circumvent regional censorship when travelling outside the U.S. But if you connect to a VPN server in the United States while you’re vacationing in Mexico, and a website thinks your IP address is from Brazil, that might not solve your problem and may even add unnecessary complications.

If you’ve encountered something similar with your VPN provider, there are several fixes you can try. Depending on why your IP location is being misinterpreted, one of these should help you access the internet from the server location of your choice.

IP geolocation isn’t infallible. Websites rely on third-party IP databases to look up your location based on your current IP address. Maxmind, which has one of the largest such databases in existence, claims that its GeoIP products have a 99.8% accuracy. Lesser-known providers with smaller IP databases may be far less accurate.

Websites can also use more than just your IP address to estimate your location. For example, they can send WebRTC requests to your browser or directly query your device’s GPS. Moreover, VPN providers often have physical servers in one country while their IP addresses are registered to another country, and this discrepancy can also create issues. Let’s take a closer look at each of these problems individually, so you can find the fix that works best for you.

WebRTC is an open-source technology that lets your browser reduce latency when engaged in high-bandwidth tasks like streaming or video calls. Based on the IETF standard RFC 8828, it lets a website choose between your VPN server and your real IP address so it can establish the quickest path to transmit large amounts of data and reduce wait times or buffering.

But the catch with WebRTC is that it exposes both your VPN server and ISP-assigned addresses to websites, which can reveal your real IP location and cause websites to reject your VPN server country. Firefox now comes with built-in protections to prevent WebRTC leaks, while Chrome and Edge support third-party extensions like WebRTC Control that you can use to eliminate these issues. To check if your browser is leaking your real IP address during WebRTC requests, you can use a free tool like BrowserLeaks.

Even when a browser isn’t leaking your real IP address, DNS resolvers may fetch inaccurate location information if their nearest servers are too far from your current location. For example, a user in São Paulo may be geolocated to Chile when using Google Public DNS because that’s where Google’s nearest resolvers are located.

If you toggle on DNS leak protection in your VPN app, this will force websites to use your VPN’s resolver to perform DNS lookups. That often solves the problem, but, again, you can confirm the fix worked through a service like BrowserLeaks or IPLeaks.

Websites rely on IP databases like Maxmind, IP2Location, IPinfo, etc. to look up your exact location, but these databases get outdated quickly and need constant updating. Most of these databases also correct errors on request, but that takes some time. Also, each website has its own rules for how often it queries IP databases for updates.

Even when locations are updated in the actual database, a website may be sitting with outdated information unless it actively has refreshed it recently. MaxMind recommends doing this at least twice a week, but that’s ultimately up to the specific website.

VPN providers often rely on virtual servers that use IP addresses registered in a different region than the server’s physical location. For example, ExpressVPN notes that it serves IP addresses in Bolivia, Ecuador, Peru, Uruguay, and Venezuela through servers located physically in Brazil.

While this is usually to help with the lack of local infrastructure or strict surveillance laws in the region, many databases and analytics tools will flag the discrepancy for websites, leading to confusion and inconsistency regarding your actual server location. In these cases, your best bet is to switch your VPN server or use a dedicated IP address by signing up for a paid add-on for your VPN.

Before investing in a specific solution, it’s better to do a thorough lookup to make sure why your IP address is pointing to the wrong location and whether a WebRTC or DNS issue, virtual servers, or something else is the cause. Here’s how I’d go about it, step by step:

We’ll start by recording your baseline IP address, country, city, and ASN. With your VPN disconnected, navigate to IPConfig.co on your browser to grab your default IP details. I like this tool because it’s free and uses echoip to pull your location data straight from Maxmind. If you prefer using Terminal instead of your browser, you can also run curl ifconfig.co/json to grab these details in plain text format.

Now connect your VPN server. Then visit IPConfig.co again to note down the changed details.

Make sure the Country and Timezone fields match your current VPN server location. Also make sure the ASN (organization) field does not list your home ISP.

In case these details do not match your VPN server, run a WebRTC leak test and a DNS leak test using BrowserLeaks. If either of these tests doesn’t return your VPN server’s IP address, you’ve found your culprit.

If both the leak tests come back clean but a specific site still gets your location wrong, the issue is likely originating from an outdated database or virtual server.

There’s no surefire way to solve IP location mismatches for good. But if it happens often enough to disrupt your internet use, you can consider switching to a different VPN server and getting a browser add-on that prevents WebRTC leaks. If that doesn’t work, I’d consider buying a dedicated IP address that isn’t based on a virtual server. While many IP databases like MaxMind or IP2Location also have ways to request a location correction, that takes a while to go through and isn’t worth the effort unless it’s a permanent IP address registered through your ISP.

#3350. iFixit tears down touchscreen MacBook Pro, reveals light-up Apple logo details

iFixit published its teardown of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display today, revealing interesting details about how Apple brought back its illuminated logo on the lid. Watch it below.

iFixit’s teardown of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is now live, and it explores not only how the new illuminated Apple logo works, but also its tandem OLED and how Apple managed to trim its weight down to 3 pounds (1.38 kg) from 3.4 pounds (1.55 kg) on the standard 14-inch model.

The teardown opens with a close look at the tandem OLED, which stacks two light-emitting layers to deliver higher brightness than conventional single-layer OLED displays.

Under a microscope, iFixit found that the blue subpixels are larger than the red and green ones, which they say should help reduce strain on the materials and potentially extend the display’s lifespan.

Most of the teardown process is quite familiar from past models, though iFixit noted that replacing the USB-C ports or fans still requires removing the entire logic board, despite both components being independently replaceable.

iFixit noted that the headphone jack also requires logic board removal, while the HDMI port, SDXC port, RAM, and storage remain soldered to the board.

As with past teardowns, iFixit also tested what happens when swapping logic boards between two MacBooks.

While last year’s M5 MacBook Pro failed to complete Touch ID calibration through Apple’s Repair Assistant, iFixit noted that the new model successfully recognized the battery, display, and Touch ID sensor after a logic board swap, with True Tone, brightness controls, and the touchscreen all working as expected.

iFixit was also able to enroll a fingerprint with the donor board installed from another MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.

As for the illuminated Apple logo, iFixit had a bit of a rough time getting to it, destroying the OLED panel in the process and even asking whether anyone had managed to remove it intact.

Once inside, iFixit found that the Apple logo is illuminated by a strip of four LEDs, which work in conjunction with a reflective layer and a diffuser to distribute the light evenly.

The Apple logo itself, in turn, has a two-way mirror coating that gives it a shiny, reflective appearance when the LEDs are off, while allowing light to pass through when they’re on.

When it comes to weight, Apple shaved 92 grams off the chassis and 101 grams off the display assembly, despite adding touch and an illuminated logo. The battery is just 2 grams lighter, while the slightly smaller trackpad saves another 8 grams.

Finally, iFixit gave the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display a repairability score of 5 out of 10. That was one point higher than last year’s M5 MacBook Pro, but one point below the cheaper MacBook Neo.

#3348. The 10 Best American Shows in TV History, Ranked

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

My favorite thing about television is that it can make somebody's stupid little habits feel important. A man adjusts his tie before lying to his wife. A child keeps waiting for a parent to say something encouraging. Or Kieran Culkin’s Roman Roy does disgusting things in the bathroom to continue living depressed.

American television has given us extraordinary spectacles, groundbreaking comedy, and dramas that changed the entire medium. But the shows I return to most aren't necessarily the ones with the biggest twists or most prestigious reputations. They're the ones that give me excellent lessons. That understands people so precisely that I feel personally implicated in their decisions. And yes, I'm still furious about things certain fictional characters did twenty years ago.

Lucy Ricardo (Lucille Ball) wants something more exciting than being a New York housewife, much to the exhaustion of her bandleader husband Ricky (Desi Arnaz). I Love Lucy turns that simple conflict into magnificent comedy, frequently involving their neighbors Fred (William Frawley) and Ethel Mertz (Vivian Vance). Lucy's ambitions aren't unreasonable. It's her methods of achieving them that tend to become spectacular disasters.

I still laugh watching Lucy and Ethel desperately stuff chocolates into their mouths when the candy factory's conveyor belt speeds up. There's no complicated joke to explain. Two brilliant performers gradually lose control of an increasingly ridiculous situation. But Ball's real achievement was making Lucy's desperate hunger for attention strangely lovable. She could be selfish, dishonest, and gloriously theatrical, yet her disappointments felt recognizable. Seventy years later, that physical comedy remains unbelievably sharp. Some sitcoms owe this show practically their entire existence.

Homer Simpson (Dan Castellaneta) works at a nuclear power plant despite demonstrating little evidence that he should be trusted near one. His long-suffering wife Marge (Julie Kavner) keeps their household functioning, while Bart (Nancy Cartwright), Lisa (Yeardley Smith), and Maggie navigate childhood in the delightfully dysfunctional town of Springfield. The Simpsons transforms an ordinary American family into a bottomless source of cultural satire, absurdity, and occasionally surprising tenderness.

Give me “Marge vs. the Monorail” and I'll happily defend the show's funniest writing for an hour. The town is talked into buying an obviously suspicious transportation system, and practically every exchange contains a joke worth remembering. Yet “Lisa's Substitute” affects me more deeply. Mr. Bergstrom recognizes Lisa's intelligence and loneliness, and his farewell note tells her something she's desperately needed to hear. That's the magic of the show's greatest years. It can make Homer an unbelievable idiot, then have him express genuine love for his daughter in a way that completely destroys me.

A man boards an airplane and becomes convinced something is destroying its wing. Another discovers that his childhood hometown might offer an escape from his unhappy adult life. Ordinary people encounter extraordinary situations in The Twilight Zone, Rod Serling's anthology series about fear, morality, loneliness, and humanity's talent for making terrible decisions.

I have an enormous soft spot for “Walking Distance.” Martin Sloan (Gig Young) returns to the town where he grew up and somehow encounters his younger self. What begins as a beautiful fantasy about recovering childhood becomes a painful lesson about the impossibility of living in the past. Serling understood that a science-fiction premise didn't need elaborate machinery to become unforgettable. Sometimes all it required was a lonely man desperately wanting one more afternoon of happiness. The show can be terrifying, funny, devastating, or cruelly ironic. Its imagination still embarrasses productions with a hundred times the resources.

There are practically no respectable people in the lawless mining settlement of Deadwood, and I wouldn't have them any other way. Saloon owner Al Swearengen (Ian McShane) controls much of the town through intimidation and cunning, while former marshal Seth Bullock (Timothy Olyphant) struggles to establish something resembling order. Deadwood watches a filthy collection of opportunists, fugitives, workers, and fortune seekers slowly become a community.

McShane is absolutely magnificent. Al can threaten somebody's life, deliver an outrageously profane monologue, and then demonstrate an unexpected concern for the town's survival. David Milch, who created the series, writes dialogue that sounds almost Shakespearean without diminishing the characters' vulgarity. I particularly love how Bullock and Al gradually recognize the necessity of cooperating despite despising each other's methods. There's something strangely beautiful about civilization emerging from such unpleasant circumstances. Nobody becomes a saint. They simply begin recognizing that other people's lives are connected to their own.

Logan Roy (Brian Cox) has built a media empire, and his four children have spent their lives competing for his approval and eventually his position. Succession introduces Kendall (Jeremy Strong), Shiv (Sarah Snook), Roman (Kieran Culkin), and Connor (Alan Ruck) as extraordinarily wealthy adults whose emotional development appears to have stopped somewhere around adolescence.

A phone call from an airplane abruptly forces the siblings into a situation that their money, influence, and practiced cruelty cannot control. They stumble over words, interrupt each other, and desperately try to communicate feelings they've spent their entire lives avoiding. It's breathtaking acting. I love how Jesse Armstrong's writing makes these people simultaneously hilarious and pathetic. Their boardroom victories are often elaborate attempts to win a father's affection. They possess practically everything imaginable, except the emotional security that might allow them to enjoy any of it. The ending was heartbreaking. This is probably one of the greatest shows of all time.

Don Draper (Jon Hamm) is an extraordinarily successful advertising executive whose polished appearance conceals a carefully constructed identity. At Sterling Cooper, he sells beautiful versions of American life while struggling to maintain anything resembling genuine happiness in his own. Mad Men also follows Peggy Olson (Elisabeth Moss), Joan Holloway (Christina Hendricks), and the colleagues navigating an industry transformed by social change during the 1960s.

I will never stop thinking about the Kodak Carousel pitch. Don uses photographs of his family to sell nostalgia, describing the emotional power of returning to a place where we felt loved. It's a wonderful presentation, made devastating by how badly he's damaging those very relationships. Matthew Weiner, who created the show, understood that Don's professional brilliance came partly from recognizing desires he could never satisfy himself. And Peggy's growth is equally extraordinary. She enters the agency as a secretary and slowly discovers how much of herself she's unwilling to surrender for approval. This show understands ambition, loneliness, and the exhausting business of pretending to be somebody else.

Before becoming Saul Goodman, Jimmy McGill (Bob Odenkirk) is a struggling lawyer desperate to establish himself while living under the judgment of his successful older brother Chuck (Michael McKean). His relationship with fellow attorney Kim Wexler (Rhea Seehorn) offers something dangerously close to stability. Better Call Saul follows Jimmy's transformation while demonstrating how much damage two intelligent, affectionate people can cause when they start enjoying their own dishonesty.

I genuinely think “Chicanery” contains some of the finest acting ever produced for television. Chuck's courtroom testimony deteriorates into an eruption of resentment, exposing how deeply his feelings toward Jimmy have shaped both their lives. Yet the tragedy belongs to both brothers. Jimmy wants Chuck's respect, but his methods keep justifying Chuck's worst assumptions. And Kim! Seehorn makes her gradual moral compromises almost physically painful to witness. Vince Gilligan and Peter Gould created a prequel that somehow made the destination more heartbreaking because we understood exactly what Jimmy was throwing away. I could watch these people negotiate a legal technicality for an entire hour.

Walter White (Bryan Cranston) is a high-school chemistry teacher diagnosed with lung cancer who begins manufacturing methamphetamine to provide financial security for his family. He partners with former student Jesse Pinkman (Aaron Paul), gradually building a criminal enterprise that places everybody around him in danger. Breaking Bad turns a desperate financial decision into one of television's most horrifying studies of pride.

What absolutely destroys me is watching Jesse continue searching for affection from a man who repeatedly manipulates him. Walt recognizes Jesse's need for approval and exploits it whenever convenient. Meanwhile, his wife Skyler (Anna Gunn) becomes trapped in circumstances that Walt keeps insisting are for the family's benefit. Cranston makes Walt's transformation frightening because each terrible decision arrives with an explanation that sounds reasonable to him. By the time he finally acknowledges how much he enjoyed the power, the damage is almost impossible to comprehend. I love this show for refusing to let intelligence excuse cruelty. Walt's greatest talent becomes the weapon he uses to ruin everything.

Four criminal masterminds. One of them was always going to be yours. Here is who comes for you, why they picked you out of everyone available, and what they want from the encounter.

Your nemesis does not want to beat you. He wants to know you completely, and he is patient enough to wait for it. The frightening part is how good the conversation is.

Your nemesis is not after money, territory or revenge. He is after a demonstration, and you are the person he has chosen to prove his point on.

Your nemesis respects you, which sounds flattering until you work out what it means. He chose you because nobody else was worth his time.

Your nemesis has no personal interest in you whatsoever, and that is precisely what makes him unsurvivable. You are not a rival. You are a stop on the way.

Tony Soprano (James Gandolfini) runs a New Jersey criminal organization while attending therapy for panic attacks. His psychiatrist Dr. Jennifer Melfi (Lorraine Bracco) attempts to understand a patient whose anxieties involve his mother, his marriage, his children, and the people he's ordered killed. The Sopranos places a deeply troubled family man inside a profession that rewards practically every one of his worst instincts.

The argument between Tony and Carmela (Edie Falco) in “Whitecaps” is devastating. Years of resentment come pouring out, and neither can escape the uncomfortable truths the other knows. They're married people who understand exactly where to hurt one another. Gandolfini and Falco make the confrontation feel almost indecent to witness. That's David Chase's extraordinary achievement. He never lets us forget Tony's brutality, even while making his personal struggles painfully recognizable. I can laugh at Tony complaining about his family, then feel revolted when he inflicts suffering upon somebody else. Few television characters have demanded so much sympathy while doing so little to deserve it.

Baltimore's drug trade, police department, shipping industry, political establishment, schools, and newspapers become the interconnected subjects of The Wire. Detective Jimmy McNulty (Dominic West) initially investigates a drug organization led by Avon Barksdale (Wood Harris), but the series gradually expands far beyond any single investigation. The institutions remain, even as the people attempting to change them come and go.

Season 4 is the reason I will defend this show forever. Four boys enter a school system where their futures are already being shaped by poverty, street violence, and decisions made by adults who rarely understand their lives. Watching Randy (Maestro Harrell) desperately seek help as his circumstances deteriorate is heartbreaking. And Bubbles (Andre Royo), a man struggling with addiction, eventually reaching a point where he can join his sister's family upstairs for dinner feels like an extraordinary victory. The police may celebrate an arrest, politicians may announce progress, but somebody's child still has to walk home through the same dangerous neighborhood. That's why The Wire belongs at number one.

#3346. Hackers Now Want Your Browser Sessions More Than Your Passwords, but You Can Stop Them

There’s a very organized dark web supply chain that attackers use to trade in stealer logs. Russian Market has effectively replaced Genesis Market as the new storefront for black hat cybercriminals, although much of the market has also shifted to private channels on Telegram.

According to threat analysts at DarkOwl, approximately 180,000 stealer logs were sold on Russian Market in just the first half of 2025. What's more, Russian Market is a well-designed storefront that users can access even without Onion links or the Tor browser. That means anyone could go there and buy a bunch of stealer logs to start attempting account takeovers at scale.

Meanwhile, Flare Research estimates that this isn’t even close to the actual scale of the threat, because 90% of stealer logs now surface privately on Telegram. There, automated chatbots let scammers shop for stealer logs like it’s Amazon, with options to filter by country, app, and account privilege. Logs sell for anywhere between $5 and $500 a piece, depending on the estimated value of the target accounts.

The easiest way to go about this is to take a look through all your active devices and their locations in your account settings on most websites. If you see a device or location you don’t recognize, you are likely the subject of an ongoing breach. However, keep in mind that this may not always be a reliable method if you use iCloud Private Relay or a VPN. Still, it's generally best practice to log out of all active sessions every once in a while and perform a fresh login to invalidate any unauthorized sessions.

Reset the passwords on your email account, enable two-factor authentication for added protection, and sign out of all sessions before doing a fresh login. Your email inbox is the single point of entry for most attacks because that’s where most websites send their verification codes or magic links.

Sign out of all active sessions on every account that you suspect is compromised. This will log out any attackers who are currently on a hijacked browsing session.

Change your passwords on every platform in order of priority. Start with banking websites, cloud storage providers, and password managers first.

Look through each compromised account’s third-party integrations and app permissions. Revoke access if you can’t recognize an app, or it looks suspicious. Also make sure to rotate any API keys that you’re currently using, since those may have been compromised as well.

But while the initiative has already been open-sourced, no other major online provider has begun offering native support for it as of this article. That means DBSC’s security benefits are limited to Google services like Gmail and Docs, Chrome for Windows, and third-party websites that offer single sign-on (SSO) options for your Google account. We might see a wider rollout in the near future, though.

#3345. Johnny Depp's 'Ebenezer' a Box Office Hit, Fan-Favorite Years After Court Drama

Johnny Depp's return to the big screen landed at No. 1 at the international and domestic box offices this weekend years after his court drama ... despite a wide divide between critics and regular moviegoers.

"Ebenezer" opened domestically to the tune of $19 million and earned an additional $23 million overseas ... according to Variety and Deadline. Not bad for a budget of $38 million!

While the movie has split critics down the middle -- with the film sporting a 54% Tomatometer -- audiences have raved over it.

Currently the comeback flick is verified hot on Rotten Tomatoes with an 89% Popcornmeter rating ... and an A- CinemaScore.

The divide between fan reaction and critical response comes amid a flurry of analytical pieces that have tied the movie to some sort of PR power play by Johnny.

Take the Wall Street Journal's feature that says the film is the perfect PR vehicle for the star, while in a separate review, the WSJ claims the film fails to find its tone and that Johnny is "ridiculously blustery and loud as Ebenezer, as if trying to get laughs."

In another review ... Vanity Fair drew parallels further between Ebenezer and Johnny, characterizing the movie as "Christmas-washing" his reputation.

Johnny's return to Hollywood comes after he levied a defamation lawsuit against ex-wife Amber Heard over her 2018 Washington Post op-ed, in which she described herself as a "public figure representing domestic abuse." He claimed the piece falsely implied he was the abuser.

While a jury awarded Johnny millions in damages after siding with him, Heard won one count in her countersuit.

All in all ... it seems that Scrooges aside, Johnny has done it all in one weekend, returning to screens all over the world in a triumphant way.

I finally get why people love traditional Zelda games so much

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In February 2021, I wrote an op-ed titled “Breath of the Wild ruined traditional Zelda for me.” Back then, I mused that Breath of the Wild being my first-ever Zelda game had made going back to the older titles in the beloved Nintendo franchise difficult. Flash-forward to now, and I’m roughly halfway through the new Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on Nintendo Switch 2, and I’m loving it.

I’ll cut my past self a little slack. February 2021 was more than five years ago, and a person’s tastes can change a lot in that amount of time. Heck, in those days, I also thought Souls games weren’t for me. Now in 2026, I’ve beaten every modern title FromSoftware has released (bar Dark Souls 2; it’s in my overflowing backlog) and am basically obsessed with the Soulslike genre.

Nevertheless, I definitely wrote off classic Zelda games too hastily. Turns out all it took was pretty much the most acclaimed video game of all time getting a stunning remake for me to see just how foolish I had been. Consider this follow-up article my formal apology to Link.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has been remade for the Nintendo Switch 2, and in a word, it's stunning. This complete remake of the classic Nintendo 64 offers overhauled visuals, improved controls, and a few smart tweaks to make the timeless game even more modern. Ocarina of Time was considered a masterpiece back in 1998, and this new version on Switch 2 has earned the same plaudits.

Ocarina of Time starts a little slow. Lots of text boxes and simple tutorials. But once the adventure really begins, and Young Link is tasked with finding three Spiritual Stones (the first is obtained during the prologue chapter), I started to discover exactly why longtime fans bemoan Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom’s lack of “proper” Zelda dungeons.

But it was only once I had obtained all three stones and transformed into grown-up Link that I really understood what makes these dungeons so special, and why fans still beg for the series to bring them back. Nintendo’s penchant for creative and satisfying puzzles is on full display in the Forest, Fire and Water Temple, and I’m very excited to head to the remaining dungeons and discover what’s hiding within their twisting corridors.

The Fire Temple is a great example of phenomenal design, as the underground lava-laden cavern loops back on itself in surprising and creative ways. The infamous Water Temple might actually be my frontrunner favorite, probably because the remake has stripped away the friction of the original.

Best of all is the way each dungeon gives you a new tool to play with, which is then vital to unlocking the dungeon’s many secrets; it is a consistently brilliant way of asking players to make use of their entire arsenal of tools.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

My favorite aspect of Breath of the Wild (and sequel Tears of the Kingdom) has always been the puzzle shrines. While it’s not an original opinion, the dungeons in Ocarina of Time feel like a couple dozen BOTW puzzle shrines stitched together in an environmentally cohesive manner.

Delving into a dungeon feels appropriately epic, and each one (or at least, each one I’ve experienced so far) begs to be fully explored with treasure chests and secrets for those willing to look in every corner. They’re just a blast, and yes, I can finally admit, they flow better than Breath of the Wild’s pretty repetitive Divine Beast dungeons.

While I’ve at long last come around to the strengths of the traditional Zelda formula, that doesn’t mean I’ve suddenly lost my intense love for Breath of the Wild and its own acclaimed formula. Sorry, Ocarina stans, but Link’s 2017 adventure remains my favorite game in the series (of the ones I’ve played).

If there is one element where Ocarina of Time can’t compete with Breath of the Wild, it’s in the latter's ability to let you solve puzzles in a multitude of ways. In Ocarina of Time, the tools at Link’s disposal are more rudimentary (understandable, it’s ultimately a remake of a game from 1998), typically giving players a singular way to progress. In Breath of the Wild (and especially Tears of the Kingdom), you can “break” puzzles in ingenious ways.

While playing modern Zelda, I’ve found myself looking up online guides, not even because I need help with a puzzle, but merely to see the different ways other players solved the various roadblocks in Link’s path. In Ocarina of Time, players will reach the exit in pretty much the same way.

But that's not necessarily to say there's no appeal to Ocarina of Time's more linear progression. As mentioned, the way tools like the hookshot are slowly dished out, giving you incentive to return to previous areas with a larger arsenal, is something that Breath of the Wild lacks. In that case, you get pretty much all your traversal and puzzle-solving abilities in the first area.

I think both classic and modern Zelda have huge strengths, and opting for one over the other in any future Zelda games would be disappointing. I hope the development team at Nintendo mashes the two design philosophies together. Imagine a Zelda game with an exploration-focused open Hyrule but also containing lengthy, tightly crafted dungeons? Best of both worlds.

Tears of the Kingdom was a step in this direction, but its dungeons still don’t compare to those in Ocarina of Time. So, I don’t know if what would now be my “dream” Zelda game will ever exist, and it’ll probably be a good few years now before Nintendo is ready to talk about the next mainline 3D game in the series. But I really hope Link’s next flagship adventure takes the best part of both traditional and modern Zelda games and satisfies fans of both camps.

A great example of blending the new and old is FromSoftware's Elden Ring, which offers a refreshing sense of freedom in its expansive overworld but also contains several "Legacy Dungeons." These are designed more like the smaller-scale areas found in the Dark Souls series. I hope that the Zelda team takes a similar approach when crafting whatever is next for the franchise.

In the meantime, I should probably circle back and give other classic Zelda games a chance, or maybe I’ll just keep my fingers crossed that the rumored Majora’s Mask remake materializes. I hear some fans consider it even better.

#3340. Forget 'Peaky Blinders,' Titus Welliver's 8-Episode Crime Thriller Is Perfect From Start to Finish

Jeffrey is a freelance features writer at Collider. He is an MPA-accredited entertainment journalist and a Tomatometer-approved critic based in the LA area. He graduated from the University of Texas at Austin with a Bachelor of Science in Radio, TV, & Film and a Bachelor of Arts in Theater.

If you're in the mood for a deliciously fun drama and a fan of shows like Peaky Blinders, it's time to check out The Westies. Set in the early 1980s, the MGM+ series presents a fictionalized account of the real-life Irish crime syndicate that operated out of Hell’s Kitchen. A combination of slick storytelling with crime drama thrills, along with a terrific cast of compelling characters, makes this show a must-watch experience.

The Westies mixes fact and fiction, with the series' main characters drawn from members of the real crime syndicate. Although the Italian mafia outnumbers the Westies five-to-one, the construction of the Javits Center in the latter's territory stands to give them a lucrative payout. J.K. Simmons stars as Eamon Sweeney, inspired by real Westies mob boss, Mickey Spillane. One of Sweeney's top lieutenants is Jimmy Roarke (Tom Brittney), based on real-life mobster James Coonan, whose loyalty to both the gang and its leader appears to be reaching its limits in the first season.

What did it take to bring the infamous Westies to television? J.K. Simmons, Tom Brittney, Titus Welliver, and co-creator/showrunner Chris Brancato pull back the curtain on how The Westies recreated 1980s Hell's Kitchen while balancing real history with dramatic storytelling.

When The Westies begins, Sweeney is attempting to navigate the finer points of the Javits construction deal while maintaining an uneasy peace with the Gambino crime family, led by Paul Castellano (Ron Lea) and underboss John Gotti (Hamish Allan-Headly) — and the series nicely juxtaposes these real-life figures against the story's more fictionalized interpretations. Although The Westies isn't aiming for a straightforward history lesson, with some elements of the show changed for storytelling purposes, series co-creators Chris Brancato and Michael Panes have crafted an immersive crime drama that exceptionally transports the audience back to the early 1980s.

Alongside the crime thriller's many twists and turns, The Westies boasts an incredible ensemble cast. The show has to juggle characters, factions, and subplots, but each still receives proper room to breathe. The actors wonderfully bring their characters to life, inhabiting a brutal world where one wrong move can bring ruin, and you are never sure who to trust. In addition to the intriguing chess game between Sweeney and Jimmy, another riveting subplot follows Jimmy's girlfriend, Bridget Walsh (Sarah Bolger), a former IRA soldier who now resides in the U.S. and runs into trouble when her former IRA contact and lover, Brendan Cahill (Allen Leech), arrives in New York City, seeking assistance with the IRA's ongoing activities.

Titus Welliver of Bosch fame is another standout within the cast as Glenn Keenan, a morally ambiguous NYPD officer who has a long-standing relationship with Sweeney. When FBI agent Birdie Polk (Jessica Frances Duke) recruits him to join her task force with the intention of bringing down organized crime, Keenan is torn between his ties to Sweeney and his love for his son, who is becoming involved with the Westies. Instead of choosing one, Keenan plays both sides of the law, and the actor portrays his character’s moral complexity exceptionally well. It's a different side of his acting strengths, and fans can watch him play someone totally different from his arguably most iconic role as Detective Harry Bosch.

The Westies hasn't yet been renewed for a second season, so its future is still up in the air. The first season ended on a shocking note with huge story implications, and it would be a shame if the finale served as the end of the road for the series. Brancato spoke optimistically about the show's fate in a July interview with Deadline, stating, 'We're very confident there will be a second season of The Westies."

The titular gang's rise to power has only just begun, and based on the first season's ending, there are many more great storylines to come. Nevertheless, The Westies provides a throwback crime drama experience reminiscent of movies like Goodfellas and Casino, albeit in a nostalgic 1980s setting.

#3336. End of an era: Apple Support Community forums will permanently close on November 20

Users visiting the Apple Support Community tonight were greeted with a message informing them that the platform will permanently shut down on November 20. Here are the details.

If you have ever had a question or ran into a problem with an Apple product, chances are you have come across the Apple Support Community, the company’s official discussion forums where users from around the world help each other troubleshoot issues and share tips.

The platform has a history dating back to at least 1998, when it was known as Apple Tech Exchange. Since then, it was renamed Apple Discussions before relaunching as Apple Support Communities in April 2011, with a redesigned interface, personalized profiles, and a reputation system that rewarded users for helping others.

Tonight, however, users who tried to access the platform were greeted with the following message:

The AppleCare Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state.

You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site.

We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products.

Right now, the portal still shows a “Sign in” button, though it leads only to an AppleConnect login page labeled “AC Communities Web – Internal,” suggesting that access is now restricted to Apple employees.

Interestingly, Apple’s message refers to the “AppleCare Support Community,” rather than the “Apple Support Community,” which is how the platform is officially branded.

These forums were often far up when searching for Apple problems, but I’m not sure I ever found a real answer there. So often the threads went no where or someone would link an unhelpful Apple support page.

Still, the forums are already in read-only mode, with users able to browse existing discussions, search for answers, and interact with posts through the “Me too” and voting buttons, but no longer submit new questions or replies.

At the time of writing, the most recent post was published just 57 minutes earlier, suggesting that Apple only recently disabled new submissions.

9to5Mac has reached out to Apple for comment and clarification on the scope of the shutdown, and we’ll update this story if we hear back.
